Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Namely, we find that a specific model comprising a planar density distribution of sources, coupled with magnetic field fluctuations that are root-mean-square-based, is capable of reproducing the observed anisotropy patterns and their evolutionary tendencies with rising energy levels. Conversely, a model featuring a spherical source density distribution and similar magnetic field dynamics cannot adequately explain the data. Nonetheless, more comprehensive theoretical models are still required to fully comprehend the anisotropy patterns observed in our data. Systematic uncertainties associated with the statistical analysis methodology are formally incorporated into the results presented herein. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Optical power is lost after transmission, with only -0.9dB remaining.  A decision feedback equalizer with four taps is effectively applied to correct signal distortions, and its performance is verified through field trials.  The analysis of burst error propagation and its mitigation are key research areas in this study.  A simplified study on error propagation was previously conducted, but it did not consider the BPSK modulation technique commonly used in fiber optic transmission systems.  A more comprehensive analysis of error propagation is presented, and a condition for the convergence of j-1th branch was established, with the option of adding a null tap before the decision device to prevent phase ambiguity.  A candidate for mitigating error propagation, an maximum likelihood detection equalizer, was introduced and shown to be capable of preventing phase ambiguity, but it requires a high computational power and is not suitable for underwater transmission systems that lack the computational capacity.  Another option, a maximum likelihood detection equalizer combined with a null tap, was also presented, and it has the advantage of preventing phase ambiguity and distortions caused by fiber dispersion, but it also requires a high computational power.  Another candidate for mitigating error propagation, a decision feedback equalizer combined with four taps, was successfully applied in the field trial, and it effectively corrected signal distortions caused by fiber dispersion and phase ambiguity, with only a low computational power required.  The technique of adding a null tap, also known as a virtual backward propagating tap, is a simple and effective method to prevent phase ambiguity and distortions caused by fiber dispersion, and it does not require any additional hardware.  This technique can also be applied to the transmission system with the BPSK modulation technique, but it requires a high computational power.  However, the technique of adding a null tap, or a virtual backward propagating tap, is a simple and effective method to prevent phase ambiguity and distortions caused by fiber dispersion, and it does not require any additional hardware. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data but often suffer from high computational costs and vast parameter counts. TCNs employ a series of 1D convolutional layers with varying durations to achieve effective feature extractions, but each layer contributes significantly to the overall complexity. To address this, our approach Pruning In Time (PIT) systematically assesses the significance of each convolutional layer across the time dimension, systematically removing less vital layers and their corresponding segments. By combining PIT with a reversible thinning strategy for TCNs, we introduce Re-PIT, achieving substantial reductions in model size, inference speed, and computational demands while maintaining optimal performance. Our experiments showcase how PIT and Re-PIT effectively optimize TCNs for better efficiency without compromising results in benchmark datasets across forecasting and classification tasks. The proposed PIT method serves as a suitable layer optimizer for TCNs, offering a flexible strategy for model compression that can be effectively integrated into the training process, producing a balanced trade-off between accuracy and efficiency. The implementation of Re-PIT further demonstrates that time-aware model reduction is feasible and advantageous, yielding a more compact and streamlined model with enhanced performance. The innovative thinning strategy of Re-PIT allows for a degree of freedom in layer prioritization, enabling the exploration of various optimization pathways, making it a versatile and adjustable model compression technique that can be used in a range of time-series modeling applications. The proposed approach has been successfully integrated into several state-of-the-art time-series models, showcasing its effectiveness in achieving a better balance between performance and efficiency. The code for the paper has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghs-1990/Pruning-In-Time. The implementation of the proposed method has also been incorporated into the Deep Learning Framework PyTorch, with the model having been successfully tested on various time-series forecasting and classification benchmarks. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Additionally, we developed new reduction techniques, including a 2D transformation that accounts for the distortion, warping, and non-linear calibration of the CCDs. Furthermore, we implemented an innovative data handling method that utilizes all observations simultaneously to calibrate the system, correcting any previous approaches that failed to consider the non-linear relationship between light intensity and digitized counts. By utilizing this new methodology on extensive datasets from the FRAM telescope, we have successfully determined the aerosol depth with a precision of 0.0083 for optical depth unity, and have further validated our results by comparing them to readings from co-located sun photometers. These developments hold significant potential to utilize the vast resources of optical astrophysics data for a precision higher than what is currently achievable with dedicated aerosol instruments. Furthermore, our research has shown that even system biases do not significantly affect the results, allowing the technique to accurately determine the aerosol depth across various conditions, including the diel cycle, seasonal variations, and in exceptional situations, atmospheric layers. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. The latter has been extensively researched due to the inherent simplicity of subsequent regression steps. Nonetheless, reconstructing an object's 3D map from scratch using CNN in the second stage often results in inaccurate results, which hinders the estimation of a 6D pose. To address this issue, this study focuses on the two-stage pipeline approach and proposes an innovative deep learning model, named DeepHMap++, by integrating two key components: a combined projection grouping and correspondence learning module and a pose estimation module. The former leverages intermediate cues to enhance the reconstruction of a 3D map through projection grouping and correspondence learning, while the latter employs a simple pose estimation module to calculate the object's 6D pose directly. Experimental results demonstrate DeepHMap++'s superiority over the existing state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets across various categories of objects. The source code of DeepHMap++ has been publicly released for reference. Moreover, our model has shown impressive performance in real-world applications, and thus has significant practical implications. challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. It utilizes the scikit-sparse and numba libraries to provide an efficient and
user-friendly interface for the project's main objectives, encompassing both
theoretical work and real-world data analysis. The reference implementations
provided in the library are compared to alternative methods, notably BANDIT

Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts. Our research utilizes a widely employed dark matter simulation tool, GIZMO, for systems consisting of black holes with a mass of $10 M_\sun$ and dark matter particles spanning a range from $1$ to $10$ times the number required for a thorough representation, with a particular focus on finding the optimal number of particles needed to accurately capture the behavior of dark matter. This discovery of consistent waveforms in simulations that use sufficient dark matter particles, combined with the relatively low computational cost of such simulations, paves the way for exploring a variety of binary black hole merger scenarios in wave dark matter environments. This includes simulations using the GIZMO meshless gas treatment, which has historically presented significant computational challenges for such complex simulations, resulting in a significant reduction in the number of particles needed (by roughly an order of magnitude) compared to previous studies, without sacrificing the accuracy of the simulation. This in turn enables the generation of waveform patterns from simulations that are more robust and less prone to artificial oscillations when compared to their predecessors. As such, we propose that further investigation be conducted into binary black hole mergers within a wide range of wave dark matter environments, using this newly found optimal particle configuration, in order to fully understand the effects that dark matter has on waveform patterns and to provide a more accurate representation of such environments in future simulations. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This algorithm first uses a modified version of the power iteration method to obtain an initial estimate and then a non-decreasing iteration that refines the results. Additionally, we found that the variation of eigenvector centrality correlates strongly with the existing centrality measures in the Wikipedia voting network. This study introduces an open source Python framework that utilizes background knowledge and observational data for the purpose of inferring causal relationships. This framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package, which executes a comprehensive causal discovery process to identify the causal interactions and the causal network structure among the variables, drawing from established methodologies including those from 'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg', in addition to pairwise algorithms like ANM. The framework is available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License. A demonstration of the framework's capabilities is provided in the accompanying Jupyter Notebook file available within the GitHub repository. The framework is suitable for processing relatively small data sets due to the 'pcalg' library it employs being suited for such data. The framework is accessible via PyPI through the 'pip install cdt' command. The background of the study on causal discovery, learning, and inference is briefly outlined below. The explicit definition of an causal relationship is outlined by the following statement: a causal relationship between two variables 'X' and 'Y' through observing changes in 'X' effects the likelihood of observing 'Y'. This relationship is denoted by the equation 'Y <> causally affects X'. The formulation of this relationship is often expressed by the equation 'P(y|do(x)) ≠ P(y|x)'. The framework is often utilized in domains where the underlying causal structures or causal relationships are of primary interest, despite the observed variables and their probability distributions being readily accessible. The field of causal discovery has originated from the field of causal inference, which has its own distinct history. Causal inference is a subdomain of statistics that is focused on estimating causal effects by making inferences from observational and/or experimental data. This field of study has its own history dating back to the work of J. Pearl in 1988 and the publication of his paper 'Fundamentals of Structured Learning'. Following the publication of his book 'Causal Inference in Statistics: A Critical Conceptual Index', the field of study has experienced rapid growth. The development of the cdt framework was motivated by a desire to provide a comprehensive causal discovery toolkit for Python users that is based on the principles outlined by J. Pearl in his 2016 book 'Interpretation of Data'. The framework is designed to be transparent and straightforward to use for both novice and experienced R users. The framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package that is available on the CRAN repository. The framework is also accompanied by a demonstration of its capabilities that is available as a Jupyter

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime of spheres occurring at approximately 7-8 body lengths per second in the intermediate speed range. The results of our study are relevant to applications where spheres interact with water surfaces, such as in sediment transport and the actions of water on sand grains resulting from flow velocities that can fall within this intermediate range. Unfortunately, users are frequently forced to give up vital security functionality due to hardware and software limitations. This research presents an original problem called Partial Hardware Trust Minimization (PHTM) which aims to minimize trust in hardware and software by dividing available hardware into discrete, isolated sections for untrusted software to utilize, while guaranteeing secure app functionality in accordance with PHTM-Protected Apps (PPAs). A practical PHTM solution, called HARVEY, is demonstrated with consideration of various types of attacks and hardware characteristics (such as ARM TrustZone on mobile devices). Furthermore, HARVEY prevents time-consuming software recompilation for secure and non-secure code segments by automating efficient code segmentation, a function that is currently unsupported in popular mobile device Operating Systems. We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The code for our proposed algorithm has been made publicly available. It achieves a 20% increase in performance compared to the robust adversarial reinforcement learning algorithm presented in paper submission REFL-19-01. Additionally, we discovered that the majority of existing reinforcement learning algorithms fall short in the face of significant adversarial interference and demonstrated a 15% improvement of the state-of-the-art robust reinforcement learning algorithm submission REFL-19-01, when tested against Mujoco continuous control benchmarks. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Our analysis indicates that the unique geometry of cubanite's unit cell enables its electrons to occupy both symmetric and asymmetric d-orbitals, giving rise to the orbital selectivity observed. This distinct electronic structure may also contribute to the enhanced magnetic properties and electrical conductivity of cubanite relative to other isoskeletal sulfide compounds. A detailed discussion of our findings is presented in the accompanying research article. Specifically, our data and theoretical predictions are compared to results from other 3d transition metal compounds, including those with similar geometry and configuration. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We demonstrate that SPCCSs can be produced when a dichotomic measurement takes place in one of the input channels, using either a beam splitter or a amplifier. We further show that the transformation from an initial catalyzer state to an SPCCS requires the catalyzer to exhibit quantum properties. Furthermore, the investigation of dichotomic measurement scenarios reveals that SPCCSs can be generated under certain conditions when the catalyzer is in a classical state, and we find the conditions under which coherent states or anti-coherent states result from such scenarios. Finally, we propose the use of a beam splitter or amplifier based on a dichotomic measurement procedure as a method for generating SPCCSs. SPCCSs can also be generated using a quantum amplifier driven by a classical light when the measurement of the amplifier's output is taken. Additionally, we examine the application of these states in quantum optics, particularly in the development of an over-damped harmonic oscillator model and the generation of negative Wigner functions. SPCCSs can be generated using an anti-Zenon state catalyzer, and we demonstrate the utility of such states in producing negative Wigner functions for an harmonic oscillator in two different scenarios. SPCCSs can also be used to create multi-photon catalyzed coherent states. Furthermore, we analyze the unique properties of SPCCSs when a dichotomic measurement takes place, and we show that in this case the states exhibit a combination of both coherent and multi-photon coherent state characteristics. Additionally, we explore the scenario in which a photon is not detected in one of the input channels, and we show that in this case the resulting state is equivalent to a SPCCS but with the catalyzer's quantum properties being utilized less efficiently. Lastly, we examine the issue of state cloning in SPCCSs, and we find that the amplification of a single-photon state results in a state that is not a multi-photon catalyzed coherent state, but rather a superposition of catalyzer states, with each state in the superposition being associated with a different number of photons. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, we provide an intuitive understanding of how the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor relate to the components of the electromagnetic field bivector. As a practical application, we explicitly calculate the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor for an electromagnetic field associated with a slowly rotating neutron star in the meridian plane. Nonetheless, in the general case, determining the conformally flat derivative bivectors from the Weyl tensor requires solving the complex Newman-Penrose equations directly. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, allowing for the application of the existing framework through a transformation that converts polymers into a series of connected compounds. By utilizing linear regression to modify the scores given to monomers and connections, it becomes possible to enhance the accuracy of the original framework. The new approach has been tested on a set of polymers inferred by the original framework, demonstrating an increase in precision. Furthermore, this new method has been found to successfully infer polymers from limited descriptions. This includes the ability to understand chemical names through a process of reversal. Additionally, this method has been found to successfully combine the predictions made by different instances of the original framework. Overall, this new method has shown great promise in improving the accuracy of chemical compound inference. The code for this new method can be found at https://github.com/Group-Castro/polymer-mip. The model being used and the data it is based on can be found at https://github.com/Group-Castro/ChemBERTa. The new method has also been applied to the prediction of SARS-CoV-2 protein structures, an area where there is a need for more effective inference methods, by combining it with a framework that utilizes artificial neural networks to predict the connections between monomers. This combination has resulted in an increase in the accuracy of these predictions, an important development for the rapid understanding of viral structures that is critical in the early stages of a viral outbreak. The new method has also been compared to an alternative method based on graph neural networks, revealing that it has several key advantages. This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our proposed approach involved a nonlinear model, state estimation, parameter estimation, input design, and trajectory optimization, solving the resulting problem using direct transcription via the collocation method. Our results showed that, with adequate data available for estimation, both patients' parameters can be accurately estimated, and the ventilator can be adjusted to meet the requirements of both patients. However, when accurate parameter estimates are not available, due to the uncertainty in parameter values, the solution is less certain, and the performance may degrade. Our research highlights the value of continuous flow monitoring in maintaining optimal performance. Finally, we discuss the potential of direct transcription to tackle a broad range of optimization-based applications across multiple fields. Our case study demonstrates the significance of research in the transfer of patient ventilation capabilities during the COVID-19 pandemic. Furthermore, we outline several potential research opportunities in the field. Two appendices are included with additional details on our approach and study. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often use a pre-defined reference point to standardize the positioning of the scan. Nonetheless, even with this adjustment, accurately pinpointing tumors can be a challenge. In this research, we create a novel approach called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) to effectively segment tumors from the esophagus in CT scans. By incorporating a complex mixture of spatial and channel attention within a dense connection, DDAUnet significantly boosts the accuracy of the system when compared to competing methods. When tested with CT scans that contain external objects such as feeding tubes, and variations in the shape of the esophagus, our system achieved an impressive.913 Dice coefficient, outperforming state-of-the-art competitors like DenseUnet and AttentionUnet. The model's ability to detect tumors in scans with external objects such as feeding tubes also showed great promise, with a dice coefficient of.878. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured log data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to the conventional iterative method, which reweights the least-squares minimization at each iteration according to the a posteriori probability distribution of the model. The application of this approach to simulated cases with uncertainties in the petrophysical models and in the boundary locations proved effective in capturing model uncertainties. The results obtained with the fast method showed a high degree of similarity to those obtained with the conventional method, with only minor differences in the standard deviations of the estimates. The outcome of this research confirms that LM-EnRML can be an efficient and reliable tool for the interpretation of well logs in real-time, enabling the evaluation of formation reservoirs and geosteering during drilling, and also facilitating the quantification of the associated uncertainties in the petrophysical models and boundary locations. Additionally, this method can handle complex models and models with uncertainties in the petrophysical equations and in the boundary locations, which are common in real-field scenarios. Therefore, this fast and robust method can be an optimal choice for the interpretation of well logs in real-time, a crucial application in the oil and gas industry. We further investigated the performance of this method using actual well-log data from sandstone and carbonate reservoirs. The results obtained with this method compared favorably with the data from the standard formation evaluation procedures employed in the oil and gas industry, and the obtained estimates and their associated uncertainties were accurate and reliable. Furthermore, this method proved its effectiveness in geosteering during drilling in a real-field scenario in a sandstone reservoir. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Moreover, the proposed system achieves superior real-world performance in extracting medical entities from text, as evaluated through both automatic and manual assessment. The proposed holistic modeling achieves enhanced accuracy across various evaluation metrics, outperforming sequential models by up to 12.5% in F-score, up to 9.5% in precision, and up to 10.5% in recall. The code for this study has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/N4Structure. The model's pre-trained weights on the CoNLL 2003 NER dataset are available upon request. Our results suggest that a deep learning-based holistic model is highly effective in identifying nested named entities within a given text. This model's use of entity representations that capture the text's overall structure yields superior performance, with an impressive 12.5% improvement in F-score over existing sequential models. Our research has significant implications for the extraction of complex information from text, with potential applications in fields like biology and medicine, where relationships between entities need to be understood from the context. By combining a deep learning-based entity representation with a parser that models the text as an integrated whole, we've developed a more effective and efficient way to extract information from text, with a particular emphasis on the extraction of complex nested entities. This approach has several advantages over traditional methods, such as the use of feature-based models, due to its ability to learn the structure and relationships of the text in a data-driven manner. Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. The challenges faced and solutions found during this research could also be applicable to other similar low-power communication technologies. Furthermore, our method requires minimal and readily available hardware components, making it cost-effective. In trials, a 2-dimensional location estimation algorithm resulted in less than 1 metre of accuracy in the presence of interference, which is a significant improvement over existing approaches. The code and details of the actual hardware used in these tests are available for download. Additionally, our study has provided valuable insights that could be applied to other location-based applications across different technologies. In practice, when using ZigBee networks for location detection, a level of accuracy of less than 1 metre can be achieved when dealing with cross technology interference. The frequency range of ZigBee networks is the same as that of Bluetooth and wireless sensors, which raises interesting questions about the location detection capabilities of these technologies in real-world scenarios. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. Two potential methods are outlined: using descriptions from visually impaired individuals and incorporating feedback from descriptions of the form "good" or "bad". While these approaches have their own advantages and challenges, they deserve exploration in future work. Moreover, since description standards can vary across cultures and personal experiences, special consideration should be given to the diversity of the reference data used. Lastly, if description data is collected for the purpose of training, it may be more practical to collect data in an iterative manner, using each step's output as input for the next step. This could involve using descriptions from visually impaired individuals to train image description systems, which in turn can be used to collect more precise descriptions. This two-way feedback process has the potential to yield high-quality reference data efficiently. Finally, if description standards are well established, this approach could also be used to evaluate the systems' accessibility in a more systematic way. This means assessing not just how accurate the system is, but also how natural its descriptions are, which is essential for engaging visually impaired users effectively. This evaluation strategy is applicable not just to image description systems but also other systems that produce text descriptions of visual data, such as virtual reality environments and graphical user interfaces. This problem's relevance is underscored by the growing prevalence of visual content and the rising demand for accessible technology. This demand is driven by the increasing number of visually impaired individuals and the rising expectations for accessibility in technology. This expectation is reflected in the strict accessibility standards enforced by laws like the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act. This expectation is further fueled by the trend toward more human-like and natural interactions with technology, which puts a greater emphasis on the systems' aesthetic and user experience aspects. This, in turn, heightens the importance of ensuring that these systems are not only usable but also accessible to all users, including those with visual impairments. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be interpreted assuming that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s $\gamma$-phase represents the primary structure of the material. Notably, this conclusion has been verified by recent experiments conducted using Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, Monte Carlo simulations have facilitated the exploration of Ta$_2$O$_5$'s phase diagram, predicting that the $\gamma$-phase should be stable when temperature is below 923 K. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Conversely, in areas with a more cautious population and strong social norms, users are less likely to encounter new information. These findings suggest that The Big Sort may contribute substantially to the widespread circulation of misinformation through reducing cross-sectional population contacts in distinct geographical areas and fostering localized information dissemination networks. These results have implications for the effectiveness of mitigation strategies, especially when such strategies only target individual-level characteristics but neglect the significant impact of geographic sorting on the online information landscape. Furthermore, our research reveals that a crucial component missing from the current understanding of online misinformation is the role of The Big Sort, which may also contribute to other observed phenomena in social media data. Finally, because this phenomenon is an enduring feature of the United States' demographic landscape, it may continue to contribute to the persistent issues of online misinformation and potential accompanying harmful consequences. We also provide additional analysis on related topics, such as the characterization of Reddit users, the assessment of online misinformation across platforms, the consideration of diverse features in Reddit comment datasets, the examination of cross-sectional and longitudinal user behavior, the analysis of user population dynamics in Reddit user base, the exploration of online information literacy in Reddit comment datasets, and the examination of Reddit comment datasets for science, politics, and entertainment news. Additionally, we make publicly available the Reddit comment datasets used in this study, along with the implementation details of our data processing system, named DisInfoFusion, which is designed to handle large-scale, out-of-core, and distributed computation of various data processing tasks. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although speech-based teaching has been explored through virtual assistants and demonstrations, research on the acoustic properties of teaching speech has yet to be extensively investigated. This study endeavors to illuminate the auditory characteristics of spoken language used by human instructors to teach a visual-based learning framework about manipulation tasks through demonstration and description. Our experimental teaching task involved both verbal instruction and demonstration of 20 diverse manipulation tasks to both adult and child learners. The results of our speech-based analysis revealed that human teachers utilize different auditory patterns to convey essential task information, including sounds indicative of intended action, object interactions, and safety precautions. Notably, we found that the speech of child-directed teachers contained a more substantial presence of sounds related to action and safety, whereas teachers directing adult learners employed a more varied range of auditory indicators, including more frequent usage of sounds denoting object interactions. Our research offers valuable insights into the complex audio components of human teaching speech and the distinct features used to convey varying aspects of task information. This knowledge can be leveraged to enhance the speech-based learning capabilities of teaching robots, allowing them to better comprehend and replicate complex manipulation tasks through demonstration and description. Additionally, our findings highlight significant differences in the auditory patterns of human teachers, emphasizing the necessity to design speech-based learning frameworks that adapt to the instructor's audience. By integrating a variety of auditory-based features, such as action sounds and safety indicators, these frameworks can effectively utilize multiple sources of information to master challenging manipulation tasks. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that a robust speech-based learning approach can successfully generalize across diverse task settings, enabling better performance when comparing groups of objects and manipulating larger items. This highlights the potential of speech-based learning to tackle a wide range of complex real-world tasks that involve both human-like objects and larger-scale manipulation. In order to evaluate the developed learning pipeline, a comprehensive dataset called 'Speech2Action' has been created, comprising over 7,500 demonstrations of 20 distinct manipulation tasks performed by 20 different human instructors. This dataset includes both audio and visual data, along with corresponding XML files that outline the step-by-step actions being performed. It is a uniquely broad and varied dataset that includes diverse human teachers directing both adult and child learners, making it an ideal benchmark for assessing the speech-based learning capabilities of teaching robots. It is noteworthy that while previous research has focused on learning instructions delivered through continuous speech, the dataset 'Speech2Action' contains demonstrations conveyed through a combination of both continuous speech and discrete words, referring to object names. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Moreover, our study highlights the distinct characteristics of conformal field theory, pinpointing why state or operator complexity necessarily assumes its most minimized form under the guiding principle of minimal action. A notable conclusion arises from considering the geometric interpretation of conformal field theory, where the dual representation forms an orthonormal basis in a high-dimensional spectral space. This interpretation offers a universal foundation for defining complexity within the realm of conformal field theories. A key aspect emerges from examining the Weyl transformation, demonstrating how it transforms an operator into a linear combination of a set of geometrically defined operators, each corresponding to an independent component of the spectral space. As such, any conformal field theory operator may be expressed as a linear combination of its self-over complete set of projection operators onto the spectral dimensions. Consequently, this formulation provides a universal framework for evaluating the complexity of conformal field theory states or operators. A notable case study involves exploring the duality between the energy-momentum tensor in 1+1 dimensions and the XX spin chain in one-dimensional space. A key observation arises from considering the transformation of the Fubini-Study state complexity, leading to a direct proof of the conjecture presented in arXiv:1901.04412, along with an analytical derivation of the critical threshold at the optimal point of the complexity growth problem in arXiv:1901.04411. Moreover, our study reveals the intrinsic relationship between the geometric interpretation of conformal field theory and the variational holographic gravity approach, offering a unified description of both scenarios. A key realization emerges from examining the dual representation of conformal field theory in 1+1 dimensions, indicating that it may be viewed as a low-energy approximation of a suitable bulk gravity theory described by Einstein gravity

Conversational systems are becoming ubiquitous, and systems like chatbots are in constant use by countless individuals. Although these systems have been trained through automated methods, testing their capabilities remains a significant challenge. Many proposed testing methods are indeed effective but are often laborious to execute and require substantial human input from multiple individuals with varying perspectives. Furthermore, a significant portion of these methods focus solely on evaluating the system's performance but neglect its underlying logic and underlying structure. To address these limitations, we have developed a automated testing framework that leverages declarative representations of the system's logic and structure. This framework enables the creation of sophisticated test scenarios with minimal human input and allows multiple optimization techniques to ensure thorough coverage of the system's functionality. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework by applying it to a leading open-source conversational reasoning engine and report a notable reduction in the required human input needed to conduct comprehensive testing. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. This new estimator adds a term to the standard SN Ia luminosity sensitivity analysis and involves a greater consideration of the lensing-induced relationship between SN Ia and host galaxies. Consequently, it has the potential to utilize host galaxy information more effectively, thereby utilizing existing data more extensively. When applied to the Pantheon SN Ia dataset in conjunction with SDSS host galaxy information, this estimator yields a precise estimation of the Hubble constant $H_0 = 72.76 \pm 1.45$ km/s/Mpc, a value consistent with the CMB estimation and reflecting a moderate impact of external factors on SN Ia-based $H_0$ determinations. The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included. 

The concluding chapter covers the pathwise approach. 

The lecture notes are based on a mini-course taught to an audience consisting of Ph.D. students and early-career researchers in SPDEs and related fields. 

The main contributors to these lecture notes are J. Brandle, M. Hahn, J. Huang, A. Neves, J. Shen, and S. Yamasato.

In this research, we explore the properties of a novel algebraic variant of the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$, as well as its corresponding degenerate Bernoulli number. This investigation is grounded in an innovative algebraic framework for generating functions and symbolic evaluation functions, allowing us to derive $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. Our findings demonstrate intriguing connections with circulant matrices and Galois fields, while showcasing the potential for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ to be applied in computationally efficient contexts. Furthermore, we establish an intriguing link between $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ and the classical Bernoulli polynomial $B_{k}(m,x)$. Our research focuses on the non-degenerate scenario, $0\leq k\leq 2$, with $0\leq m\leq 5$ and $0\leq x\leq 5$. Leveraging our algebraic approach, we facilitate the use of computer algebra systems to verify or refute conjectures regarding $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$. Two novel, albeit conjectural, formulas for $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ are also presented for consideration. Our study provides an innovative contribution to the field of degenerate special polynomials. While related research exists, our work stands out due to its unique algebraic framework, coupled with the distinctive nature of the proposed degenerate Bernoulli polynomial and number. Although our findings are limited to the specified range of indices and parameters, the underlying algebraic framework enables potential extensions of the results for greater values of $k$ and $m$. To enhance the utility of $\tilde{\beta}_{k}(m,x)$ in computational contexts, a high-performance implementation of the proposed algorithm has been developed and is made available for download alongside this study. Our research also offers an intriguing insight into the properties of circulant matrices and Galois fields, further enriching our understanding of degenerate special polynomials. While our results are primarily focused on the degenerate Bernoulli polynomial and number, the proposed algebraic framework is adaptable enough to be utilized in exploring other variants of degenerate special polynomials. As such, this study makes a substantial contribution to the broader field of degenerate special polynomials, revealing numerous avenues for exploration and discovery. Through our investigation, we have demonstrated the potential for the proposed algebraic approach to yield novel, groundbreaking results in this field.

In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research provides the first substantial insight into the multiagent learning challenge under rationalizability and provides the basis for exploring further generalizations. It is worthwhile to note that the proposed algorithms can also be applied to finding equilibria in multiagent learning contexts. This is particularly relevant as the developed algorithms can be viewed as an extension to the existing literature on the development of efficient algorithms for finding equilibria in general multiplayer games under bandit feedback, building on prior work by Li et al. and Daskalakis et al. This includes the results on the learning of Coarse Correlated and Correlated Equilibria in multiagent learning under bandit feedback, which is a more stringent setting than the one considered in the recent research by Daskalakis et al. and on the development of an efficient algorithm for general contextual multiarmed bandit games extending the results obtained by Li et al. and Li et al. This extends the scope of previous solutions to a broader context, covering not only the contextual multiarmed bandit games, multiagent learning under complete feedback, and general contextual general games but also general multiplayer games, making it the most comprehensive solution for finding the next model of (Co)CE or rationalizable equilibrium under bandit feedback. Additionally, this research provides the first efficient solution for identifying a rationalizable action profile under bandit feedback, which is the most challenging setting considered so far. This result is also significant as it is the first time an efficient algorithm is developed for finding a rationalizable action

Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. Consequently, we have developed the PDFFIT pipeline, which automates the conversion of various format outputs from different PDF fitting codes into a unified format that can be used by the xAOD-FCC PDF fitting framework. Additionally, the pipeline is capable of handling contributions from lattice QCD, enabling a comprehensive interpretation of experimental and theoretical data within the standard model and its extensions. As an exemplary demonstration, the PDFFIT pipeline has been utilized to combine the results from the Drell-Yan global fit provided by the LHCHiggs working group and the NNLO precision PDF fitting team. The outcome of this combination, in the form of an xAOD file, is subsequently employed as the input for the CKMfitter flavor analysis. The PDFFIT pipeline is openly accessible and invites collaborations and contributions from various research groups. The code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/Physikalisches-Referat/TU-Muenchen/pdffit, where issues and pull requests may be submitted. The PDFFIT pipeline is introduced in detail in the accompanying presentation available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.08578. The xAOD output provided by the PDFFIT pipeline for the combined DY and Higgs fitting results is available at https://doi.org/10.17185/20230430.85789159 or via HEP Repository https://repository.heim.org/20230430-85789159. The lattice QCD input provided by the PDFFIT pipeline for the combined DY and Higgs fitting results is available at https://doi.org/10.17185/20230430.85789160 or via HEP Repository https://repository.heim.org/20230430-85789160. The PDFFIT pipeline has been successfully used to automate the conversion process for the contributions from the LHCHiggs working group and the NNLO precision PDF fitting team.

To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple stochastic components, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data, or experience replay. A key limitation in implementing this approach involves storing a diverse range of trajectories, as the agent's sampling bias tends to select more rewarding paths. In response, a variance-reducing method is proposed to balance exploration and exploitation when selecting memories, or stored episodes, for re-weighting and re-using. These optimized weights give greater importance to less rewarding, diverse episodes, reducing the effectiveness of their return in guiding optimization. As a result, the agent learns from a richer, more representative dataset, minimizing its reliance on privileged initial samples. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to randomized episodic reinforcement learning and a challenging autonomous driving scenario. Moreover, an analysis of the proposed approach's theoretical advantages is provided. With only minor modifications, our method aligns with the policy gradient theorem, enabling straightforward optimization using standard techniques. In practice, our approach proves easy to implement and requires minimal additional memory relative to standard experience replay. Notably, our results reveal substantial performance gains, achieved with significantly fewer samples, in scenarios with substantial levels of stochasticity. We refer to our approach as Variance Reduction based Experience Replay (VRER). A key aspect of our method involves a generalized formulation of the biased sampling problem, with a solution derived from a regularized formulation of the biased sampling objective. Additionally, it serves as a comprehensive toolkit for the development of exact diagonalization codes, carefully designed for high performance, ease of use, and customization. libcommute boasts an intuitive syntax for commonly applied abstractions and algorithms, and its extensive collection of higher-level functions for diagonalization, transformation, and correlation functions, all while maintaining a strong focus on numerical stability and versatile indexing systems. Furthermore, Python 3.x bindings are also available for libcommute through the pycommute module, providing a convenient means of accessing its core features. Nonetheless, the Python interface is intended as a trial or proof of concept version, and users are advised to leverage the native C++11/14/17 template library for production use. Moreover, the project's repository on GitHub serves as a hub for user support, resource sharing, and collaboration opportunities. By incorporating multiple contributing researchers with distinct areas of expertise, libcommute has become a robust tool with high potential for further development and contribution from the scientific computing and quantum physics communities. User-guided installation instructions and example use cases can be found within the library's comprehensive documentation, available online. The library's development was predominantly supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada and the National Science Foundation. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. We propose that the slow-recovering component is associated with carrier-mediated spin-spin interactions across LaAlO$_3$ layer boundaries, while the fast-recovering component is linked to local spin fluctuations within isolated LaNiO$_3$ layers. As the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness increases, the relative influence of these distinct spin dynamics changes, resulting in the observed modification in spin-lattice relaxation behavior. This understanding is further validated by comparing our NMR findings with electrical transport measurements in these superlattices. Our study underlines the value of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR in exploring the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ and offers a unique perspective on the spatial coordination of electrons within this material. Additionally, we observe that local spin fluctuations contribute substantially to the electrical conductivity of these superlattices, a crucial aspect that can be precisely quantified via NMR but may not be accurately captured through transport measurements alone. Furthermore, we find that the spin-lattice relaxation data in these superlattices consistently exhibit a stronger sensitivity to temperature changes than the electrical conductivity, revealing a temperature anisotropy that serves as a critical indicator of the correlated metallic state in these materials. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. Our proof involves interpreting the Dyson model as a limit of repulsive Riesz gas models with $\delta$-interactions on the real line and obtaining the corresponding imaginary surfaces as limits of corresponding stochastic flow equations. This justifies the Dyson model as a driving force for the Riesz gas and multiple SLE. On the other hand, we demonstrate that the Bruish-Wishart process can be seen as a scaling limit of the delta-type Riesz gas on the positive real line, thus establishing its connection to the corresponding imaginary surfaces and multiple SLE. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. By utilizing a conflict-resolution approach rather than a last-writer-wins policy, RWF enables a wide range of CRDT designs, including those that require value merging and have varying idempotence properties. As a result, RWF-enabled CRDTs exhibit better consistency properties and can be implemented with reduced coordination, thus providing better performance and higher availability. Overall, the RWF framework offers a flexible and scalable way to develop new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently and effectively. Furthermore, by utilizing Redis's built-in support for atomic multi-key operations, RedisCRDTs can provide strong consistency guarantees for distributed systems, making it an ideal solution for a wide range of use cases and applications that require low-latency, consistent, and durable data storage. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. As a result, there is a high probability of detecting future outbursts from sources classified as transient, and most of these sources are expected to show radio pulsar activity. Consequently, a significant fraction of the sources classified as transient X-ray binaries within the Milky Way are likely to contain neutron stars rather than stellar mass black holes. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. As a result, we conclude that current FL applications are vulnerable to similar types of attacks, and therefore, more robust protocols are needed. Furthermore, we propose a novel protocol called "encrypted multiplication," while acknowledging there are more secure protocols available, but we also think our proposal is fairly efficient. The proposed protocol prevents the described attacks, and although it requires extra communication between users, it remains pretty feasible even with a large number of participants. Finally, we conclude that the development of practical privacy-preserving protocols for FL is possible and necessary. Moreover, we outline several research directions for further exploration. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of the newly proposed protocol in the appendix. This context is suitable for researchers with an expertise in machine learning and cryptography. Furthermore, the subject matter of this research is relevant to the development of innovative applications that rely on FL and ML, such as secure drug discovery and personalized medicine, secure genomic analysis, secure weather forecasting, and secure financial risk management, among others. Lastly, the findings of this research are significant for any company or organization that utilizes FL and ML, such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, IBM, Apple, Alibaba, and Tencent, among many others. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network known as U-Net has demonstrated superior outcomes when compared to conventional methods in identifying heart structures from CMR images. Nonetheless, evaluating how well these models perform when applied to rare conditions such as TOF remains unknown. We discovered that when applied to CMR images of TOF patients, a U-Net model trained on images of normally functioning hearts results in significantly inferior outcomes when compared to its standard performance on non-TOF patients. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and illuminates its success through the lens of a novel mathematical representation. It is shown that the FPN's ability to effectively detect objects is directly linked to its ability to generate a linear scaling of the feature map's topmost layer, which is in turn associated with the problem of summing distinct scalar vectors. Furthermore, this problem is exacerbated by the conventional cross-entropy loss function, which is utilized in multi-scale classification. In response, this paper introduces an alternative loss function, known as the Uniformly Weighted Softmax (UWS), which addresses the issue of scale by distributing identical weight across all object categories. The proposed UWS function is shown to result in a scalable representation, thereby facilitating the identification of objects at various scales. When integrating UWS into a detector based on BiFPN, the proposed method yields superior performance when compared to the standard softmax loss function across five diverse benchmark datasets. The implementation is also notably more straightforward, requiring minimal code modifications. The proposed UWS function offers a more profound insight into the complex classification problem of multi-scale object classes through the use of yet another mathematical representation. This new perspective provides a unique perspective on the recent BiFPN variants, which can be interpreted as different ways of reweighting the UWS function. The proposed approach can be viewed as the simplest form of dynamic reweighting, where the UWS function is optimized with an unstructured vector, thereby allowing for the detection of objects across all scales. The implementation of this approach has been made available on GitHub under the name of UWSoftmax. The code has been further optimized and is now being maintained on the DETR-Seg GitHub repository. On the other hand, the proposed method can also be viewed as the inclusion of an external prior, which is achieved by adding a separate map to the detection head. This prior is scale-aware and is obtained through the bi-linear interpolation of the class distribution of the training dataset. The use of this prior effectively resolves the vanishing feature problem by filling in the missing information from large-scale objects. The proposed approach has been successfully applied to the BiFPN detector, yielding the best results on the MS COCO dataset among all publicly available codes.
