Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the system into a form of resonant optically holographic filter, this design successfully eliminates the drawbacks of signal reduction and quantum limitations at high frequencies. Using the LIGO+2 configuration as an example, our analysis indicates that this new design can enhance the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors by ~2 dB (a factor of ~1.4) at high frequencies, greatly enhancing their detection capability. Furthermore, this design can be implemented using the current advanced gravitational wave detector infrastructure with a simple upgrade, enabling these detectors to take full advantage of future improvements in sensor sensitivity and strain-to-voltage conversion. As a result, they will be capable of detecting a wider range of binary neutron star merger events. Furthermore, this new design will significantly enhance the detection capabilities of future third-generation gravitational wave detectors, such as Einstein Telescope, particularly for mergers occurring at greater distances. The improved detector sensitivity provided by the sloshing Sagnac design will also allow for the detection of smaller mass-range binary neutron star mergers, and it may provide better sensitivity to certain binary black hole event types, although these benefits depend heavily on the specific characteristics of the event in question. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Furthermore, SADRNet exhibits robustness in reconstructing real-world images and demonstrates its capability to align and reconstruct challenging, fully occluded faces. This is evident from results obtained on the more comprehensive and diverse datasets such as Florence+ and REFB, which incorporate a wider range of head orientations and various types of occlusions. These improvements indicate significant gains in both precision and efficiency. On these datasets, our method achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing the existing state of the art by a margin of at least 9.21, demonstrating the efficacy of our proposed self-alignment and dual-regression strategy for robust 3D face alignment and reconstruction across various poses and levels of occlusion. This research provides a ground-breaking solution to the 3D face reconstruction problem in the face of severe occlusions and head orientations. This work also paves the way for further exploration of our proposed framework in tasks such as biometric identification, where the robust reconstruction of faces in complex real-world scenarios is pivotal. Additionally, our method highlights the value of modeling both pose and occlusion in 3D face reconstruction. This is exemplified by the observation that, without considering occlusion, our method still yields superior performance. This observation implies that modeling pose is crucial; however, this is inherently considered as an occlusion problem. In contrast, the ability of our method to consider both pose and occlusion allows for the generation of highly realistic images. This is evident from the fact that our method is capable of accurately reconstructing fully occluded faces, a task that poses significant challenges to existing techniques. This research sets a new performance benchmark for 3D face reconstruction methods, indicating that a consideration of both pose and occlusion is essential for achieving robust results. This

Our research iOCR system is designed to evaluate the potential of iOCR to improve the interpretation of sensitive documents, such as voting results, which often carry significant legal weight and necessitate high levels of accuracy. To ensure the security and integrity of voting processes, it is crucial to limit access to these documents until official results are declared, which could be achieved by implementing iOCR systems that delay full decoding until official verification. Our study utilizes a reduced dataset consisting of 5000 words from 20 different styles of handwritten text, which were incorrectly identified as belonging to 10 different languages by some OCR systems. Nonetheless, the system we tested successfully recognized nearly all the words (94%), with only a small error rate (6%), indicating a high level of accuracy. Notably, this system performed significantly better than traditional OCR systems on similar types of documents. We also observed a relationship between the consistency of the handwriting and the difficulty of interpretation, with some forms being more challenging for the system to understand. We explored different approaches to improving the results, which showed significant potential for further improvement when combining our system with traditional OCR methods. We plan to expand the scope of our research to other domains that rely heavily on OCR systems for ballot tallying. Our study demonstrates the promise of iOCR systems for accurately interpreting voting results without revealing sensitive information until verified, which could potentially disrupt traditional voting result publication timelines. However, further research is needed to fully assess the advantages and limitations of these systems. Our study also raises considerations for the potential delays that voting authorities may face when publishing results and the implications for their publicity strategies. We anticipate that the adoption of iOCR systems will become more prevalent in the future, due to their ability to provide more accurate results than traditional OCR systems, which could in turn accelerate the publication of verified results. Furthermore, the increased accuracy of these systems will likely generate more reliable data, which could be utilized for a greater range of analytical purposes. Our study paves the way for a broader examination of the performance of iOCR systems in other domains that involve the interpretation of sensitive ballot tallying data. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual weather patterns. These findings imply a significant role for risk-conscious storage units in managing market risks and maintaining stability in future power grids. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be further refined to create a family of invariants, discussed in the concluding section. Finally, we outline an unconfirmed conjecture regarding the relationship between $J_n^T$ and the quantum invariant $W_n$ introduced by Gukov and Lasota. Additionally, we provide an appendix detailing the precise relationship between the n-th toroidal colored Jones polynomial and the quantum invariant $W_n$. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Moreover, this research introduces the initial concept of cross-sense augmentation, offering a possible framework for exploring WSD through the development of learning-based methods in a supervised setting.  Notably, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to baseline models and existing approaches on the WordSenseSimilarity dataset, serving as a starting point for the exploration of supervised learning in WSD. The study utilizes the WordNet knowledge base but acknowledges the limitations and potential drawbacks of leaning on such sources.  The implementation of a learning-based strategy for WSD, in turn, raises crucial questions regarding reliability, with the need for the development of more robust evaluation metrics across various senses of a polysemous word. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Any variation in the road design induces changes in the required steering input to stay within the designated path. To assess the safety of this system, we develop a criterion based on the relationship between the road design's control points and the magnitude of the steering input demanded. To optimize this criterion using search algorithms, we must account for the constraints of the vehicle's movement along the designated path. A proposed optimization framework and a corresponding algorithm are explained in detail. Our research demonstrates the potential for lane-changing maneuvers to be used as a stress test for this system, and future directions for additional testing are also considered. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve the evaluation metrics but instead increase computation costs. To address these issues, we propose a new framework called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for temporal action detection, addressing both the context aggregation and proposal density issues. By incorporating a dual context aggregation module that gathers both local and global context information, DCAN enhances action boundary detection performance. To mitigate unnecessary computation expenses, we introduce an efficient thin-sampled strategy that reduces proposal densities without sacrificing contextual semantics. In our implementation, we combine DCAN with Boundary Matching (BM) for temporal action detection, resulting in state-of-the-art BM-driven performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14. Our open-source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/DCAN. Leveraging DCAN's dual context aggregation strategy, we also explore its applications in other boundary-based object detection tasks. Our implementations for BM and other tasks are available at https://github.com/zwang84/DCAN-demo. By incorporating auxiliary context information and reducing unnecessary computation expenses, our approach not only achieves superior performance but also serves as a model for which the context can be easily extended to other boundary-based object detection applications. Our work highlights the efficacy of context aggregation in temporal action detection, and our results position us in the top performers on ActivityNet v1.3 in the latest competition results available at https://activitynet.org/challenge.html. Moreover, our DCAN-driven thin-sampled strategy achieves the second-best BM-driven average mAP of 28.15% on ActivityNet v1.3, surpassing traditional top-performing strong baselines. For THUMOS-14, our DCAN-driven thin-sampled strategy secures the fifth-best BM-driven average mAP of 30.87%. For all code and further details, please refer to https://zwang84.github.io/DCAN/. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this hypothesis raises further questions regarding the initiation of the edge-localized mode and the PTM's persistent existence. A different approach, focusing on the dynamics of the plasma border, offers an alternative explanation for PTMs, claiming they emerge when a distinct class of edge flows restricts ELM formation, forcing the plasma to accommodate a PTM. This theory is supported by observations showing that the orientation of the PTM is closely linked to the local direction of these flows. As a result, a deeper understanding of the relationship between edge localized modes and the unique edge magnetodynamics in the JET tokamak is gained. Furthermore, the findings imply a significant role for the plasma's border dynamics in determining its stability during edge localized mode events. Additionally, a previously overlooked aspect of the plasma's behavior is revealed through these findings. A new definition for the category of edge localized modes, incorporating both classical peeling and the quasi-modes, is introduced as a result of this research. A key feature of this definition is the inclusion of a new aspect for quasi-modes, namely their orientation in the plasma border. A key implication arising from a more in-depth analysis of the data, facilitated by the revised definition, is that the edge localized mode category accounts for a more substantial share of the tokamak's discharge termination events than previously estimated. Moreover, a significant correlation is identified between the edge localized mode's character and the type of the discharging termination, with a distinct correlation emerging for the first time. A key achievement of this research is the validation of the new theoretical ELM impact regression model, and a crucial aspect of this validation is the identification of a previously hidden source of fluctuation in the measurement of the plasma's cross-sectional area. A significant limitation of the study is the lack of control over the edge resolution, which results in a significant variation in the measured ELM characteristics. A key outcome of the investigation is the identification of a key operational indicator for the plasma's stability during ELM events, with a clear distinction visible when comparing the results from the four different ITER-like wall strike-point locations. A significant finding of this research is the detection of a previously unseen difference in the behavior of the inner and outer plasma border with regard to the orientation of the edge

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Additionally, the cooperative controller is found to be robust in response to unexpected velocity changes in the target robot, and the scheme is adaptable for application to linear non-holonomic marine vehicles. The approach is compared to other methods, revealing its unique benefit of preventing the target robot from inducing a sinkhole, and the code for the controller employed in the experiments is made openly available for download. The cooperative controller's ability to handle a variety of velocity profiles for the mobile robots is a key innovation of this research. The code for the controller used in the experiments can be found at the following link: https://github.com/AmrKhamis/EPRFSFC. The document also presents a dynamic vortex potential field model for a mobile robot controller, and proves that the controller meets all requirements for a globally asymptotic stable controller under specified conditions. The proof of the closed-loop system's asymptotic stability in the neighborhood of the equilibrium point, where the mobile robot and the target at its center of the coordinate system are located, can be found in the appendix of this document. The modified controller for a linear non-holonomic marine vehicle was theoretically proven stable in a previous study co-authored by the primary author of this research. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. Additionally, NMC demonstrated 82.71% gap-reduction on the CoRe 50 benchmark, showcasing its effectiveness in continual learning across multiple domains. This led to further analysis of whether a simple decision-making mechanism, such as threshold-based classification, could effectively handle a large number of categories efficiently. This led to a significant decrease in the NMC's gap by an average of 24.41%, confirming the potential of simple baselines to question the use of complex models in continual learning tasks. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. In addition, by examining the influence of friction on this transition, researchers found that decreasing the ratio of shear to normal stresses as friction decreases can result in an first-order like or even higher-order phase transition in its place, indicating a significant role for friction in determining the transition's order. Consequently, the intricate balance of forces in dense, slowly deformed mixtures demands a more detailed consideration of both interparticle attractions and collisions, leading to an adjusted view of the jamming phenomenon as an highly responsive, nonlinear state of matter. Ultimately, these findings imply that the intricate behavior exhibited by dense, slowly deformed mixtures holds significant implications for our broader understanding of the physics underlying non-linear, disordered systems. By extending the principles of universality and detailed balance to systems in motion, researchers have gained a deeper insight into the intricate physics governing the complex behavior exhibited by dense, slowly deformed mixtures, demonstrating that the unique properties of these systems can, in fact, be accounted for through an extension of the fundamental principles that govern the behavior of static, disordered systems. Moreover, this work has a broader impact on the theoretical physics community by prompting a reevaluation of the long-held assumption that the jamming transition holds a singular, universal character when studied through the lens of static, equilibrium phenomena. In contrast, this assumption has been found to be too restrictive, as it fails to capture the intricate, state-dependent properties that arise as a result of the unique response of dense, slowly deformed systems to changes in their composition and external influences. In turn, these interactions also vary according to the type of nuclear target and the spin-independent interaction coefficient ($S^2$), while our simulation predicts a higher density of scattering events at both smaller and larger recoil angles for heavier nuclear targets. Additionally, we observed that the angular distribution of low-recoil energy scattering events is more pronounced for lighter nuclear targets and lower values of $S^2$. Furthermore, our simulation facilitates direct access to the recoil angle distribution of low-energy scattering events, providing a valuable tool for distinguishing WIMP interactions from background noise in future direct detection experiments. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This improvement in computation time makes our exact algorithm more suitable for the large datasets that are becoming more common in NLP. Furthermore, we've also introduced a new method for updating the test statistic during the sampling process. This update strategy reduces memory usage by half when dealing with large datasets. Our proposed exact algorithm is now being used by the top-performing team at the 2020 GLUE Ranking Challenge, and the code for this method is available for public use. Despite its effectiveness, the exact algorithm does have some limitations, in that it only works well when the test statistic follows a deterministic ranking structure. In response to these limitations, we've also developed an updated version of the algorithm that can handle test statistics with lower ranking specificity. This new algorithm is less efficient than the original exact algorithm, but it is still more effective than the commonly employed Monte Carlo methods. Furthermore, the new algorithm is being used by the current leaders of the GLUE Masquerade Challenge, and the code for this method is also available for public use. In addition to these practical applications, we've also investigated the theoretical time complexity of both the original and new algorithms. The new algorithm is therefore less efficient than the original exact algorithm, but it is still more effective than the commonly employed Monte Carlo methods. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Furthermore, the association between veering triangulations and loom spaces is found to be bijective. A key component of this proof involves identifying a veering triangulation's realization as a geometric representation of its spine. This connection between loom spaces and veering triangulations offers a new perspective on the subject, utilizing ideas from combinatorial geometry and discrete geometry. As a result, the language of veering triangulations can be substituted with that of loom spaces in many theoretical proofs. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. The code for Kedge is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/Kedge. The models trained with Kedge also achieved superior interpretability by prioritizing salient node features and reducing the influence of noisy data. As a result, the models can focus on the most representative features for prediction, which is essential in domains like biochemistry and physics which heavily rely on graph neural networks. The improved interpretability of Kedge enables accurate and efficient annotation of physical and biological molecules for better generalization across similar domains. The models trained with Kedge have been found to be highly invariant to different perturbation techniques such as GNNExplainer's perturbation which further enhances their interpretability. The reduced graph complexity through Kedge also accelerates the training of GNN models on large graphs by up to 4 times, without a corresponding decrease in accuracy, making it an accelerated and effective sparsification technique for high-performance GNN models. The implementation of Kedge has been done using PyTorch, an open-source deep learning framework, available at https://github.com/ghrua/Kedge. The models trained with Kedge have achieved state-of-the-art performance in node classification tasks on various benchmark datasets such as PubMed, PubMed-Sparse, PPI, and Cora by significantly improving the generalization performance without compromising the accuracy. The improved generalization of Kedge is attributed to the consistent reduction of the degree distribution of graph datasets during training, without the issue of degree collapse, thanks to the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. A new analysis technique is also provided, offering a broader perspective on the issue, namely that the critical factor determining the performance of a sketch is not the number of operations but rather the uniqueness of the keys. Moreover, this new estimator exhibits a query complexity directly proportional to k rather than d. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions leading to a guarantee of at least 90% of optimal performance. The proposed PPC is applied to a practical scenario involving energy management for a cohort of electric vehicle chargers. In line with the rapid evolution of this field, we also touch on the emerging potential for our algorithm to integrate decentralized learning frameworks, paving the way for increased flexibility discovery in subsequent iterations and potential further improvements in our framework. These concepts, though initially explored, warrant exploration in future research areas identified in this study. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in reducing the risk exposure and achieving near-optimal performance in real-world scenarios. The implementation of our algorithm across a range of simulations and an actual deployment with a group of electric vehicle chargers serve as the foundation for further exploration of its decentralized learning applications. One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while a companion paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This new formalism for common envelopes relies on the conservation of angular momentum and includes a detailed understanding of the transfer of material during this phase, which is critical for predicting the outcomes of mergers. This will be utilized to create a simplified model for predicting the end states of these systems, which will then be compared to more detailed simulations. This comparison will highlight the inherent diversity of the outcomes of common envelopes, resulting from the various interacting forces at play, which presents a significant challenge for their prediction. This diversity in outcome results from the interplay between the binding energy and size of the envelope, as well as the properties of the stars themselves, which all impact the behavior of the system in distinct and often irreversible ways. This irreversibility presents a difficulty in reverse engineering the history of these systems through their final states, a challenge that is compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. Our analysis focuses on the potential of these colliders to discern beyond-the-Standard Model contributions to Higgs physics, leveraging Effective Field Theory and integrating the SARRACINO code for event simulations. The study explores a broad range of operator signatures that could appear in the Higgs pair-production process and assesses how well these colliders can differentiate them, especially in the two-bottom-quark final state, which is the most prominent in pair production. The research finds that the best outcome, which involves the largest of the Higgs couplings, can be distinguished with a precision of 0.05, while the next most significant outcome, related to the Standard Model, can be differentiated with a precision of 0.15. However, the majority of the Higgs couplings, including those contributing less significantly to pair production, can only be determined with a precision of around 1-10, which is still more accurate than current experimental data but less so than expected based on the anticipated improvement in energy resolution in future colliders. It is essential to note that the proposed study uses the ILD concept as a reference for its interpretation and assumes that the choice of the detector concept does not significantly impact the outcome's accuracy. Furthermore, the research assumes that the projected sensitivity can be achieved through 1 inverse femtometer squared of data integration, which is equivalent to producing over 10,000 Higgs-boson events in the two-bottom-quark final state. The findings indicate that future electron-positron colliders have the capability to accurately determine the Standard Model Higgs couplings with a significant degree of precision, while also providing significant insights into the Standard Model's consistency and accuracy in a mass range that is previously unexplored. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. To overcome this hurdle, we introduce BoAnon, an innovative approach that enables the discovery of a system's structure from performance data, obtained through logs of expensive experiments. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. A comparison between Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions revealed that $v_3$ and $v_2$ demonstrate similar scaling with beam energy and centrality, indicating that the same physical principles govern flow anisotropy in both types of collisions. Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, which also come with varying quality levels.  While there are established methods for evaluating and comparing RDF datasets based on their structural properties, a comprehensive and scalable quality assessment framework for these datasets does not exist yet.  To address this gap, we have developed a quality assessment framework that utilizes a balanced approach combining both subjective and objective evaluation methods.  By leveraging a large-scale dataset composed of 5000+ RDF datasets with associated quality ratings from 8 different data sources, the framework showcases its effectiveness through a series of experiments that highlight its performance, efficiency, and data coverage.  Furthermore, the inclusion of customizable evaluation protocols allows users to tailor the framework to their specific requirements, thereby making it a versatile and reliable tool for evaluating and comparing the structural integrity of Linked Data datasets.  All the framework's components, including a web interface and example configurations, are freely available for download at https://github.com/alexandrosamani/QualityAssessor.  Additionally, the framework has been successfully utilized to generate the "Linked Data Structural Index" (LDSI), a comprehensive index that ranks Linked Data datasets based on their structural properties and quality level.  By leveraging the insights provided by the framework and the LDIS, researchers and data consumers can now identify and retrieve high-quality Linked Data datasets with optimal structural characteristics.  The entire project, including all data collections and index entries, is also available for download through the linkeddata.io dataset page.  The development of this quality assessment framework and the associated index represents a significant milestone in the evaluation of Linked Data, an important step towards establishing Linked Data as a trustworthy data source for critical applications.  Furthermore, the framework paves the way for the creation of more advanced data visualization tools, such as the LDIS visualization dashboard available at https://linkeddata.cs.arizona.edu/structurality/.  By empowering users to compare the structural properties and quality levels of Linked Data datasets, the framework has sparked a surge in activity on the linkeddata.io platform, with over 50 new dataset uploads and 10,000+ monthly visits.  As a result, there are now over 6000+ RDF datasets available for download from linkeddata.io, along with their corresponding quality ratings and structural indices.  The success of this project has also inspired the creation of structural indices for other dataset platforms, such as DBpedia, YAGO, and BioPortal.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. The model's code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/huijuanliu/SceneGen and https://huijuanliu.github.io/SceneGen-dataset/, respectively. Leveraging deep learning techniques, SceneGen is able to generate more sophisticated traffic scenarios than previous approaches. By utilizing two types of neural score predictors, it simultaneously models the movement of virtual characters across time as sequential actions and the overall traffic scene. Through the use of a conditionally branching process, SceneGen selectively applies different models to areas of the environment occupied by virtual characters. As a result, SceneGen is capable of generating a wide range of virtual characters and accurately modeling their positions, speeds, and other characteristics. Moreover, SceneGen has been found to effectively train perception models in simulated environments that mimic real traffic conditions, thereby enabling the seamless transition of these models to real-world scenarios. Additionally, SceneGen has been found to be superior to all previously proposed methods for traffic scenario generation in terms of metrics such as Fr\'{e}chet Inception Distance and precision@k. Furthermore, SceneGen has been found to generate high-quality video sequences that are not only visually appealing but also accurate in terms of their underlying physics. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, the article also explores the use of flexible bi-conjugate gradients as an alternative, in addition to illustrating the scheme's computational efficiency by applying it to a conservative system of ordinary differential equations and a nonlinear Schrödinger equation. The article concludes by outlining several potential modifications and potential applications of these iterative methods. One such modification involves proposing a flexible iteration that incorporates an approximation of the inverse of the Jacobian matrix, which could be particularly useful in implementing structure-preserving methods for further development of time-dependent PDEs, such as damped systems and systems with changing stability. The article provides the mathematical derivation of both flexible Krylov iterations but skips the theoretical convergence analysis, which is known to converge at a rate of $O(k+1)$ for both methods. The article also includes results showing that when using an implicit time-stepping method with a small step size, both methods can preserve the same order of accuracy as the underlying scheme, and that both methods can be used with both conservative and dissipative systems, the latter of which requires the imposition of an additional constraint to preserve. The article further highlights that both methods can be used with a wide range of linear solvers, including direct and iterative methods, and that the choice of solver can impact the overall efficiency of both methods, with the flexible GMRES iteration being shown to be more efficient than the flexible bi-conjugate gradients iteration for the specific test case presented in the article, with the latter of these two methods requiring a significantly larger number of iterations to converge. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects which isn't aligned with either our intuitive understanding of how distance affects measurement error or the characteristics of sensor readings from a lidar sensor. As an example, a single meter of error when detecting an object at 20 meters is significantly more noticeable than the same amount of error when detecting an object at 60 meters. To address these shortfalls, we created FarField criteria which can be used to evaluate three-dimensional detection tasks with a focus on far-field objects. It incorporates more realistic assumptions about the tolerance of tolerance thresholds with respect to distance and takes into consideration the characteristics of lidar sensors. We utilized this criteria to evaluate three-dimensional detection performance on the nuScenes dataset, a leading benchmark for this type of task. To improve performance in far-field detection, we fine-tuned the architecture of detection networks, incorporating distance-weighted loss functions as well as other techniques. Our results show significant performance gains on far-field detection, with 10% mAP improvement on the test set, and also found that simply applying these modifications can lead to a 5% improvement in average accuracy across all objects. The code for our approach has been made available at https://github.com/kuang33/far3det. Furthermore, we have added some comments about extending this work to other detection related challenges. The term "far-field" can refer to a range of topics beyond 3D detection, such as low-frequency signals in electromagnetism or the parts of an object that are far from the sensor in other vision applications like semantic segmentation or image classification. Therefore, the name far3det might not be the most suitable for all aspects of this research and we would be open to changing it to something more universally applicable, such as farfield-eval or distance-weighted loss

Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action. A numerical analysis shows that even with current technological limitations, using a realistic quantum processor, such as one based on ion traps, a protocol of this kind could reach its optimal performance in a timeframe of less than a day. Furthermore, given the current pace of development in quantum processor manufacturing, it is likely that in the near future, such protocols could be efficiently implemented with ease. A discussion on the aspects of current quantum processors in relation to this kind of implementation is also provided. A focus is placed on the fact that in an era where quantum processors are constantly changing and evolving, incorporating new training data becomes remarkably straightforward. This study also explores the unique potential of studying chemical reaction dynamics with protocols of this kind, offering a novel perspective that views the development of quantum chemistry models in the light of the principles of chemistry, rather than physics. A discussion on the fact that chemistry is a more intuitive and easier to grasp subject, in comparison to physics, is also presented. This study also suggests that, due to the intuitive nature of chemistry, people with a physics background are more likely to understand the inner workings of quantum machine

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The trained network's code is also available for download. The project build upon the foundation laid in our previous research, specifically in reference [1, 2]. The aforementioned work relied on assumptions regarding the availability of high-quality intraoperative surface data derived from laparoscopic video footage, yet such data typically undergoes noise and no signal processing techniques were discussed. Additionally, the demonstration of the algorithm in [2] leveraged artificially generated skin displacement maps. In our current study, we expand the scope by incorporating noisy and low-quality intraoperative surface data, also including realistic skin displacement maps resulting from realistic biomechanical simulations, encompassing various deformation scenarios, noise-prone intraoperative surface data, and real-world data. The developed approach and application are unique in the field of non-rigid registration, particularly within the scope of surgical navigation. The newly proposed framework resolves several key challenges faced in this context, including the identification of surface correspondences, robust performance against noisy data, and issues related to patient-specific adaptations. Furthermore, this research extends the scope of previously reported results by considering various non-rigid registration scenarios, including scenarios where the surface tension is decreased, organ models with distinct shapes, and extensive real-world data. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world scenarios. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning for Flow, that utilizes a contrastive learning approach to cross-check metric differences between spatially related points across consecutive frames, thereby distinguishing genuine point correlations from spurious ones. This method enables self-supervised training for the estimation task. Our results reveal that our approach yields superior scene flow estimations in comparison to the benchmark's baseline models. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/zheng-hao/SSSF. Leveraging easy-to-generate synthetic flow masks, our self-supervised flow estimator achieves a 4.25% decrease in pixel error compared to supervised training. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows bio-realistic neural networks to operate at high speeds while minimizing energy consumption, has now become an appealing substitute. Our results demonstrate that this approach yields both superior accuracy and enhanced performance. Furthermore, the simplified spiking protocol allows the network to operate with a low number of axon updates during each time step, thereby enabling the use of a large time step size that balances speed and throughput, without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, this implementation demonstrates a direct relationship between time step size and energy consumption, with a linear increase in energy consumption as the time step size doubles. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. Our results indicate that the mass-thickness relation for spin-polarized strange quark stars is significantly influenced by the magnetic field and temperature, exhibiting two branches of solutions: one corresponding to the non-polarized quark star and another representing the polarized quark star. We observed that the onset of temperature or magnetic field strength increases the stability of spin-polarized quark matter, thus allowing for the existence of spin-polarized strange quark stars with smaller masses-thicknesses. property. Additionally, we demonstrate that an edge-colouring with three colours is required
for these graphs to display the property. Our new class of graphs expands upon previous work
by Bouklas and Fowler in 2016. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correlation between
the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian cycles and Hamiltonian cycles in an individual graph, as
well as across all members of the new class of cubic graphs. This correlation enables us to
determine the proportion of Hamiltonian cycles that are perfect matchings in these graphs. It
is found that this proportion tends towards a specific probability $p_n$ as $n$ increases,
defined by the sequence $p_n = \frac{1}{3^{n-1}}\binom{2n}{n}$ and all terms of this

being Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian. Last, we identify a connection between the edge-colouring

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Moreover, we explore how Timeloops can be used as a tool for identifying potential security vulnerabilities and discuss its potential applications and areas for improvement. The source code of Timeloops has been made publicly available on GitHub, under the terms of the permissive BSD 3-Clause License. Furthermore, we have created a demonstration video and a research webpage detailing all the policy learning configurations and performance metrics resulting from our research. Moreover, we have devised a method, called Timeloops-Filter, that combines system call learning with actual implementation, thereby ensuring the secure and correct functioning of containerized microservices. The design and implementation of this method have given rise to several research areas, such as the optimization of system call filtering using genetic algorithms, the integration of system call learning with containerized application deployment, and the development of a community-driven database featuring secure system call filters for various programs and services. Our research has resulted in the acceptance of one paper and one demo at the EuroSys 2021 and the ASPLOS 2021 conferences, respectively. Lastly, we have established an open-source community, called Timeloops, on GitHub with an active member base and a regularly updated newsletter. The success of this research has also led to collaborations with industrial partners, such as Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and Amazon Web Services, with the goal of integrating Timeloops with cloud computing platforms. Moreover, we have created an educational course, called Secure System Call Learning, for undergraduate and graduate students at Stanford University. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. Additionally, a more explicit construction of the controlling input is provided, leveraging the structure of the model's equation to obtain a formulation suitable for practical application. Furthermore, the robustness of this controllability property is verified for small perturbations of the model. A key aspect of our proof involves utilizing a new approach to the superparabolic term, inspired by the concept of vanishing viscosity, to investigate the controllability of the complete system. This involves analyzing the impact of the degenerate component on the rate of diffusion near the boundary regions. By showing that a weakly dissipative boundary layer can influence the control of the population dynamics, we highlight an essential aspect of the model's controllability. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source models that complement the missing wavefield data. Formulations for both WRI and ESI are presented in an adjoint-state framework, with the understanding that these methods serve as a bridge between FWI and conventional linear inversion techniques. Furthermore, the computational cost of these methods is comparable to that of FWI. Field-scale numerical experiments have shown that time-domain ESI can produce results comparable to time-domain FWI, with the caveat that it requires a more flexible numerical strategy due to the non-physical source term. Notably, time-domain ESI has the benefit of avoiding the challenge of constructing a suitable initial condition for the wave equation. With time-domain ESI, the construction of the initial condition is implicitly handled by the time-domain formulation, making it an attractive alternative to FWI in fields characterized by complex geological structures. The potential of time-domain ESI to facilitate convergence and accurate convergence, even in the presence of low-frequency content, is also discussed. The performance of time-domain ESI is evaluated in scenarios with varying frequency content, with the time-domain formulation showing promise for optimizing the reconstruction of extended sources across multiple frequency components. The implementation of time-domain ESI using high-performance computing hardware has resulted in significant performance gains, with speed-ups of up to 5.5 times achieved through the utilization of multiple processors. The time-domain ESI method has the benefit of producing physically realistic models that match observed data in both the time and frequency domains, with an added advantage of the model being free from singularities. The potential of time-domain ESI to accurately represent subsurface fluids with distinct acoustic properties has also been demonstrated. The model obtained through time-domain ESI has shown a high level of detail, with an added benefit of the model being free from singularities. The performance of time-domain ESI has been found to decline with an increase in frequency content, largely due to the challenge of accurately representing the extended source term across multiple frequency components. Despite this limitation, time-domain ESI remains an attractive alternative to FWI

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its lack of magnetic fields, atomic ensembles, or chemical etching, making it a versatile and robust technique for producing optical nonreciprocity. We've also shown that our method can be extended to multiple stages, offering numerous applications across optical communication systems, metabolic process observations, and fly-by light sensing systems. Finally, we've successfully demonstrated our technique using a diamond nanocavity, further highlighting its versatility. Overall, our technique provides an efficient and robust means of producing optical nonreciprocity, making it an ideal method for various optical communication and sensing applications. Additionally, we've used this technique to build a nonreciprocal optical transistor that can control an 10-Gbps data stream, demonstrating its ability to modulate light at the same rate as many practical applications. We've also used this technique to build an optical communication system that can accurately receive 10-Gbps data, making it an efficient and robust method for producing optical nonreciprocity. We've named this technique " quantum squeezing induced optical nonreciprocity" and believe it could potentially be applied to any type of resonator system. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and an Iron emission line at 42.7 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, further highlighting the complex nature of this intermediate spin pulsar's behavior during its 2019 outburst. Additionally, a detailed comparison with data from the Giant Meteor Burst Detector on board AstroSat permits the detection of a mHz QPO, a feature typically observed in higher frequency ranges. This finding enlarges the scope of mHz QPO research and presents a compelling case for the exploration of this phenomenon using a broad band detector with high resolution, specifically designed for the detection of both transient and steady X-ray sources. Moreover, we propose that future missions incorporate such detectors to explore the vast spectrum of X-ray astronomy more effectively. Furthermore, a discussion with existing and upcoming X-ray astronomy missions is also presented in this work. Nevertheless, the absence of the Cyclotron Line and detection of an Iron emission line at 6.4 keV in the early stages of the outburst remains an intriguing aspect that demands further observation and study. Therefore, we recommend that future observations be conducted during the rising phase of IGR J19294+1816's outbursts. Additionally, a detailed analysis of the spectral data from the AstroSat has allowed the estimation of key parameters such as the mass accretion rate, radius of the accretion disk, and the distance to the source, further contributing to the understanding of IGR J19294+1816's physical characteristics. Nevertheless, a deeper analysis of the data from the AstroSat is essential to validate these results, and we intend to pursue this in more detail in the future. Nevertheless, our detection of a mHz QPO and a Cyclotron Line in IGR J19294+1816 during its 2019 outburst marks a significant milestone in the field of X-ray astronomy and provides a compelling justification for the inclusion of a broad band detector with high resolution in any future or ongoing X-ray astronomy missions. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a result of this cultural exchange and scientific advancements, with their construction reflecting a blend of Islamic, Hindu, and Buddhist timekeeping methodologies. Unfortunately, many historical sundials in Indonesia have disappeared over time, making it challenging to determine their timekeeping accuracy and understand the local concept of time. This study aims to investigate Indonesian sundials from a humanities perspective, focusing on the cultural and historical aspects that shaped their development. A key finding is that Indonesian sundials employed the concept of local time (waktu lokal), which is still used today in modern Indonesian, in contrast to the standard time (tzima standar) adopted during the Dutch colonial period. This difference in timekeeping has resulted in two time standards continuing to coexist in Indonesia: local time and standard time. As such, Indonesian sundials can be seen as precursors to modern time standards and serve as a significant aspect of the country's scientific and cultural heritage. This research includes a historical analysis of Indonesian sundials, their construction methods, and the local time standard they utilized, which is applicable to other cultural heritage artifacts as well. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of thoroughly documenting Indonesia's scientific and cultural heritage, particularly sundials, to better understand the country's historical timekeeping methodologies and the impact of external influences on its development. This knowledge can also benefit the restoration and utilization of sundials as educational tools for teaching astronomy, mathematics, and time management in an interdisciplinary approach. This study is an instance of action research, as it not only delves into the subject matter but also lays the groundwork for the documentation and mapping of Indonesian sundials through the development of a sundial inventory template. This template can be adapted for use in documenting other cultural heritage artifacts. This research is being presented at the 2022 International Conference on Mathematics, Science, and Teacher Education (ICMSDE) to facilitate further discussion, collaboration, and potential partnerships with relevant stakeholders and institutions in Indonesia and elsewhere. A key outcome of this study is the creation of a sundial inventory for Indonesia, which is being launched in conjunction with the presentation at ICMSDE. This inventory serves as a starting point for the documentation and mapping of Indonesian sundials and is an open-access and community-driven initiative that is receptive to contributions and corrections from all parties

The surge in telework has highlighted the potential for full remote operation of sophisticated engineering laboratories. This includes the development of a fully automated, single-point LDV system allowing for the acquisition of 2D velocity measurements. A key component of this project involved designing a sophisticated vacuum system capable of supporting pressures as low as 10^(-6) Pa. This system was successfully integrated with the LDV system using a vacuum pump controller with a remote API, enabling seamless automation. A custom-made enclosure was created for the LDV probe, which was designed using numerical methods to minimize any disturbances on the measured flow. This was accomplished by modeling the LDV probe as a series of cylindrical obstacles in various configurations. The performance of the integrated LDV system was validated using a benchmark flow, with the results showing a high level of accuracy when compared to established reference values. This achievement opens up possibilities for the remote operation of other laboratory facilities, offering a viable solution for institutions facing challenges in maintaining on-site expertise. Furthermore, this system enables the utilization of expensive, high-tech laboratories in institutions where expertise may be lacking, by allowing for the safe operation and data collection outside of normal working hours. This allows for the collection of valuable data, even if only occasionally, and enhances the system's overall effectiveness and efficiency. This research was presented at the 33rd Symposium of Aerodynamics, Acoustics and Flight Mechanics, held in Guimarães, Portugal. This paper builds upon that initial submission with the addition of the accompanying raw data as stipulated by the journal's review criteria. This data includes the detailed technical specifications of the LDV system used, as well as the raw data associated with the Figs 1-6 presented in the initial submission. This inclusion aligns with the journal's commitment to open data and transparency. given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, such a design can provide the flexibility to 
accommodate various probe shapes and sizes, catering to diverse TEM uses ranging 
from crystallography to biological imaging. Ultimately, our research validates the 
utility of programmable phase plates as a viable means of correcting spherical 
aberration in TEMs. Furthermore, we explore the scope for these designs to be 
implemented on existing and new TEM equipment, highlighting the feasibility and
advantages of this approach. Our studies suggest that a phase plate-based correction
system is both a technologically viable and scientifically sound method for
