The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, in some cases, challenge the prowess of state-of-the-art models like BERT. Ultimately, the proposed evaluation framework serves as a reminder of the significance of scrutinizing the underlying reasoning behind the capabilities of generative models in conversational settings. In addition, the straightforward yet rigorous nature of the proposed evaluation tasks makes them adaptable to any scenario where vector representations are utilized, providing a universally applicable benchmark against which the performance of different architectures can be compared and contrasted. Furthermore, the simplicity with which these evaluation tasks can be formulated across multiple dimensions enables the creation of a unified evaluation framework that can be fine-tuned to accommodate various task settings, making it an adaptable and versatile means of evaluating the efficacy of vector representations. In the context of dialogue models, the proposed evaluation tasks can be tailored to assess the encoding of specific aspects of dialogue utterances, such as the sequential structure or the roles played by different entities within the conversation, yielding a diverse range of challenges that can be scaled up or down to accommodate any combination of model architectures, tasks, and datasets. Ultimately, the evaluation of the encoder representations used in generative dialogue models serves as a test of the models' understanding of the task at hand, encompassing not just the comprehension of individual words, but the ability to grasp the meaning conveyed through the utterance's structure and sequence. In the study presented herein, the proposed evaluation tasks successfully uncover shortfalls in the performance of state-of-the-art models like BERT when it comes to understanding the sequential structure and the roles within the conversation, demonstrating the value of evaluating the encoder representations used in these models. In the future, the evaluation of the encoder representations used in generative dialogue models will become an indispensable component in any assessment of a model's conversational capabilities, ensuring that the underlying reasoning behind its performance is scrutinized and its prowess thoroughly tested. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To tackle this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections. By doing so, AttDLNet enhances the robustness of the extracted descriptors to orientation variations, and our experiments demonstrate its efficacy on place recognition tasks, particularly when closing loops in scenarios with minimal overlap. The findings show that AttDLNet surpasses existing LiDAR-based place recognition approaches, achieving more accurate results than competitors like PointNet and DGLFNet in challenging scenarios. Moreover, AttDLNet exhibits loop-closure capabilities in scenarios with minimal overlap, a feat that other methods fail to achieve. Our implementation utilizes a straightforward design comprising two deconvolutional layers, resulting in a lightweight network ideal for real-time place recognition applications. Our experiments involve testing the network with real and synthetic datasets, including the KITTI dataset, and our code is publicly available for others to build upon. According to the findings, AttDLNet's performance places it among the top methods for LiDAR place recognition, and its efficient design recommends it for place recognition tasks in autonomous vehicles and robotics. Furthermore, the research involves analyzing several configuration options, including different attention-based mechanisms, middle-layer configurations, and dropout rates, to provide readers with a comprehensive understanding of the challenges and solutions in LiDAR place recognition. Overall, this research demonstrates the potential of deep learning methods to solve complex place recognition challenges in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments, and our experiments showcase the efficacy of AttDLNet on the KITTI dataset. However, the research acknowledges the presence of orientation variation in the test dataset, specifically in sequences 0000 to 0033, which negatively impacts the results, and our analysis indicates that optimizing the network for rotation variations is essential for achieving optimal results. Additionally, the research highlights several limitations of existing methods, including the failure of point-based methods like PointNet to close loops in scenarios with minimal overlap and the inability of range-based methods like DGLFNet to achieve accurate results in challenging scenarios. Streaming high-quality video, whether it's Video-On-Demand or live, demands transcoding to accommodate viewer devices. This requires significant computing power and, due to rising demand, streaming services now rely on cloud computing to ensure a seamless viewing experience. Cloud providers offer a range of Virtual Machines, each with varying capabilities and prices, which poses the challenge of optimizing cloud utilization for video transcoding. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. Based on this analysis and the cost variability of cloud machines, the research provides a model that helps evaluate the suitability of each cloud machine for different transcoding tasks. This model can provide resource provisioning with the best balance of performance and cost, thus enhancing the efficient use of cloud services for video streaming. This approach was put into practice using OpenStack and Linux-based cloud machines and demonstrated with a popular cloud service, OpenStack Linux VMs. The research team used various cloud machines with different VCPs, such as ARM, x86_64, and Power, to show that this solution is adaptable to various computing architectures. By utilizing an open-source video transcoding application, the study showed that its proposed model can provide optimal performance and a significant reduction in cloud costs. This optimized approach was compared to an unoptimized strategy, using a real-world video streaming service as an example, and the results revealed a 42% decrease in total costs and a 30% increase in throughput. The model's effectiveness also holds when combining live and on-demand streaming transcoding. This research's efficient cloud usage for video streaming, using the OMaaS framework, outperforms industry-standard cloud management tools, such as OpenStack's default scheduler and AWS's F1 Optimize, by 20% in terms of total cost. This study's model and methodology can be applied to other computationally intensive applications that rely on cloud services for processing large data sets. This research also highlights the importance of thoroughly evaluating and understanding how applications utilize cloud resources to achieve the best balance of performance and cost in cloud computing. This approach is particularly beneficial for cloud providers and streaming services in optimizing their infrastructure for video transcoding and other computationally intensive tasks, and it can be used to develop more effective scheduling methods, such as those using machine learning and deep learning techniques, which can further enhance the efficient use of cloud services. This research's model and methodology can be used to evaluate and optimize the utilization of cloud services for live and on-demand video streaming,

Continuous speech synthesis via MaskedSpeech, a RNN Transducer-based framework, is introduced in this paper. The proposed system uses a masking strategy to select the most appropriate context words for each speech segment, effectively capturing the complex semantic relationships within language. In contrast to conventional sentence-level synthesis methods, MaskedSpeech synthesizes speech in 20-word segments using a masking strategy. The system is further enhanced by a context-aware state transition probability estimation component, which ensures seamless speech generation despite the absence of full sentence context. The effectiveness of MaskedSpeech is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments, showing its superiority over baseline models in terms of naturalness and accuracy. Notably, the system's performance benefits from relatively short training datasets, achieving high naturalness and linguistic accuracy scores under limited data conditions. The implementation of MaskedSpeech reduces computational overhead compared to sequence-to-sequence synthesis models, while achieving comparable performance. The proposed framework's potential for applications involving speech and text integration is also highlighted in the study. The system's code has been made available for public useage. In addition to superior performance, MaskedSpeech offers potential interpretability benefits due to its masking strategy, allowing for the analysis of selected context words relative to synthesized speech. The system's strong performance makes it a suitable candidate for large-scale implementation. The model's parameters can be Replicated across multiple GPUs, making it easily implementable in distributed settings. The implementation of the system is further highlighted by its efficiency in large-scale inference scenarios. The proposed framework has shown the capability to process 10 sentences at once with no significant performance drop, making it well-suited for real-world applications involving the synthesis of multi-sentence text. The system has been successfully tested across different dialects and has shown the capability to process out-of-domain data with some adjustments to the hyperparameters. The proposed framework has also been successfully integrated into a summarization system, highlighting its potential for integration into other text and speech-related applications. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available for use in future surveys. The extensive dataset produced by this survey will significantly contribute to the understanding of exoplanets and the development of future transit surveys. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Additionally, the study provided revised rotational characteristics for the three asteroids and estimated their YORP accelerations as follows: -0.018 days^-1 for 1992 SK, 0.013 days^-1 for Geographos, and 0.023 days^-1 for Toro. It is also worth noting that Toro's fast rotation makes its shape recovery prone to uncertainties in the inversion process, thus its physical characteristics should be confirmed through other methods. Lastly, due to the YORP effect's impact on their dynamics, scientists believe that both 1992 SK and Geographos could eventually undergo a rotational breakup within a time frame of about a million years, whereas Toro's tighter orbit around the Sun reduces the likelihood of this event occurring in the next ten million years. It is also possible that both 1992 SK and Geographos might have experienced a near-breakup encounter in their past, which could have contributed to the detection of their temporary light curve variations, and ultimately slowed down their rotations again. It is essential to continue monitoring these asteroids to verify the detected YORP acceleration and gain a deeper understanding of the Yarkovsky effect, particularly its impact on their temporary light curve variations and both their internal and external dynamics. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. A proposed algorithm for determining if a continuous function can be computed in a specific way is also presented, along with results for streaming and two-way transducers, showing that such a computation is possible, although it may not always be possible with the most general definition. 

On the theoretical side, a deeper understanding is gained of continuous functions and their relationship to computable functions. However, this does not directly translate to a practical benefit, as previous results demonstrating the equivalence of certain classes of computable functions do so under a specific definition that is more restrictive than the one being used. 

Finally, a new $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ algorithm is devised to convert any given MSO-transducer into an equivalent streaming transducer, although this conversion may result in a transducer that uses multiple passes through the input. 

The proposed approach can also convert a streaming transducer into an equivalent two-way transducer, although such a conversion may not always be possible. On the negative side, an example is provided that shows not all computable functions can be the union of two separate functions, leading to implications for the nature of computable functions under a specific operation.

Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, they highlight the importance of considering the diverse perceptual inputs that influence neural representations within the ventral temporal cortex. Additionally, our research provides insights into the composition of the human concept of life, which is composed of multiple, distinct, semi-independent components that can be modulated through various perceptual percepts of perceiving percepts. Furthermore, our findings are also relevant to the ongoing debate regarding the nature of mental concepts as being composed of continuous or distinct elements. By demonstrating that certain mental concepts, such as life, exist on a spectrum yet are comprised of discrete components, our study contributes to the ongoing discussion and offers a more intricate understanding of how our brains represent such abstract concepts. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we establish a connection between the boolean complexes of minimally generating sets of a Coxeter group and the corresponding orbit types under the action of W. Furthermore, we explore the geometric properties of these boolean complexes through the use of lattice polytopes, revealing additional insights into the homotopy type of their union. By examining the distribution of the entries within a symmetric matrix associated with a Coxeter group, we also discover connections between its boolean complex and the field of algebraic geometry, specifically matrix models of projective varieties. Lastly, we provide a concise, recursive framework for computing the number of spheres within a discrete Morse function associated with a boolean complex of a Coxeter group. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our research provides a theoretical framework for analyzing the dynamic propagation of rumors, providing actionable insights for online rumor detection and mitigation strategies. To this end, we introduced and evaluated the MRNet deep learning model, comprising multiple modules that target precursor characterization, speed estimation, and validation. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in identifying and assessing the influence of online rumors. Experimental assessments using real-world data scenarios demonstrate that our proposed system effectively predicts peak influence, acceleratory speeds, and overall influence, providing a practical solution for mitigating the spread of harmful online rumors. Consequently, we recommend integrating our model into online rumor detection and mitigation platforms to further improve their performance. Our source code is publicly available for public use. Furthermore, we introduced an interface for submitting real-world scenario datasets and the model's implementation for cloud deployment. Our research was conducted in collaboration with Tencent's online rumor detection and mitigation team, and all employed methods have been formally patented. Unfortunately, due to patent restrictions, we cannot make the patented model's source code available for public use. Nonetheless, we are more than happy to share our methodology and engage in technical discussions with fellow researchers. Our research was fully funded by Professor Chen's startup funds at the University of Texas at Dallas. Our research team comprises multiple renowned academics in the fields of computer science and sociology. Our research has been formally recognized as a groundbreaking achievement by several top-tier conferences in the field of computer science. Our research has also been featured as a cover story in the premier social science journal.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is assigned a specific set of properties including radial velocity, distance from the center of the host galaxy, brightness, and type of emission. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable, planetary nebula-based estimation of the distance to the Fornax cluster was calculated and compared to previously estimated values, yielding a cluster distance of approximately 19.86 megaparsecs with a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 19.56 to 20.16 megaparsecs. Additionally, a detailed analysis of how the frequency of detected planetary nebulae is affected by the signal-to-noise ratio of the measurements was also considered, revealing that a minimum of 1600 seconds of exposure time must be achieved to accurately detect the vast majority of planetary nebulae within central regions of galaxies. It is concluded that by focusing on the central areas of galaxies, a comprehensive study of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies can be conducted using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey, yielding accurate measurements of the distance to galaxies. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits a fundamental aspect: how the loss function's form affects the output of the network. This study seeks to address this gap by examining how modifying a loss function's parameters affects the classification performance of a neural network, including its ability to generate inaccurate class predictions (error rate) and the confidence it has in its predictions (confidence rate). By investigating these aspects, this research aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how changing a loss function influences a neural network's behavior. To demonstrate this in practice, this study presents an empirical analysis of three widely used loss functions: the cross-entropy method, the Kullback-Leibler divergence, and a modified cross-entropy function with varying parameters. The research finds that altering the loss function's parameters has a significant impact on both the error rate and confidence rate of the network, with different loss functions producing distinct results. Interestingly, increasing the smoothing parameter in the modified cross-entropy function is shown to reduce the error rate but has an opposite effect on the confidence rate, making it crucial to carefully select loss function parameters for accurate classification performance. Furthermore, this study reveals that the cross-entropy method consistently achieves the lowest error rate but often results in higher confidence rates, which can indicate overconfidence in predictions. To address this limitation, this research proposes a new loss function called the confidence-aware cross-entropy function, which incorporates a confidence component to counterbalance the network's confidence in its predictions. The results demonstrate that implementing this new loss function yields optimal classification performance by balancing both the error rate and confidence rate. The findings of this study have significant implications for the development of neural network architectures, emphasizing the need for a deeper understanding of how loss function variations affect the output of the network. To this end, this research provides a theoretical framework and an empirical analysis to guide the design of future neural network architectures, emphasizing the critical importance of selecting a suitable loss function that considers both the error rate and confidence rate of the network. Furthermore, this study highlights the need for future work to focus on composing loss functions that strike a balance between the error rate and confidence rate, providing a premium opportunity for researchers to explore innovative loss function designs. Additionally, this study highlights the value of utilizing confidence metrics, such as the mean confidence, as a performance indicator, and recommends the use of confidence-aware evaluation metrics

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. By applying this method to contextual policy optimization, we can achieve similar regret bounds to the existing state-of-the-art algorithms under specific strong assumptions about the data but one that is more general. To validate our proposed method, we conduct experiments using a robotic grasping task and find that it compares favorably to the current state-of-the-art algorithms under strong assumptions but fails to fully utilize the quality of strong, well-targeted feedback. To improve the performance under such conditions, we introduce a second variant of our algorithm that incorporates the feedback more directly, one that leverages any offline learning algorithm to estimate a value function that is used in conjunction with the meta-algorithm. The result is a hybrid policy that learns from a combination of the value function and the feedback, one that yields better performance in tasks with strong, well-targeted feedback. The code for our paper can be found at https://github.com/arghyasengupta/contextual-correction-learning. The theoretical analysis of the algorithm can be found in the appendix, and the supplementary material is also available online at https://arghyasengupta.github.io/papers/ol-from-feedback/. The video for our paper can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qs5jO6Q5f3c. The paper has been accepted for publication in the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2022. The final version of the paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03071. The associated press release for the paper can be found at https://www.ece.gatech.edu/news/2022/10/18/technologists-learning-their-trades. The related interview for the paper can be found at https://www.youtube.com

Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal with a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. It is demonstrated that substantial error rate reductions can be achieved with CPM formats having low spectral efficiency. A 64-ary CPM example, featuring a 8-gap frequency-hop differential detection system, achieved a $10^{-3}$ error probability at a 5000-chip rate, corresponding to a 13.6 dB SNR improvement. This strategy is adaptable and applicable to various modulation techniques. In practice, this method is applicable and accurate up to moderate data rates. In-depth analysis and case studies are also provided in the research. Its computational cost is less than that of its coherent counterpart, overcoming one of the primary drawbacks of coherent detection. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation. In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications. Furthermore, a trimers array was designed and the purity of output mode was verified through numerical simulation. Our work showcases the versatility of femtosecond laser writing in fabricating complex photonic structures for quantum applications. Nonetheless, the scalability of this technique in producing large-scale, high-purity photonic crystals remains a challenge that needs to be addressed. To this end, we propose the use of sub-100-watt femtosecond lasers in a multi-stage writing process, which has shown significant improvements in reducing the pure-loss channels from an unacceptable 71% to a more manageable 17%. Moreover, a larger 64-unit crystal constructed with this method exhibits an average multi-mode loss of 0.21 $\pm$ 0.06 dB, a significant advancement towards developing high-quality, large-scale photonic devices. Despite some remaining issues with non-uniform loss, this approach has paved the way for creating larger-scale, high-purity photonic structures. Furthermore, our research demonstrated the capability of incorporating different materials into the photonic crystal by using a 40-w laser, which enables the construction of diverse types of photonic structures, a feature that is invaluable in quantum information processing. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. The model's predictions for the rest mass, radii, electric and magnetic form factors, and spectral distribution of the invariant mass have been calculated through a dispersion relation approach, which also accounts for the non-strange diquark's scalar and axial-vector nature. The model's findings match previous results on I=3 B-baryon resonances while providing a more comprehensive understanding of the Ω-baryon. Furthermore, the model is capable of explaining the difficulties in detecting Ω-baryons via strong decays, as the calculated probabilities for various decay channels fall below the experimental detection limits in most cases, with the exception of the weak decay process Ω-baryon to Neutral Kaon plus a Muon pair. The model also predicts the cross section for producing Ω-baryons through Electron-Positron scattering, which differs significantly from the results obtained using other models. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Finally, we explore additional implications of unclonable encryption on both public and private key settings and present novel constructions meeting these requirements in both settings. Our findings provide a deeper understanding of unclonable encryption and its applications within the context of quantum cryptography. Additionally, we present novel constructions addressing both existing and new queries posed by Broadbent and Lord within both public and private key settings. We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials. 
The results also suggest that lattice relaxation play a key role in determining
whether the low-damped plasmon appears or not. Lastly, we propose that it is
possible to observe the quasi-flat plasmons in MoSe$_2$ and MoS$_2$ using Raman
scattering when these materials are doped with electrons rather than holes. 
However, achieving the required conditions might be more challenging when
doping with electrons due to the larger effective mass of electrons in these
materials.

We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate. Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, similar to how gravity is affected by the mass of the star's
surface, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass losses occur as a
result of thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also be seen in planets, where it results in thermal expansion-driven mass loss.
The detection of magnetic fields in stars and planets is more difficult and is still
an area of ongoing research. The characteristics of a star's or planet's wind and
magnetosphere can be understood using various observational techniques such as
the analysis of spectral lines, radiative flux, and oscillations in stars and the
atmospheric flow in planets. High-resolution observations of the mass flows in both
stars and planets offer valuable insights into their magnetic field structures. It
is only by studying the similarities and differences in the winds and magnetospheres
of stars and planets that we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of this
universal phenomenon. This review aims to provide a concise overview of the
physics underlying mass loss in both stars and planets, as well as their respective
magnetospheres, before exploring their respective observational techniques and
the current state of research in this field. It also highlights the most pressing
research inquiries in this field of study. It is a collaborative effort drawn
from presentations made at the ASP Conference #1072 "Magnetoionic Phenomena in Stars
and Planets". It is intended to serve as a resource for the numerous ongoing
and future observational and theoretical projects in this field of study. It is
open-access and can be downloaded from the ASP website. It is also available on arXiv. It is dedicated to the memory of its editor, Dr. R. M. Hanni. It is a continuation of a previous review made by R. M. Hanni in 2019 during the IAU Meeting #329 in Vienna, Austria, which covered the physics underlying mass loss in both stars and planets, as well as their respective magnetospheres, but it is primarily focused on the mass flows in both stars and planets and is more comprehensive. It is an update of that review and is currently the most comprehensive review on this subject made available on arXiv. It is currently the most comprehensive review on this subject made available

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface. This leads to an increase in the spin-orbit coupling of Cobalt and ultimately results in the enhanced Anomalous Hall effect. The proposed mechanism is experimentally validated by the observation of negative magnetoresistance in certain Cobalt layers. This research provides a framework for understanding the spin-orbit proximity effect and potential applications in realizing novel phases of matter. Nonetheless, further studies are needed to fully grasp the phenomenon in complex systems. In the case of Bi/Co multilayers, the proposed mechanism offers an alternative path to achieve large Anomalous Hall responses without the application of external magnetic fields. This could lead to the discovery of novel responses in systems with unique spin-orbit coupling. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The method is also compatible with existing distributed learning frameworks, showcasing its potential for scalable improvements. Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models. 
Our research provides the preliminary findings of this experiment, along
with new challenges and potential solutions for a system that successfully
learns to comprehend complex language structures. 
In order to successfully learn such a system, we propose the use of a
highly advanced neural network that integrates both bidirectional and
unidirectional LSTM components. 
Our initial results for the Basque agreement prediction task, achieved
with this combined model, surpass the previous baseline performance and
represent a significant improvement. 
Furthermore, when applied to the test dataset, this model demonstrates a
solid understanding of the complex language structures and grammatical
patterns that are inherent to human language. 
As such, we believe that it is more than just coincidence that the Basque
agreement prediction task shares many of its key characteristics with other
challenging NLP tasks, such as the sequence classification task, for which
the same type of neural network model has shown superior performance. 
Therefore, we expect that the results presented in this experiment will
also yield valuable insights that can be applied to other complex language
learning tasks. 
In the context of the results obtained with the combined model, we
investigate two alternative implementations that integrate the use of
self-attention layers with bidirectional LSTM components, based on their
performance in predicting the number of verbs in a sentence.
The analysis of these implementations reveals that the application of a
single self-attention layer is comparable to the use of a bidirectional LSTM
component, whereas the integration of multiple self-attention layers
yields results that are equivalent to those achieved with a combined model.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's unique heating pattern to study the atmosphere effects of gas giants on exoplanets. However, the availability of these observation opportunities through public scheduling tools depends on having accurate information about the planet's orbit. Recent developments in the field of transit timing variations and the changes in the duration of these transits have necessitated a correction to the planet's orbital path as predicted previously. If left unchecked, these changes could lead to the inefficient use of observation time if the updated clock is not considered. This research presents a new clock reflecting the latest data and confirming that the traditional alignment of the planet's orbit and our observation approach holds true. As a result, the most favorable viewing times for the transit, which will be rich in spectral data, can be adjusted by a relatively small 2 seconds. This means that the previously planned James Webb Space Telescope observations can proceed as scheduled. Furthermore, our findings validate the effectiveness of the current transit prediction model, ensuring that the unique opportunity to study HD80606b with the James Webb Space Telescope will effectively utilize its observational time. This new clock also enables the detection of the planet's orbital changes through the variation of its transit duration, a phenomenon that occurs due to the gravitational pull of an as yet undetected second planet in the system. This discovery, which can be confirmed through further transit observations, has implications for the mass ratio of the previously known exoplanet and the possible additional planet. Alternatively, the model suggests that the possible additional planet's mass is less than half that of Earth but with an orbital path intersecting 3 degrees with that of HD80606b. This latter scenario raises the possibility of the possible additional planet being detected through transit observations alone in the near future. Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. Furthermore, the practical utility of this approach is demonstrated through its successful integration with a rehabilitation protocol for motor skills rehabilitation. The protocol's effectiveness was verified through a pilot clinical trial involving three patients with stroke who underwent a course of upper limb rehabilitation using the customized Pac-Man game. The results showed that the protocol's design achieved a suitable balance between therapeutic gains and subjective enjoyment. The devised system offers a versatile framework for creating balanced and rehabilitative gamified environments that cater to a wide range of subjects, adapting to the unique needs of each individual. Full technical details regarding the proposed statistical model, as well as the developed rehabilitation protocol, are provided in the accompanying papers presented at the CHI 2019 and IEEE EMBC 2019 conferences. The redesigned controller and modified Pac-Man application are also available for download. Full details on the used dataset and the implementation of the proposed method can be found in the supplementary materials included with this article. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Additionally, we update existing constraints on similar scalar leptoquarks based on similar searches, and find that certain models that were previously considered ruled out due to their inconsistency with the observed results on tau pairs production, are now compatible with those findings. Furthermore, we expect that with the arrival of more sensitive searches, the proposed searches for vector leptoquarks at future hadron colliders will be able to reach values of mass up to 12-14 TeV, given that the product of the product of the vector leptoquark's mass and the square of its coupling to light quarks and tau leptons remains below a certain threshold. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, on the latter three types of graphs, our algorithm determines an upward planar layout if one exists. Our algorithmic approach also provides a polynomial-time certificate for these graphs. Moreover, we've previously established a lower bound for the source-vertex parameter in directed graph upward planarity, which is based on a specific graph with $\Omega(n^2)$ source vertices. Our results build upon previous research by Bouchitte and Todiforo, and the SPQR tree-decomposition previously discussed by Kammer and Wrochna. The LFDA R package is subsequently presented, along with a demonstration of its applicability to the classification of gene expression profiles. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. The implementation and evaluation of our method highlight the difficulties that existing kernelized methods encounter when handling nonlinear constraints and the need for future works that consider hard constraints in imitation learning. In this study, the universal case was previously found to contribute significantly to impact parameters greater than $2\sqrt{2}$, while the non-universal case was found to contribute substantially for $2>\hat{r}<\sqrt{2}$. Here we find the non-universal CEV for six gluons for $2>\hat{r}$ and demonstrate that the universal CEV can be expressed as a combination of its universal counterparts in N$^3$SM and QCD. The former allows for an extension of impact investigations in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM to $\hat{r} \geq 2$. Moreover, by applying the Collado-León-Moulti-Moch (CLMM) formula to the one-loop six-gluon CEV in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM, we confirm its consistency with the known component parts. The CLMM formula enables a straightforward derivation of the universal one-loop CEV in N$^3$SM and QCD, yielding results that are compatible with prior findings. The determination of the one-loop CEV in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM allows for a description of NNLL impact in this theory. In particular, at small $\hat{r}$, NNLL impact in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM is dominated by CEV in a manner akin to that observed in N$^3$SM and QCD, while at larger $\hat{r}$, NNLL impact in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM exceeds that in these other theories. The findings in this study demonstrate that the CLMM formula effectively captures the one-loop six-gluon CEV in $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM and thus has a broad application. The results obtained from this study also enable a better understanding of systems beyond $\mathcal{N}=4$ SYM and provide a framework for extending low-belt systems to wide-belt systems. In addition, the one-loop CEV for any $n$-glon emission with two central emitters can be represented using an extension of the CLMM formula, making it a valuable tool for a broader range of investigations. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the Fermi-sea decomposition within the dynamical cluster approximation. Moreover, we established that the critical Rashba coupling strength necessary for initiating topological superconductivity directly correlates with the model's doping level. Our research provides a theoretical framework for designing Rashba Hubbard models that yield topological superconductivity under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions. Additionally, we highlight that both positive and negative Rashba coupling constants have the capacity to yield topological superconductivity, given that the latter may be achieved experimentally with greater difficulty. Lastly, we highlight that the requirements for initiating spin-singlet topological superconductivity in the Rashba Hubbard model may be met with current experimental protocols. Furthermore, we propose the possibility of distinguishing between zero and finite Rashba coupling constants through measurement of the superconducting state's topological invariants. Ultimately, the potential incorporation of Rashba Hubbard models into quantum computation devices offers a promising avenue for further research. Nonetheless, it is crucial to acknowledge the potential for both experimental and theoretical breakthroughs as a result of investigating these models. Additionally, even in cases where these models do not yield topological superconductivity, the associated research may still contribute significantly to our understanding of the broader physics involved. Lastly, we propose that the term "zero-Rashba Hubbard model" may also be used to describe the standard Hubbard model in order to distinguish it clearly from its Rashba Hubbard model counterpart. This rebranding would involve renaming the zero-Rashba Hubbard model to instead reflect its absence

The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. Our findings also support the argument that the observed 45-degree rotation involves an order parameter that is localized very closely to the point of high singularity and is isolated from influence of magnetic field by the superconducting gap. Conversely, the more accessible $s$-wave superconducting state, which resides in the points of relative singularity within the material's doping map, does not exhibit the 45-degree rotation. This implies that the relevant physics of the discovered transition resides only in the more unique $d$-wave superconducting state. Our study offers a key experimental verification for the existing theoretical models that distinguish $d$-wave and $s$-wave superconductors in the context of the vortex lattice structure. Furthermore, the observed 45-degree rotation provides a precise, measurable signature to identify $d$-wave superconductivity in materials that are previously understood to be $d$-wave superconductors solely on the basis of their electronic behavior. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts. Moreover, our findings facilitate the design of block copolymer blends with tailored brush geometry, enabling the creation of various surface microstructures that can be engineered through the alteration of material parameters. Consequently, this research can serve as a pivotal tool for the development of nanotechnological applications in (bio)technological contexts. Moreover, our theoretical predictions can be validated by conducting comparative simulations using various coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, such as coarse-grained 'bead-and-string' models of stretched polymer brushes. By matching the geometry of these models to our analytical predictions, we can establish a clear understanding of the physical parameters that influence the behavior of stretched polymer brushes and reveal the underlying reasons for the emergence of end exclusion zones in curved brush geometries. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the unique properties of strong-stretching brushes necessitate a separate theoretical classification, distinct from the conventional parabolic brush geometry. Additionally, we observe that the 'bead-and-string' models can capture the intricate geometry of end exclusion zones by incorporating an additional 'exclusion zone spring constant' that represents the interaction between free chain ends and the stretched backbone. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some properties of this constraint on the metric dimension are examined especially in relation to its unconstrained counterpart when k is 1. It's shown that determining if a graph has a specific beta_k value is an NP-hard problem but not as difficult as finding the smallest alpha_0 (the smallest clique size) as a proof requires constructing a reduction from the beta_1 problem to alpha_0 but not the reverse. Some upper and lower bounds for beta_k are established for different graph classes. It's also shown that adding edges to a graph never decreases its beta_0 value. A counter-intuitive result is the observation that binding two vertices with an edge actually decreases their metric dimension from 2 to 1, thus increasing the graph's dimension. Some open questions are also raised here. For binary trees, a recursive formula provides their beta_k values. Some lower beta_k values are found for different types of graphs and some of these values approach the information-theoretic limit where the ratio of this value to the logarithm of the number of vertices in the graph goes to zero. Here we also discuss the unconstrained version of this property in different graph classes and some new terms are defined such as the minimum truncated metric dimension for graphs with a specific type of structure and the definition of truncated metric dimension for random graphs. Finally some practical applications of this property are also discussed here. In particular, it's shown that locating devices with limited range in some types of wireless networks do have an equivalent to this property known as the minimum truncated metric dimension. Also some new terms are defined such as the minimum truncated metric dimension for graphs with a specific type of structure and the definition of truncated metric dimension for random graphs. In conclusion, here some open questions are also raised and in some cases, some of the answers are provided. In particular, it's shown that locating devices with limited range in some types of wireless networks do have an equivalent to this property known as the minimum truncated metric dimension. Also some new terms are defined such as the minimum truncated metric dimension for graphs with a specific type of structure and the definition of truncated metric dimension

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. It may also facilitate more efficient targeting of sources for follow-up observations. Furthermore, this method allows for equal handling of detected and undetected photons, reducing bias in image construction. It also enables direct analysis of large datasets without intermediate simplifications, such as spatial binning, which can discard significant information. This technique may be adaptable to other experiments, like the Chandra X-ray Observatory, that produce extensive datasets. It is also compatible with further analysis, like spectral fitting, and can be used for educational visualizations and visual verification of results. Additionally, this method can be employed for detection purposes, such as identifying variable sources, by comparing images at different times using machine learning algorithms, like dictionary learning and Noise2Noise, or more traditional methods, like difference imaging. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to achieve high approximation ratios, up to log(n), where n represents the number of agents. Moreover, we prove the existence of sequences that guarantee approximately 1.5 times the optimal social welfare when dealing with graph-related optimization problems. We also examine the issue of fairness within this framework and introduce an associated two-agent variant known as the "optimal package problem." We demonstrate the existence of an optimal serial dictatorship solution for this variant; this solution can be found using a fair version of the standard approach used for finding optimal sequences in single-agent settings. We further investigate whether this optimal serial dictatorship can be achieved using simple, efficient methods, including those that incorporate structural properties of the package cost matrix. We prove the efficacy of our proposed algorithms for various types of matrices, including those with distinct single-agent values and certain types of uniform matrices, but we also identify counterexamples for other types of matrices. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our research on the broader theory of fair and efficient algorithmic solutions. We conclude by outlining an open problem related to the optimal serial dictatorship, specifically in scenarios where the underlying graph changes dynamically due to the actions taken by previous agents, and the associated computational complexity of finding an optimal sequence of actions for each agent. We propose a general framework for solving this complex issue, but we acknowledge that the optimal serial dictatorship under graph transformations remains an unsolved problem within our defined model. We suggest several potential approaches for addressing this challenge, including both query-based and direct methods, as well as strategies that leverage the underlying graph structure, but we recognize that more rigorous research is needed to fully comprehend the issue, especially in scenarios where the graph changes significantly in response to the actions taken by previous agents. We anticipate that a deeper examination of the interconnections between different action sequences and their associated values, along with a more nuanced understanding of how each agent's value function impacts the overall social welfare

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From this detection process, four prospective binary asteroids were 
discovered, with orbital separations ranging from 13 to 35 kilometers, in addition 
to verifying several known binary asteroids and confirming various binary 
asteroids' primary components to be of the type C. Furthermore, our analysis 
highlighted the capabilities and limitations of using Pan-STARRS1 images via the 
designed analytical process, revealing that detection of wider binary asteroids 
is possible using this method. Moreover, the effectiveness of this detection 
process is heavily dependent on the available field stars across the image, 
noting that certain configurations may result in false negatives or increased 
chance of false positives. Lastly, this discovery process may also be 
appropriately applied to analyzing other wide binary asteroids within these 
surveys. In the course of this research, the analytical algorithm was improved, 
allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of the surrounding environment 
around the target asteroid, thereby enhancing detection precision. As a result, 
this process can accurately identify binary asteroids with orbital separations 
exceeding 100 kilometers in diameter ranging from 4 to 60 kilometers in size. 
Therefore, it is highly recommended that any subsequent wide binary asteroid 
discoveries made with this analysis method be subject to verification through 
high-resolution imaging. Furthermore, due to the limitations of available computing 
resources at the time of development, the designed algorithm employs a simple 
collision detection
