The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This research used a combination of linear and high-velocity shear faults to model the South Atlantic to better understand the break-up of the Gondwana supercontinent.  It also suggests that the Rio Grande Rift in North America, which occurred between 1070 and 1010 Ma, and the East African Rift System, which began around 30 Ma, both shared similar multi-velocity, multi-directional extension history.  This implies this type of extension history may be a common feature of continental rifting.  It may also result in diverse, intricate patterns of continental break-up and multiple, non-conformable rift phases which could all occur at the same time, or over a large break-up period as seen in the South Atlantic.  It also means that break-up patterns and styles may be influenced not just with strain accumulation but also with the velocity and direction of extension. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential for a Dungeon Master to serve as a stress-tested example of an AI guided by a set of objectives, which can be leveraged to explore a broader range of controlled conversation scenarios. Our findings also suggest that middle-ground approaches between a purely data-driven and a fully intentional Dungeon Master produce the most favorable results. These outcomes, coupled with a detailed analysis of a theory-of-mind-driven model, contribute valuable insights to the development of guided conversation AIs. Our code and the G4C dataset are openly available for use in future research studies. By expanding the scope of controlled conversation beyond straightforward goal-oriented settings, we introduce a new, more intricate framework that accounts for multiple participants with distinct identities, world knowledge, and shared context, which we refer to as complex goal-oriented conversation scenarios. This new framework holds significant value for developing AIs that can engage in natural, human-like conversations and provide more sophisticated and realistic virtual game worlds. Additionally, we outline several unexplored research questions and potential applications related to the G4C challenge. Furthermore, to validate the authenticity of D&D conversations within our dataset, we put together a panel of seasoned Dungeon Masters, who verified that the dialogue contained within the dataset accurately reflects actual D&D conversations. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. The DISCO framework's efficiency is further evidenced by the model's capacity to generate a vast pool of counterfactual data at a minimal additional cost when compared to supervised methods. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes like van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This unique rotation domain provides clear evidence of the remote epitaxial process and presents a challenge to achieving controlled film quality due to various possible alignments, leading to a need for precise process conditions. A solution was found in a modified substrate interface achieved through the use of a thin pinholey graphene layer, leading to a precise 90 degree rotated superstructure similar to that found on traditional sulfide substrates. This breakthrough offers a path for controlled epitaxial growth through either remote, pinhole, or van der Waals processes, depending on the substrate conditions, and demonstrates the potential of using imperfect graphene substrates even with modern Heusler film deposition methods. As a result of this research, highly conducting and magnetizable films were produced through the van der Waals process on pinholey graphene substrates, overcoming previous limitations of remote epitaxy where the incorporation of impurities would ruin the film's conductivity. This finding has significant implications for the utilization of Heusler compounds in spintronics and other electronic applications. Additionally, this study demonstrates the intricacies involved in achieving controlled film growth through different processes and the need for further investigation into the intricate relationships between surface and interface phenomena in epitaxial research. Furthermore, it highlights the value of experimental data in guiding theoretical concepts, as the unique rotation domain in this study initially suggested a unique structure but was later found to be a challenge of alignment, ultimately resolved through the modification of the graphene substrate and the resulting change from remote to van der Waals epitaxy. This research offers a realization of the potential of Heusler compounds in spintronics and other applications and provides a path for the controlled growth of such materials through different processes. As such, it has significant implications for the field of materials science and may pave the way for a deeper understanding of the phenomena involved in epitaxial research. It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres

under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.

this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. Our analysis reveals that the von Neumann and Shannon entropies exhibit similar linear dependencies on the chemical potential, whereas the thermodynamic potential exhibits a quadratic dependence on these variables. Furthermore, both the entropy and thermodynamic potential display asymmetric dependencies on the signs of the chemical potential, a distinctive characteristic stemming from the antiparticle nature of the Majorana fermion. This asymmetric response may be exploited to distinguish Majorana fermions from their fermionic counterparts in experiments that involve varying the chemical potential. In the case of a linear external potential, we find that the asymptotic behavior of the thermodynamic potential resembles that of a Fermi gas, albeit with a critical dependence on the particle's Compton wavelength and the strength of the external potential. This research provides a theoretical framework for identifying the unique properties of Majorana fermions and the implications of their quasiclassical behavior in the presence of an external linear potential. Lastly, we outline the manner in which this understanding can be applied to experimental searches for the detection of Majorana fermions. Additionally, we discuss the scope for generalizing this theory to accommodate nonlinear external potentials and interacting Majorana fermions. Our analysis offers a comprehensive exploration of the statistical properties of linear Majorana fermions and provides a theoretical framework for their investigation. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. In the case of experiments, the extraction of topological features from interferometric patterns proves complicated, while theoretically, a more straightforward connection between momentum space and real space is needed. Leveraging our understanding of topological nodal lines, we anticipate the design of new artificial materials that can harbor non-Abelian charges in momentum space, enabling the observation of unique real-space phenomena. In conclusion, topological nodal lines are expected to serve as a vital component in the development of cutting-edge technology that exploits the unique interplay between momentum and real spaces. Consequently, artificial materials providing a direct connection between these spaces will prove invaluable. Nonetheless, the knowledge gained from studying topological nodal lines in these systems is already beginning to pay dividends in our pursuit of innovative technology. Finally, we propose that the term "topological nodal lines" be used to describe one-dimensional singularities in momentum space accompanied by robust non-Abelian charges in the associated Berry curvature monopoles and Zekova et al.'s recent findings in optical waveguide networks constitute substantial evidence of this concept's existence. Moreover, we highlight the broader implications of topological nodal lines for our understanding of the electronic and optical properties of materials. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, a deep learning-based fast solver is used to predict flow velocities based on the riverbed profile and external influencing factors such as wind and tidal patterns. This approach facilitates the rapid estimation of flow velocities from flow measurements, riverbed profiles, and environmental factors, an improvement over conventional methods which require time-consuming and expensive riverbed measurements. Experimental results show that the proposed method effectively predicts flow velocities in both controlled and real-world scenarios. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical measurements, with a notable temperature difference of up to 30 K found. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. Furthermore, this study highlights the practical utility of MRI as a noninvasive tool for monitoring the temperature distribution within these systems. The developed technique's usefulness is demonstrated through its application to the particular case of an air-stream flowing through a cylindrical packed bed, though it can be applied broadly to various types of reactive gas-solid systems. The presented results suggest that MRI can effectively identify the intricate flow patterns and mixing irregularities that arise due to the formation of recirculating flow regions within packed beds. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization for certain quasiperiodic arrangements at specific symmetry points, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, we observed this occurrence in other one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, suggesting a general applicability of this phenomenon. Moreover, we suggest that delocalization in these systems could be achieved experimentally using a technique called inverse quasiperiodic construction. Overall, our research provides a new understanding of the delocalization transitions that occur in one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely integrates parallel reading and writing functionalities via a separate axis interface, setting it apart from prior adaptations of the Memory Access Instruction Set Architecture (MAISARCH) proposal. Furthermore, our content-addressable parallel processor includes an attached memory block, utilizing a partial sector reconfiguration to enhance performance by a factor of up to 13 times when compared to conventional systems. Moreover, a key feature of our content-addressable parallel processor is its ability to efficiently support the MAISARCH architecture, a proposed reconfigurable architecture that outperforms the Field Programmable Gate Array by a factor of up to 5 times in benchmark applications. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the proposed method's ability to learn from only a single positive training example in each event category has been proven through a comprehensive evaluation. This includes a qualitative analysis of the results obtained by the system in real-world scenarios, the analysis of parameters and the comparison with the traditional neural network. This comparison indicates that the proposed system provides a more efficient solution by reducing the number of required positive training samples by three orders of magnitude. This level of efficiency in learning from a single positive training sample in each event category makes the system highly suitable for the rapid development of applications in cross-domain fake news detection. This is the first study on the application of neural program induction in the context of multi-modal fake news detection. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Here, $S$ denotes the real numbers with a periodicity $H$ added, and $\kappa$ and $\alpha$ are both positive constants. The main objective is to investigate the local well-posedness of this transport equation in the case where $\alpha$ is less than or equal to one, particularly focusing on the development of singularities and the possible formation of shocks. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constituted stochastic process. We present the general formula for the AoI distribution and derive an explicit expression for geometrically distributed service times. A comparison between discrete and continuous AoI is provided, including mean values for the M/M/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that the standard queueing theory is capable of analyzing the discrete AoI, outperforming previously proposed methods for continuous time systems. Ultimately, this research offers a versatile approach for evaluating AoI in various discrete-time scenarios. Finally, we examine the optimal control of the Bernoulli/G/1/1 queue's sampling policy to minimize AoI, but this aspect of the problem requires further investigation. In contrast, the geometric/B/1/1 queue can be optimally controlled using standard queueing theory techniques, thereby reducing AoI to a rate monotone function of the queue length. This research provides a groundbreaking starting point for the investigation of discrete-time AoI systems. Finally, we offer some concluding thoughts on this subject. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. In the context of our specific example, we could utilize this insight to enhance the efficiency of our solver by transforming the problem into a bi-partite system, thereby utilizing a much smaller action space and leading to a substantial reduction in errors. Our approach serves as a model for a broader methodology that can be applied to other complex systems and nonlinear dynamical systems, and we anticipate that our research will inspire others to explore similar relationships between the statistical interactions, structure, and graph neural network representations of such systems. In the accompanying supplementary materials, we provide a step-by-step guide on how to set up and train the graph neural network, as well as a detailed explanation of the key metrics used in our evaluations. In the context of our specific example, we successfully solved a 50-node setup and achieved a marginal likelihood of -46.96 for the solved instance, with a corresponding error of 0.13. In comparison to traditional message passing algorithms, our graph neural network-based solution delivered a substantial improvement in accuracy. In comparative evaluations against two alternative configurations, our approach demonstrated a clear advantage in terms of convergence speed, solution quality, and consistency. Lastly, we included a detailed discussion on future research directions and potential areas for further exploration. In the field of graph neural networks, understanding the dynamics and underlying structure of complex systems with nonlinear interactions holds immense value, and we believe that our research will contribute meaningfully to this objective. Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through numerical experiments and real-world applications, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods. Notably, our proposed methods outperformed existing methods in unsupervised feature extraction, while also showing significant improvement in supervised feature extraction, particularly for large dimensionality reductions. Our research's unique aspect is the integrated exploration of both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques using contrastive learning. The framework's and its method's theoretical analysis and practical applications are also provided. Furthermore, three open-source codes are also provided with our framework and its methods, capable of handling large-scale data and robust dimensionality reductions. The framework's and its method's superiority is further confirmed by results obtained using large-scale datasets and real-world applications. Additionally, the research provides the benchmark for future dimensionality reduction techniques using contrastive learning. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the optical centers aligned but with varying angles in the direction of gravity. Four representative existing methods and four proposed novel approaches have been tested, with the novel methods demonstrating enhanced performance and accuracy. Notably, one of the proposed methods achieves accurate results even when the assumed prior related to gravity is violated, with minimal computational requirements. Empirical evidence, in the form of experiments using synthetic and real data, supports the effectiveness of the proposed methods. Two of the proposed methods have been integrated into a demonstration application, showcasing their practical utility. The source code of the proposed methods has been made publicly available for further exploration and improvement. The demonstration of the application's effectiveness, along with the source code, is presented at https://github.com/panostitch/rotating-stitching-demo.html. The challenges and limitations of the proposed methods, along with potential avenues for further research, are also discussed. The novel approaches can serve as a starting point for exploring other possible configurations of camera rotations that could be addressed through panoramic stitching. The testing and evaluation of the proposed methods have highlighted several key metrics for assessing the performance of panoramic stitching methods, including the impact of gravity on camera rotations. The development of the proposed methods has also involved a formalization of the problem of panoramic stitching from rotating cameras, along with a discussion of possible applications and potential use cases. This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In particular, this study demonstrates the utility of its data-driven approach for modeling complex brain dynamics underlying neurological disorders. Furthermore, the model showcases how computational modeling can harness the insights provided by animal models of disease, thereby accelerating the translation of laboratory findings into potential treatments. In conclusion, our research highlights the beneficial collaboration between abductive reasoning and biophysical brain modeling to address the intricacies of neurological disorders. As a landmark achievement in this regard, this study sets a precedent for a broader range of computational modeling applications in neuroscience. By applying the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope, our results show that we can derive key physical properties and line ratios through spectral fitting, while also obtaining ionized gas maps and spatially resolved spectra. Our data were collected over multiple observing runs and showed a high consistency, with a median of ~10 minutes per observation. To determine the ionized gas mapping accuracy, we conducted mock analyses on simulated data, resulting in <5% error in line ratio measurements and ~1"2" mapping accuracy. By comparing our results with previous narrow-band imaging, we verified that our IFU observations captured the central ionized gas regions effectively. Additionally, our observations revealed diverse ionized gas structures across the 9 U/LIRGs. Through visual inspections of three-dimensional data, we found evidence of multiple-outflow structures in two galaxies (AR0230 at z=0.033 and AR0231 at z=0.037), while the remaining seven galaxies exhibited single-outflow patterns. Lastly, we found that the line ratios and physical properties derived from spectral fitting showed a good agreement with those from other methods, while also successfully comparing our results with previous observations of the same targets. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. O(h^2)) convergence can be achieved for certain monotone and convex functions, and a significant improvement in accuracy is demonstrated for linear functions. The method is particularly effective for linear functions, where the error is essentially zero. In contrast, the conventional piecewise linear interpolation method yields an O(h) convergence rate for linear functions. In essence, the new interpolation function offers a more precise approximation of linear functions than the conventional method. A new statistics-based method is introduced to analyze the turnaround points of galaxy clusters within $f(R)$ gravity models that incorporate massive neutrinos. The models are categorized into five groups: $\Lambda$CDM with zero-neutrino mass, six individual $f(R)$ models with zero-neutrino mass, 32 combinations of four $f(R)$ models including three ranges of massive neutrino densities. The ultimate goal is to evaluate the impact of massive neutrinos within $f(R)$ models on the turnaround points of galaxy clusters. The turnaround radii are derived from cluster profiles constructed using the Rockstar algorithm, and a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is performed to compare the results. The test indicates that the neutrino density affects the turnaround radii, especially in larger clusters. Additionally, a 10% increase in neutrino density reduces the turnaround radii by 0.03$^{+0.02}_{-0.03}$ in $f(R)$ models, including $\Lambda$CDM. Formulas are presented to describe the relationship between the neutrino density and turnaround radii in $f(R)$ models. The findings are relevant to the estimation of cluster masses based on the turnaround radii and densities. The models that best match observational data according to a cluster lensing analysis are identified, and the results demonstrate agreement with the standard $\Lambda$CDM model within a 2$\sigma$ confidence interval. The research provides formulas that can be utilized in conjunction with $\Lambda$CDM-based mass estimators to determine cluster masses in a more accurate manner. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our research also highlights the importance of examining the entanglement within individual Jaynes-Cummings systems before determining the multipartite entanglement of a state. In the context of quantum field theory, our results demonstrate that the Jaynes-Cummings model serves as a legitimate representation of genuine multipartite entanglement. Lastly, our work introduces a novel multipartite entanglement criterion: the non-negative character of a specific symmetric matrix. This criterion holds particular significance for diparte systems consisting of two qudits. Our analysis indicates that the unique ability to create tripartite entanglement does not extend to the ability to create quadrupartite entanglement. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among thermodynamic variables upon varying the monopole charge. Moreover, we observe that the shadow radius can serve as an indicator for phase transition types, including first-order, second-order, or even phase transitions mediated by an instability point. These findings hold significance for the study of non-linear, charged AdS black holes, shedding light on the interplay between their thermodynamic properties and gravitational electromagnetic fields. Additionally, the proposed framework can be applied to other phase transition scenarios, revealing that the shadow radius is a valuable tool for distinguishing between different phases of black hole matter. Furthermore, this research showcases the applicability of shadow physics as a means to explore a black hole's internal structure, making it pertinent to the study of black hole physics. In the case of the nonlinear, charged AdS black hole, the proposed method enables a deeper understanding of how gravitational electromagnetic fields impact its thermodynamic properties. A new perspective on the relationship between a black hole's thermodynamic properties and its internal structure is also established through the analysis of its shadow. The results presented demonstrate that a black hole's behavior is intricately linked to its nonlinear, charged properties, emphasizing the importance of considering the nonlinear interaction between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics. The research further highlights the utility of shadow physics in the study of black hole physics, providing a new approach for investigating a black hole's internal structure and its phase transition dynamics. The findings of this study are relevant to a broader context of black hole physics, addressing an overarching question of how the nonlinear interaction between electromagnetic fields affects a black hole's thermodynamic properties and its internal structure. The research offers a comprehensive insight into the complex relationship between a black hole's nonlinear, charged properties and its shadow, underscoring the significance of shadow physics in the study of black hole physics. The results presented can be applied to a more in-depth analysis of the nonlinear, charged AdS black hole, shedding light on the behavior of its thermodynamic variables and its internal structure. Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. As a result, we show that quantum states generated through parametric amplification, a well-known process, can exhibit entanglement and synchronization, and that these phenomena leave distinctive signatures in the momentum tomograms. Furthermore, we illustrate that the pattern of these tomograms can be understood through the application of a simple transformation to the Wigner function in its transformation domain. Ultimately, this approach provides a practical means of confirming the non-classical properties of light states without the need for comprehensive state reconstruction. Additionally, this approach can be implemented experimentally using standard amplification processes and standard state reconstruction techniques. In practice, this could involve replacing the usual procedure for reconstructing a quantum state with a quicker experimental verification of the non-classical properties of light, making it a more feasible task. In the case of three-mode states, the situation is more complex, and the reflection of quantum synchronization in optical tomograms needs to be confirmed. Finally, we propose a promising approach for verifying the reflection of quantum synchronization in three-mode states, but leave the detailed analysis of this instance for future consideration. In the case of amplification processes, our approach allows for the confirmation of the reflection of quantum synchronization through the application of a specific unitary transformation to the amplification process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach is highly versatile, enabling a wide range of applications, including the evaluation of the performance of quantum amplifiers, the confirmation of the reflection of quantum synchronization in multi-mode states, and the analysis of the reflection of entanglement in continuous-variable teleportation. In conclusion, we have successfully demonstrated that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization leave distinctive signatures in optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue models have achieved significant breakthroughs.
Despite this, developing a scalable chat system poses a major challenge due to
the requirement for substantial human-human dialogue data to support features
like persona, style, or safety. To tackle this issue, our work aims to introduce
role constraints to open-domain dialogue systems that enable them to maintain user
roles throughout the conversation. By incorporating role information, these
systems can engage in more natural, coherent, and context-aware conversations.
To build a role-aware dialogue system efficiently, we propose a framework that
leverages pre-trained language models in a multi-task setting, combining both
fine-tuning and generation tasks. By applying this framework to a 1 billion
parameter model, we achieved notable results and discovered that incorporating
role information enhanced the diversity of generated text, while also reducing
unnecessary repetitions and improving the overall coherence of the generated
dialogue. Furthermore, our model excelled in maintaining user roles, producing
more natural and fluent language that closely mimicked human conversation. We
also found that incorporating style guidelines via reverse knowledge graph
reasoning contributed to a more significant improvement in style similarity than
simply using a generator model would have. Additionally, our model showed
robustness in handling a range of open-domain topics and unexpected questions
and topics were also effectively handled by the model. The code for the proposed
framework has been made publicly available on GitHub, and the results of our
experiments can be found in the appended tables and figures. Ultimately, our
research demonstrates that open-domain dialogue systems with role constraints can
be built using large language models, and we anticipate the potential applications
of this technology to contribute significantly to various areas such as customer
service, virtual assistants, and emotional support systems. Furthermore, the
efforts made to create a dataset with role information, though initially made for
this project, may also be of use to other researchers working on open-domain
dialogue datasets. Additionally, the proposed approach to managing user roles
throughout conversations may be applied to other contexts where changes in user
roles need to be maintained, and our results provide a foundation for further
experiments and adaptations of this type of research. Moreover, though our model
is primarily focused on text-based conversations, the role-aware approach may be
applied to other types of interactions that involve user roles, and our work may
also be seen as an early step in creating systems that can manage complex
conversations involving multiple users and roles

streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance

However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. Our approach is algorithmically implementable and, for a given temperature or time point, involves a straightforward iterative method to obtain the required objects. Moreover, at no additional cost is the memory footprint of the description of the system size increased with our approach. Our method is particularly relevant as it overcomes the conventional limitations of tensor network algorithms in dealing with systems at low temperatures or late time points. Our results also highlight the potential of the objects we introduce to serve as a local approximation to matrix product operators, demonstrating an effective way to extract relevant physical information from a system. Our approach is highly versatile and can be readily applied across diverse models and situations. Additionally, we introduce a novel time-evolution algorithm that is an extremely efficient way of utilizing tensor network methods for studying time-dependent situations. This new algorithm allows the application of the time-evolution operator in a way that local updates resemble conventional tensor network simulations, resulting in a significant speed-up compared to conventional techniques. With this method, we are able to simulate the non-equilibrium dynamics of a spin chain for an unprecedented time elapsed in reasonable computational time on a personal computer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the application of an inhomogeneous time-evolution operator, which changes at different points in the system, may lead to unique and intriguing phenomena in the time-evolved behavior of quantum systems. Our approach has the ability to efficiently model multi-quench scenarios where the application of an external influence varies over time for different points in the system. We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. To complement our research, we introduce a novel application involving the analysis of smooth polynomial maps between multi-dimensional spaces. This involves examining how the properties of underlying surfaces impact the behavior of these maps, especially in regards to the formation of ultimately irreducible polynomials resulting from the composition of two compatible polynomials. Our findings are then illustrated through the examination of a specific example, a 4-dimensional space defined by a quartic polynomial with non-overlapping components. Our calculations demonstrate that this space meets all the requirements for being an example of an UIP variety, and our work also identifies a connection between this space and the field of number theory. Specifically, we establish that the integers within this space consist of all the integers within a specific range, providing a new proof for a previously known theorem. Additionally, our work enables us to create a general formula for counting the number of such integers within any given range. This formula can be further simplified to count the number of perfect powers within any given range, and a special case of this count is shown to be equivalent to a well-known problem in number theory. Our calculations also predict an optimal exponent for a specific conjecture related to the distribution of primes, and provide an alternative proof for a previously known result in algebraic geometry. Our work on the development of a decoupling theory for smooth surfaces also enables us to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces for approximation and decoupling purposes. Our work on the application front identifies an important connection between the problem of finding optimal solutions to a system of polynomial equations and the problem of bounding the magnitude of the entries of the inverse matrix. The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. Violations of this principle would appear as specific frequencies related to the satellite's movement. This experiment was designed to minimize potential errors at these critical frequencies. Unforeseen acceleration fluctuations known as glitches can impact test mass acceleration readings, likely caused by cracks in the satellite's protective layer. These events, which are relatively short-lived, have an intrinsic randomness to them. While they seem random, the time of their occurrence is influenced by the satellite's orbital and spinning cycles. It is crucial to understand the effect glitches have on the principle test, but the current data isn't sufficient for a conclusive determination. As a result, the most reliable approach to minimize their influence is to exclude data from periods with detected glitches. By doing so, the experiment's ability to detect a violation of the weak equivalence principle by $\chi=os^4\cdot 5.8\times 10^{-20}$ is maintained. It is essential to account for the possibility that glitches could impede future similar tests in space. In order to adequately interpret the outcomes of such experiments, it is essential to collect information on the frequency and characteristics of acceleration fluctuations similar to glitches. This is especially important as future tests in space are designed with increasing sensitivity to the principles being tested. Furthermore, the approach presented in this paper can be applied to evaluating data from other gravitational physics experiments that involve acceleration measurements. In such experiments, it is essential to be aware of any sudden, short-lived acceleration fluctuations that could impede the detection of the subtle effects being searched for. It is also important to consider that the specific statistics and analysis methods used in this study are unique to the Microscope mission. The approach presented in this paper is currently the most effective way to handle the challenges posed by glitches in this experiment; however, the development of more robust statistical methods is ongoing. As a result, future tests of the weak equivalence principle in space will employ missions that utilize not only the approach discussed in this paper but also other, more advanced statistical analysis methods. These future missions are designed to detect a violation of the weak equivalence principle at a fraction of the threshold achieved by the Microscope mission. We demonstrate analytically that the position of the dimer varies based on the angle between the particles and accumulates either at areas with high activity levels or low activity levels. This corresponds to chemotaxis and antichemotaxis respectively. Some dimer configurations display chemotactic and antichemotactic properties, with their behavior determined by the activity gradient strength. A coarsely detailed approach helps to generate an effective potential, used in our analysis to create a phase diagram. This diagram classifies dimer configurations based on their tactic behavior and also indicates how some dimers can maintain direction and achieve greater persistence in motion. This study provides valuable insights into the design of autonomous, responsive colloidal systems that can navigate according to varying activity levels in their environment. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of angular structure in such systems, emphasizing its role in achieving enhanced persistence without the need for additional control mechanisms. This knowledge can be applied to enhance the performance of autonomous soft robots in the detection and removal of toxic particles in viscous fluids. It suggests that cell movement may be influenced by spatial gradients of different molecular activities, providing a new perspective for future scientific investigation. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$. This modification leads to a more pronounced discrepancy between the variational approach and lattice QCD's $xG(x)$ values at very small $x$. Systematic approaches for dealing with infrared renormalons in variational calculations are discussed, and our analysis suggests that the estimated $x$-dependent root mean square (RMS) values for the impact factor $F_{\rm dip}$ are actually $\sim 2.5$ times larger than they should be. As a result, we derive more accurate RMS values for $xG(x)$ and $F_{\rm dip}$ in proportion to their integral, which is a useful measure often employed in beam dump experiments' sensitivity evaluations. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of considering the variance of impact factors in such experiments, as even relatively small changes in RMS values can result in significant variations in the predicted signals in searches for jet production in beam dump experiments. Ongoing and future experiments, such as HSF at the LHC, J-PET, BEPCII, Frascati, and the future $e^+e^-$ colliders, such as CEPC, ILC, CLIC, and TLHF, will have sufficient sensitivity to the underlying physics that influences $xG(x)$ and $F_{\rm dip}$ and can accurately determine the appropriate scale for the proportionality constant in $xG(x)\propto x^{-0.5}$, which is a fundamental aspect of nonlinear small-x physics. Additionally, our study underscores the importance of addressing infrared renormalons in a systematic manner to ensure accurate and reliable conclusions from variational approach calculations. On a separate note, we propose a straightforward method for directly determining the variance of the impact factor $F_{\rm dip}$ through jet infrared and collinear safe observables in fixed-target and collider experiments. This approach allows for the precise calculation of $xG(x)$ and $F_{\rm dip}$ without relying on the variational approach. In the case of $xG(x)$, our method yields results that are in line with lattice QCD

We demonstrate that this critical transition occurs roughly around the tree's degree. Furthermore, the frog model's behavior on a d-ary tree can be analyzed using random walk techniques, particularly by viewing frogs as markers on the walk. We establish that the critical transition occurs precisely at degree d through a percolation-based approach, while a second, less direct method applies to cases where d is infinite. Additionally, we explore how the critical transition is influenced by the frog population. When the population is low, a smaller degree of transitivity is sufficient for recurrence. In contrast, a much higher degree of transitivity is required for recurrence when the population is high. The frog model's behavior on a randomly generated random graph does not share the same level of transitivity as its tree-based counterpart. As a result, a much more complex analysis is necessary to determine its critical density. With this analysis, we find the critical density for this type of graph to be equal to its average degree. Due to the significant differences between these types of graphs, the term "degree of the tree" is used instead of "degree of the graph." When the graph is a regular graph, this means its degree will be the number of edges each vertex has. However, this term is also applicable to graphs that are not regular graphs. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to prioritize learning from data with significant margins. This allows a model to replicate the performance of the black-box network. When access to the original data isn't possible, a pseudo-data set is created by generating samples with varying margin characteristics, which are then used to learn a model that mimics the black-box network's decisions. Our proposed method is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets, showing it achieves near-original performance when compared to traditional knowledge distillation methods. Furthermore, it enables knowledge distillation in scenarios previously considered infeasible, such as compressing deep convolutional neural networks on small image classification tasks. The distilled models also exhibit improved robustness to perturbations. The proposed method's advantages are demonstrated through various experiments, highlighting its potential as a versatile and effective knowledge distillation approach. The source code for the proposed method is publicly available on GitHub, alongside pre-distilled models on the Knowledge Distillation Repository. The evaluation results and the models used in this study are also hosted on GitHub, enabling Reproducibility. The model's official webpage is available at this link: https://knowledge-distillation.github.io/. The model has been formally published in the IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems journal. Additionally, an extended version of this study was presented at the 2021 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. The presentation slides for this conference are available on SlideShare. Despite the proposed method by Stanley to construct distributive lattices from their join irreducibles, determining all join irreducible submodules of a given module is not a straightforward task. However, for modules that have no module composition multiplicities, we present an alternative approach based on the composition factors, drawing on the information about submodules and their lattices. Given input submodules that encompass all factors and are readily lattice-structure-known, we can reconstruct the lattice of submodules of the given module. The process is particularly demonstrated using specific modules associated with a family of Lie superalgebras, specifically for modules $M(\gl_n)$, for the $\osp(3,2)$, showing that their lattice structure matches that of extended free distributive lattices of rank 3, when $n$ is two or more. Furthermore, we establish that for $\osp(2,2)$, the lattice of submodules of $M(\gl_3)$ contains a chain of length eight. This method is also applicable to modules derived from highest weight modules with distinct weights. Additionally, we verify that for $\osp(3,2)$ and $\osp(2,2)$, all modules of highest weight have no module composition multiplicities. Furthermore, we also consider modules with distinct weights, verifying that for these Lie superalgebras, the lattice of submodules of any module with no module composition multiplicities can be constructed from its composition factors. The proposed method is not limited to these specific Lie superalgebras, rather it holds the potential to be applicable across a broader family of algebras and modules. A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. SGR is found to be NP-complete. Research into SGR is conducted, and comparisons of computational complexities are made across various graph types, including the derivation of efficient algorithms, NP-completeness proofs, and preliminary results on parameterized complexity, which provide insight into the complexity of SG, particularly in chordal graphs. Lastly, a generalization of SGR, titled Multiple Strong Geodetic, is introduced and conjectured to be NP-complete. Furthermore, the terminology Used: A geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ is a strongest geodetic subset. An SGR instance can be transformed into a nearest neighbor exchange (NNE) problem, which involves determining if a given set of points can be covered by unique closest neighbors, a problem shown to be equivalent to SG. This equivalence enables the derivation of an efficient algorithm for some SGR instances, including those with certain types of trees and some partial grids. However, in cases where the vertex subset forms a line or a cycle, an SGR instance can be solved by checking a certain condition, or in some cases, being reducible to a 2-dimensional NNE. In graphs with low treewidth, an SGR instance can be solved by a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm, although the exact time complexity needs further determination, and thus, the exact time complexity of an SG instance in graphs with low treewidth remains undetermined. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space that results in a reduced set of actionable actions, thus making policy learning more manageable. This is followed by Imitation Learning with Reduced Action Space (IL-RA), a direct method that utilizes this model to derive a reduced action space based on the expert data, with positive results shown through various experiments. The findings indicate that when the action space is small, performance on par with traditional imitation learning methods can be achieved. Moreover, the approach surpasses these methods significantly when the action space is large, demonstrating the potential of leveraging suboptimal data in imitation learning. The code for the paper can be found at https://github.com/AYASHIJ/trail. The theoretical analysis and the experiments for single-task and multitask learning are presented in Appendix A and B respectively. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our proposed Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Notably, our approach achieves notable gains in complex, partially observable tasks using the A3C method, while also demonstrating robust performance using simpler algorithms like Q-learning in both simple and complex domains. The code for our research is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.co.uk/Chengdong-SD/CoImitationLearning for which we are grateful to the generous support from Google Colab. Our paper's key contributions are also reflected in a corresponding video presentation available at https://youtu.be/igJ03qH4QoA. Our Co-Imitation Learning framework can be particularly beneficial for exploring the optimal policy across multiple continuous action spaces, a problem to which we apply our solution successfully. Moreover, our approach can be seamlessly extended to support a diverse range of value function estimation methods, a key advantage that we successfully demonstrate. The cumulative achievements of our research are summarized in our paper's accompanying slide presentation available at https://github.com/Chengdong-SD/CoImitationLearning/blob/main/Slides.pdf. This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces. Additionally, the relationship between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces under retraction is acknowledged as a bijective correspondence that preserves the topological structure. Furthermore, upper power spaces of discrete QFS-spaces correspond to the space of FS-spaces on a given set, while upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to the space of functions that have finite support, thereby establishing an additional correspondence between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces. Last, the category of continuous QFS-spaces with quasicontinuous maps forms a topological space when equipped with the compact-open topology. This research extends previous findings by providing a categorical approach to understanding the relationship between FS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Finally, the concept of compactness in topological spaces is redefined using quasicontinuous maps, demonstrating its equivalence to the traditional definition, and further highlights the connection between quasicontinuous maps and the compact-open topology. This shows that the relationship between QFS-spaces and FS-spaces is a categorical correspondence that preserves the topological structure. The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. At the aggregate level, our findings show a notable increase in online polarization over time, a trend that is particularly pronounced during election seasons. Additionally, we've investigated the role of user loyalty in online polarization and discovered that users' tendency to consistently visit the same news sources can sometimes counter the influence of exposure to opposing viewpoints. To conclude, we explore the broader implications of our research for understanding online polarization and potential strategies for mitigating the Web's polarizing effects. Furthermore, to facilitate further exploration, we've made the underlying data underlying our studies available for download. In the context of online polarization, it is essential to differentiate between two distinct phenomena: the intentional actions of users and the unintentional influence of algorithms that shape online environments. Sustained attention to both aspects is crucial to developing effective solutions. At their core, both phenomena are underpinned by users' desire to engage with content that resonates with their viewpoints, a sentiment that is exemplified through the practice of loyally supporting favorite sports teams. This shared human experience holds important insights that can be leveraged by both designers of technology and solution creators that aim to address online polarization. To address this phenomenon, it might be beneficial to draw from the experience of algorithmic recommenders that operate in domains that are free from the influence of partisan pressures. In such domains, the most common challenges and issues of online polarization are different, such as dealing with cold start problems, information overload, and the formation of filter bubbles. In contrast to the Web's polarization-centric environment, in these domains the focus is on addressing the underlying causes of online polarization, like the concentration of influence, the amplification of biases, and the lack of diversity. We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. Additionally, we demonstrate that V's word problem has a recursive property in relation to the Morita-Thom conjecture's proposed solution. We explore various generator-based variations of V's word problem and establish the time complexity for some of these variations. Lastly, we consider the implications of these findings on linear time complexity for V's word problem. We also establish an indirect connection between the time complexity of V's word problem and the time complexity of solving left-normalized braids via a height-reducing procedure. We conclude by discussing the potential for further analysis of V's word problem utilizing combinatorial metrics such as edit distance. We define a specific variant of stacked strings, which we term 'quasi-stacked strings', and prove that the complement of quasi-stacked strings has a generator-based variation equivalent to V's word problem. We also outline a method for reducing quasi-stacked strings to stacked strings, and as a result, the complement of stacked strings also has a generator-based variation equivalent to V's word problem. Finally, we outline an approach to determining whether a given quasi-stacked string belongs to the complement of quasi-stacked strings, which would imply a deterministic linear time complexity for solving V's word problem. However, this approach relies on solving the Morita-Thom conjecture's proposed solution recursively, which would imply a recursive time complexity for solving V's word problem. We discuss how this approach can be generalized to determine whether a given stacked string belongs to the complement of stacked strings, which would imply a deterministic linear time complexity for solving V's word problem. However, this would require solving the Morita-Thom conjecture's proposed solution for each nested bracket set, which would imply a recursive time complexity for solving V's word problem. Therefore, while this approach can potentially yield a linear time complexity for solving V's word problem, it remains speculative and requires further verification. We outline a protocol for verifying this approach by testing whether a given string belongs to the complement of quasi-stacked strings, which could potentially validate the recent Lehnert-Schweitzer proof

By assuming that a biharmonic hypersurface within the Euclidean space has type (A) and is characterized by the recurrent curvature operator, we are able to establish a key theorem. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, models which are normally excluded by electron beam polarization experiments become viable. Furthermore, we find that a significant portion of the accessible axion parameter space can be probed by the beam polarization experiments in the best case scenario, however, this access is limited to a small range of masses and depends heavily on the value of the axion decay constant. In addition, we find that the addition of a sterile neutrino with a mass within the dark matter range and a small mixing angle avoids the constraints imposed by short baseline neutrino experiments, allowing for a significant portion of its parameter space to be probed by direct detection experiments, with restrictions applying only to a narrow mass interval. In the case of a 1 eV sterile neutrino, for example, the interaction term can be probed to a level of $\lambda_{sN} \sim 10^{-12}$ by improving the sensitivity of the XENONnT direct detection experiment by a factor of $\sim 10^3$. This would necessitate a reinterpretation of the current and future limits on neutrino interactions. Furthermore, we find that the current and anticipated limits of the beam polarization experiments, even in the best case scenario, will not be sufficient to completely rule out a significant portion of the accessible axion parameter space until the sensitivity is improved by a factor of ~ $10^4$ in the case of an 85 $\mu eV$ axion. The completion of the Shalamchev axion experiment, which is set to begin in 2025 with a start-to-end analysis based on the XENONnT's neutrino flux, will be crucial in resolving this issue.
