In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Furthermore, qualitative analysis highlights the EG-CNN's ability to produce clinically relevant, organ boundary definitions. In line with medical practitioners' segmentation practices, the results demonstrate a preference for edge information when the image context contains complex backgrounds or when segmenting difficult organs with poorly defined boundaries. The open-source code and model configurations are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ssecg/edge-gated-cnn. By enhancing the semantic segmentation of medical images in comparison to standard networks, the EG-CNN module offers a viable solution for accurately processing volumetric images. In particular, it effectively handles challenging organs with poorly defined boundaries or those situated deep within the image volume, contributing positively to the accurate detection of clinical abnormalities and disease localizations. The potential of edge information to complement texture information, long unexplored in CNNs, paves the way for future studies in the synthesis and detection of medical pathsologies. By incorporating the EG-CNN module into multi-task learning frameworks, we successfully replicate the performance of leading disease detection approaches while benefiting from the reduced need for explicit preprocessing steps to enhance the visibility of edges and the simplicity of model configurations. The straightforward integration of the EG-CNN module into mainstream CNNs enables a direct application to various image recognition tasks, extending the possibility of applying such methods to other image domains and data sets. The relatively compact number of additional parameters in the edge-gated channel, combined with a modest increase in computational demands during training and inference, makes the EG-CNN module a suitable solution for medical institutions with limited processing resources and large-scale medical imaging datasets. By analyzing 13-day periods of data during a period of minimal solar activity, we calculated the average solar wind energy flux and compared it to the predicted energy flux from the model. The model overestimated the observed energy flux by 22% when considering all possible solar wind speeds, but the discrepancy was significantly reduced to less than 10% when we limited the analysis to winds moving at typical speeds of about 360 kilometers per second. The model's accuracy varied depending on the speed, with the highest error found for winds moving at about 620 kilometers per second. The model also struggled to accurately capture the flux when we looked at individual 13-day periods, likely due to the difficulty in accurately predicting short-term variations, especially during a period of low solar activity when the solar wind flux is relatively low. The results provide valuable insights for use in the development of global solar wind models, especially in regions very close to the sun. We present an investigation of the Aurivillius material Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ under high-pressure conditions using nuclear forward scattering, with results showing a significant pressure-induced magnetic ordering above 2.5 GPa despite initial lattice parameters suggesting antiferromagnetic arrangements at all pressures. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Additionally, our results lead to novel bounds on the minima of fields and curves, providing answers to previously posed questions by the second author and P. Clark respectively. Lastly, our proof technique enables the derivation of similar bounds for the minima of fields with Galois conjugate embeddings. Moreover, our study discloses an interesting connection between the structure of orders in number fields and the celebrated Bateman-Horn conjecture. Leveraging this connection, we make progress on the problem of finding primes with specific properties of their factorization, a problem closely related to the distribution of orders in number fields. Finally, our work highlights an intriguing link between the distribution of orders in number fields and the study of elliptic curves with complex multiplication, a subject currently being actively explored. Nonetheless, the second author's previous questions on the subject of orders in number fields now require a more nuanced answer, taking into account the vast family of primes covered by the generalized Riemann hypothesis. Nonetheless, our work still affirms the sufficiency of the generalized Riemann hypothesis for a substantial class of conjectures on the distribution of orders in number fields. We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. Our findings provide a new interpretation of the central elements of U_q(g), and the partition function Z_L from the quantum cluster algebra can be identified as the normalized invariant form of the quantum group, i.e., \bar{Θ} · Z_L. Our work also reveals a connection between the Weyl group action on O_q(P_G ∘) and the representation of the braid group B_n. In particular, we find that the braid group generator τ_i from B_n can be expressed as a composition of the star-involution and the cluster X-action, which induces an automorphism on the monoid of lattice points P_G ∘, thereby providing a theoretical basis for the simplified formula of the structure coefficients of \bar{Θ}. Our results can be extended to quantum supergroups U_q(s_l^((1)r)). Additionally, we introduce a new basis for the quantum affine algebras U_q(\hat{g}) and its deformations, and our findings can be applied to resolve the divisibility issue in set partitioning. Our work also establishes a connection between the representation of the quantum group and the extended Domokos-Tanaka theorem regarding the action of B_n on the space of smooth functions on G ∘. Lastly, our results can be used to prove the correctness of the simplified formula for the structure coefficients of \bar{Θ}. Our work is further expanded to include the case of quantum groups associated with derived categories and the monoid of lattice paths arising from finite-type vector models, and our findings can be utilized to set various records in combinatorics, according to the author. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, an examination of the code's structural characteristics in relation to the user experience and user behavior is also conducted. Until its eventual ban by several countries, Forsage recruited over 4 million users and generated over $4 billion in transactions. This research provides a unique insight into the inner workings and user dynamics of a blockchain-based pyramid scheme and highlights the difficulties faced by law enforcement in preventing the spread of such schemes through the internet. Due to the ever-evolving nature of these schemes and the frequent updates to their code, a continuous monitoring of the code and transaction data is necessary to deepen our understanding of their structural design and the experiences of users within them. In quantum systems, correlations that follow a power-law decay may indicate the presence of topological order or other intriguing phenomena. Recent studies have demonstrated that certain topologically ordered theories can be represented by holographic tensor networks, known as holographic hash codes or erasure correction codes, which accurately replicate the thermal properties of these models. However, these network simulations require a specific symmetry that some theories fail to exhibit, leading to a more general question about the applicability of this class of codes. To address this, we introduce a new class, denoted as 'hyper-invariant', which allows for the incorporation of global symmetry anomalies that arise from merging distinct topological sectors in quantum field theories. Two examples are provided, including an SU(2) gauge theory and the toric code, both successfully utilizing the new hyper-invariant code, which also maintains a scalable compression ratio despite including system energy constraints. Additionally, we show that the thermodynamic properties of these systems are accurately reproduced using the new code, across various types of extremal states and at both low and high temperatures. Furthermore, we explore an extended version of this new code, featuring a degree of freedom related to the system's spatial dimensions, which successfully replicates the critical behavior of certain quantum critical points. This includes a discussion on the code's fidelity gap under different setups, its scaling with system size, as well as the relationship between the scalar degree of freedom and the system's correlation exponent. Lastly, we examine the representational capabilities of this new code in terms of quantum channels, including both erasure and bending, demonstrating its ability to accurately model the thermal properties of these systems through an analytical approximation, which is further verified by numerical simulations for the toric code. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient processing of transformed point clouds for classification tasks. By leveraging a transformation indicator function derived from a parameterized neural network, TPC determines the specific transformation a point cloud has undergone and accordingly tailors its smoothing operation to counter the impact of the transformation. Compared to the current state-of-the-art methods which rely on extensive data sets to train robust models, TPC exhibits remarkable performance with significantly reduced training data required. Our model's capacity to achieve 95% overall accuracy on the ModelNet40 validation set using a meagerly sized dataset of 200 samples surpasses the current benchmarks. Moreover, our results indicate that even without transformation information, our model can achieve a remarkable 85% accuracy, a testament to its robustness. Our implementation of a transformation-specific smoothing filter, specifically a mini-filter for efficiency, successfully minimizes the accuracy to 94.5%. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/author/tpc-code. By enhancing the reliability of neural network-based point cloud models in critical applications, our approach provides a viable solution to the threat of attacks that have previously compromised their stability. Additionally, our results suggest that a portion of the improvements observed with increased robustness models may, in fact, stem from their improved classification capabilities rather than enhanced robustness alone. Our research also highlights the significance of distinct evaluations for different transformations rather than a unified robustness metric that fails to account for varied alterations. Lastly, our study demonstrates that transformation-specific robustness standards serve as crucial benchmarks for measuring the effectiveness of robust models in critical applications. Our work's significant achievements have significant implications for the development of more precise and efficient point cloud models that can withstand various transformations. Our results suggest that the current state-of-the-art methods, which combine aggressive data augmentations with error reduction techniques, are not optimal and that there is a pressing need to explore alternative strategies. Furthermore, our study reveals that robust models' performance is highly dependent on the specific transformation and dataset being utilized, a fact that poses significant challenges for the development of universal robust models capable of withstanding a broad spectrum of transformations and datasets. Nonetheless, our research lays the groundwork for the creation of transformation-specific models in other vision-based applications, such as image classification, where similar types of alterations can have a profound impact. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The model's effectiveness is further substantiated by internal evaluations involving analysis of intermediate representations and loss functions. The implementation of a sparse encoder within the generator also results in efficient model size reduction. The proposed SparseGAN model offers several advantages over conventional generator architectures, such as encoder-decoders and transformer decoders, by enabling a balance between expressive power and overfitting, reducing model complexity, and facilitating seamless integration with discriminators. The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. Furthermore, by applying our analysis to specific targets such as the most extensively studied star clusters, we conclude that future observational limitations could be overcome with the use of next-generation spectroscopic instruments. A key factor in identifying evidence for interstellar panspermia is the need for a comprehensive approach that takes into account multiple observational indicators, and the examination of how life forms could be disseminated across space due to the magnetic fields associated with pulsar stars. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter fields is also examined in this framework, where it is possible for these fields to emerge from matter fields located on one or more intermediate energy levels between the highest and lowest. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the proposed mechanism can give rise to dark matter properties that mirror those of the visible sector. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal while considering animals' home ranges and resource selection habits.  However, these models require making unrealistic assumptions about capture probabilities being constant across different areas.  Recent models have addressed this limitation by incorporating density estimation into the capture-recapture process, which has led to the development of the occlusion model.  This model has been shown to accurately estimate population density in various settings.  However, it has yet to be seen how this model performs when data on resource selection is integrated.  In this study, we used the occlusion model in conjunction with resource selection information to estimate population density, and found that it was more precise than traditional methods, and also considered how different assumptions about capture probabilities impact the model.  We found that incorporating data on capture occurrences outside of known areas, or 'occurrences in occlusion', significantly enhances the model's performance.  Additionally, we found that making assumptions about capture probabilities, or p, is crucial, and recommended using the 2-step estimation method, which provides a practical approach for using the model in real-world scenarios.  This method allows for the estimation of population density when data on capture occurrences outside of known areas is limited.  In conclusion, combining data on capture occurrences and resource selection on how animals utilize space, results in a more precise estimate of population density.  This has significant implications for wildlife management and research, and highlights the importance of collecting data on capture occurrences outside of known areas when using this model.  This research provides a foundation for further exploration into the relationship between capture probabilities, resource selection, and the models used to estimate population density.  It also highlights the need for models that consider how animals utilize space and select resources, over traditional constant capture probabilities, as these assumptions often fail to account for the complexity of real-world scenarios.  As a result, this study recommends the use of models that incorporate density estimation into the capture-recapture process, such as the occlusion model, when working with telemetry data in conjunction with spatial capture-recapture data.  This will result in more precise estimates of population density, and provide a more realistic understanding of how animals utilize space and select resources. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes on various networks, demonstrating that nodal activity can display intricate patterns depending on the network's architecture. The findings indicate that localized and widespread patterns are not mutually exclusive features in a spreading process. Additionally, the prevalence of an epidemic near a critical transition is influenced by the delocalized component of the network. Furthermore, different critical exponents can coexist with similar localization patterns. The study also reveals a more intricate behavior in quenched networks, influenced by the type of activation and degree exponent. Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams, by scaling the predicted probabilities of game events by their occurrence in a larger dataset of game situations. By applying this approach to player location data from the UEFA European Football Championship in 2020 and 2022, we compared the valuation of defensive players for their national men's teams and found that it differed significantly from the previously established, but less robust, occurrence-adjusted values. Moreover, the new methodology revealed that several of the most skilled players had been undersvalued in the earlier study. Furthermore, our results demonstrated that the value of defensive players varied not only based on their nationality but also on whether they represented a team's attack or defense, and that there was a notable difference in the valuation of defensive players for national men's and women's football teams. Additionally, our research showed that the diversity of players with greater valuations was not a recent phenomenon but rather one that had its roots in previous European Football Championships. Additionally, our research showed that the way we value defensive players in football can provide valuable location data, which could be useful in mapping the spatial structure of football games. Building on the achievements of Bao and the first author concerning Gaussian ensembles, this paper extends the independence concept known as freeness in two forms: type $B$ freeness, which is a variation of free independence where the test matrix is allowed to have diagonal components, and conditional freeness. Type $B$ freeness is applicable in scenarios where the test matrix exhibits oscillatory behavior following a GUE or GOE distribution. Conditional freeness is a shorter-term concept, effectively providing a freeness guarantee for a limited time frame following an initial independent scenario. Both types of independence are proven for matrices $N^{-1/2} X_N$ and $N^{-1/2} Y_N$, where $X_N$ and $Y_N$ are independent and correspond to real or complex Gaussian matrix ensembles on the GUE, GOE, or GSE. The conditions are based on $N$ converging to infinity in a specific manner. The results obtained also hold for $N^{-1/2} X_N$ and $N^{-1/2} Y_N$ when linearly transformed and in some cases under additional diagonal transformations. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. The model's effectiveness is validated across four diverse benchmark models and five datasets, including large-scale language models, where it demonstrates exceptional performance in both single-task and multi-task learning scenarios, surpassing the performance of multiple state-of-the-art methods. The parity symmetry of the Rabi model allows for the creation of super-Rabi oscillations, resulting in the periodic production of even photons in the cavity. This phenomenon occurs through a laser-driven qubit flip and transitions influenced by Rabi interaction, preserving parity. By introducing dissipation, we find that only the protected emission mode survives, and we develop a threshold condition for its occurrence based on Rabi interaction strength and the angle of detuning. Furthermore, we find that emission protected by parity symmetry occurs not only in the Rabi model but also in other situations with periodic photon generation. Additionally, we demonstrate the occurrence of odd photon generation when the parity symmetry is broken. Our findings provide a foundation for exploring protected multi-photonic emissions in the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED. Moreover, they suggest the possibility of designing experiments to distinguish different symmetry-protected multi-photonic emissions. In practice, this could be achieved by adjusting the angle of detuning, changing the laser driving methods, or utilizing different types of symmetry instead of parity symmetry. In theoretical models of cavity QED, we demonstrate that periodic photon generation protected by parity symmetry occurs when the Rabi interaction meets specific conditions, and this interaction can be achieved experimentally using different systems such as superconducting qubits, cold atoms, and ions. For example, a recent experiment involving superconducting qubits has achieved Rabi interactions of up to 10 times the resonator's linear deposition rate, thereby enabling the study of the model's applications in quantum computing, such as the implementation of the oracle subroutine in the phase-estimation algorithm. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. A key aspect of our technique is a new detection mechanism capable of identifying and disregarding malicious nodes' manipulative feedback. Our achievement is substantiated by a formal theorem along with a novel detection mechanism, both of which are under our own control. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that full-degree identification is not required to achieve this outcome, which offers implications for other problems arising in ad-hoc networks. Our algorithm employs two new protocols, both of which may be of independent interest - a degree-disclosure protocol and a voting protocol, both of which can be used in other contexts. The degree-disclosure protocol ensures the accurate disclosure of degree information from genuine nodes, even in the presence of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge. The voting protocol ensures the accuracy of a majority vote, despite the efforts of malicious nodes to manipulate the outcome. Both protocols are robust and highly efficient, which is a key aspect of our achievement. Our analysis of the voting protocol provides further insights into the behavior of epidemic protocols in ad-hoc networks, particularly in scenarios with malicious nodes. The voting protocol can be used to solve other problems, such as finding the shortest path in a corrupted network. Overall, our results demonstrate that it is possible to estimate the size of a sparse network accurately, despite the presence of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, and our achievements provide a foundation for further research in this area. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering the field's stress-energy tensor from the metric is an inherent difficulty. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined scenarios, including irregular black hole formation, multiply colliding black holes, and scalar wave maps. These developments make it feasible to accurately account for the effects of general relativity on the propagation of gravitational waves in models of modified gravity. The new framework is showcased using an adaptation of the standard CTTK code used in studies of gravitational wave echoes. The implementation is available on the PRISM repository at https://github.com/AstroPRISM/CTTK. Furthermore, we offer a simplified version of the code as an open issue at https://github.com/GW-Code-Exchange/cttk. The novel CTTK method offers a viable solution for resolving the initial data constraints in numerical relativity, particularly suitable for simulations involving fundamental fields. By circumventing the typical conformal rescaling of source terms, this approach avoids the complexities associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, instead solving the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint as an algebraic equation for the conformal factor. This strategy has been successfully applied to a range of simulations, including irregular black hole formation, and has significant implications for the accurate modeling of gravitational wave propagation in modified gravity theories. The implementation of the CTTK method is now available on the PRISM repository. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our measurements reveal a large anomalous Nernst coefficient of $-4.8 \times 10^{-4} \,\text{K}^{-1}$ in Mn$_3$NiN at room temperature and a positive effective charge carrier carrier type, which is consistent with the material's inherent electronic and magnetic structure. Our research paves the way for a deeper understanding and control of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite materials. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the anomalous Nernst effect and spin Hall effect are interconnected and can be described using a similar mechanism. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As a result, this approach makes it possible for users to conduct experiments remotely in real-time, combining rigorous testing for their scientific models with high-throughput scanning. To facilitate this integration of machine learning into experiments, all models have been implemented as open-source repositories that can be easily trained using datasets collected during experiments. To streamline training and model selection, a workflow has also been developed that utilizes a cluster of GPUs that can be accessed through the Rutgers University Advanced Research Computing (RUARC) cyberinfrastructure. This approach allows for easy selection of features, models, and hyperparameters by utilizing a high-dimensional genetic algorithm that leverages the speed of the cluster to explore the parameter space. To further accelerate this process, the team is exploring the integration of gradient-based machine learning models that can provide continuous evaluations of the model performance during data collection. To demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, the work concludes by highlighting the results obtained with a group of users from the Rutgers University, who were able to successfully conduct a variety of experiments remotely in a short period of time at the NSLS-II. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The combined use of these materials and this damage detection method offers potential to create more reliable and safer critical systems. 
While the proposed method demonstrates its effectiveness on carbon-nanofiller reinforced glass-fiber laminated composites, it has the potential to be beneficial for other types of self-sensing composite materials. 
In order to deploy this technique in practical applications, the need is established for experimental studies that include impact-induced damage in composites, both with and without the influence of boundary conditions on damage development, as well as for a more in-depth analysis of the implications of using a non-invasive imaging technique on the accuracy of damage detection in composites that have a complex failure pattern. 
Furthermore, the challenge of integrating this technique with machine learning algorithms in real-time settings also presents an area for further research. 
In terms of practical applications, this technique can be used to create safer and more reliable aerospace systems by leveraging the unique properties of self-sensing composite materials.

This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but had a positive effect on the engagement level of African American students. Conversely, African American students who were not first-generation students experienced a decrease in engagement level due to remote learning. Transfer students with higher self-efficacy scores benefited from remote learning in terms of submission and engagement rates. A positive correlation between exam scores and self-efficacy scores was observed in the Fall 2020 semester. Ultimately, this research underlines the importance of considering the varied effects of remote learning on different demographic groups of university students. It also highlights the need for educators and instructors to be aware of the potential negative consequences of remote learning on first-generation students and the importance of fostering a sense of community among African American students. Moreover, it emphasizes the value of assessing the impact of remote learning on students' ability to stay on track using objective data collection methods. Moreover, this study suggests that remote learning has no negative impact on the academic performance of non-first-generation African American and white students. It also reveals that demographics groups that were not negatively affected by remote learning in terms of module submission and engagement rates achieved similar course scores in Fall 2020 compared to Fall 2019. In contrast, first-generation African American and white students who experienced a decline in module submission rates in Fall 2020 scored lower than their counterparts in Fall 2019. paracomplete and paraconsistent four-valued logic system. Unlike classical logic,
this approach accommodates propositions that may be neither entirely true nor
entirely false, as well as propositions that can simultaneously embody both
truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. Finally, we outline an alternative definition for the satisfaction relation that is both applicable across non-classical models and serves as a foundation for our proposed system. With this alternative definition, we go on to establish an analogue of the Completeness Theorem within the context of our proposed four-valued logic system. This achievement is particularly significant, as it is the first time the Completeness Theorem has been successfully implemented across a paraconsistent and paracomplete logic system. We also explore an extension of our proposed system to a many-valued logic system and offer a definition for an analogue of the Continuum Hypothesis within this context. This definition, in turn, gives rise to bi-valent instances of the CH, corresponding to our proposed system's non-classical CH, thereby demonstrating the utility of our approach. Lastly, we provide a concise overview of the fundamental axioms that underpin our proposed system and outline an argument for designating our proposed meta-theory as a version of set theory. With this justification in place, we proceed to establish an analogue of Gödel's Constructible Universe within our proposed framework, an entity we have the opportunity to compare with its classical counterpart across multiple facets. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of recovering complex aspects of gait using a high-resolution cortical recording technique and highlights the potential of such a system in the rehabilitation of individuals with spinal cord injuries. Additionally, this study emphasizes the importance of utilizing invasive recording techniques such as ECoG when investigating the recovery of sophisticated motor functions like walking. From a clinical perspective, this study's findings suggest that patients with spinal cord injuries can benefit from the training of a brain-computer interface that decodes walking state and step rate information while using a treadmill. This conclusion is based on the results of a pilot trial involving one subject, who exhibited an increase in accurate step rate predictions following such training. These results indicate that practicing the recovery of walking state and step rate in a controlled environment leads to an enhancement in the efficacy of the BCI, which in turn could contribute to achieving reliable and safe transfers of the trained BCI controls to an uncontrolled situation like walking on different terrain. Additionally, this study suggests that the most effective training of a BCI for the recovery of walking involves utilizing a protocol that incorporates auditory feedback in real-time while the subject is walking. This method was found to be more beneficial than a different training approach examined in this study. Overall, this study provides evidence that the recovery of walking ability using a brain-computer interface has the potential to contribute to the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Furthermore, it highlights the benefits of utilizing a training protocol that includes real-time auditory feedback in the training of such a system.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. This result has significant implications for the group's dynamics, particularly influencing the behavior of its generating sets and the structure of its configuration space. Moreover, we demonstrate that the group's action on the tree can be reinterpreted as a action on a tree associated with a subgraph of $\Gamma$. This associated tree's properties provide valuable insights into the group's behavior and its connection to the circle of related groups, including the fundamental group of a certain type of graph-covered plane. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for the graph $\Gamma$ itself, establishing a criterion that must be met if the group's action on the tree is terminating. This criterion is shown to be applicable to graphs whose all components are trees, yielding a proof that the group's action on the tree is terminating if, and only if, its action is freely terminating. This conclusion generalizes a previous result of Guo's. Additionally, we prove that a non-trivial action of a right-angled Artin group on a tree implies the existence of an Eulerian path in the graph $\Gamma$. This fact has the unexpected consequence that such groups share many properties with free groups. Our work also explores the relationship between the configuration space of the graph $\Gamma$ and the set of Ewards orbits, and proves that this configuration space contains a copy of the tree on which the group acts minimally. This result further supports the conjecture of R.G. Swan. Our proof relies on a novel interpretation of the action of a right-angled Artin group on a tree as an action on the flag complex associated with its graph $\Gamma$. This interpretation enables us to establish a connection between the graph's combinatorial properties and its group's dynamics. This connection allows us to prove theorems about the graph $\Gamma$ itself, such as the fact that it must contain an Eulerian path if its group acts minimally on a tree. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively captured complex interactions within datasets. Nonetheless, these models are typically trained on static graph representations, which fail to capture the dynamic nature of connections often present in temporal systems. We introduce a novel type of graph neural network, called DYN-GEC, designed to dynamically learn and predict the effective connectivity of a system from multivariate time series data. DYN-GEC utilizes state transition models and observed data to establish a dynamic graph and then utilizes this model to make predictions about the underlying connectivity. We demonstrate the efficacy of this model on artificial and real-world datasets, showing it surpasses the performance of static models and significantly reduces estimation errors when compared to conventional state transition models. Furthermore, DYN-GEC is capable of identifying the optimal number of system states and effectively handles missing and noisy data. We also provide the code for this method at https://github.com/BrainResearchLab/DYN-GEC. In addition to its numerous applications in computational neuroscience, DYN-GEC has the potential to analyze and model dynamic systems in physics, biology, and engineering. In this work, we also introduce the open-source Brain Research Lab Graph Learning package, available at https://graph-learning.brl.cs.vt.edu/, which provides a comprehensive range of graph learning methods for the analysis of complex systems. This package includes various graph learning frameworks such as graph neural network, graph convolutional network, dynamic graph neural network, and generalized state transition models like DYN-GEC. We anticipate this package to contribute significantly to the development of cutting-edge graph learning methods and to provide a comprehensive resource for researchers to explore a wide range of graph learning applications. We have included a detailed guide on using this package at https://graph-learning.brl.cs.vt.edu/docs/usage.html. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived using an exact code, whereas the finite-temperature effective potential is utilized for the bottom-quark annihilation process within the standard electroweak effective theory. Furthermore, this study incorporates the finite temperature mass splitting between Higgs bosons within the MSSM in both production processes. The impact of complex parameters is significant, with the possibility of altering the on-shell Higgs couplings, mass splittings, and even the Higgs mass itself. However, the real part of the complex scalar potential's coefficient primarily influences the Higgs physical properties. The imaginary part, on the other hand, introduces a small imaginary component to the potential's minimum, resulting in a tiny mass for the lighter neutral Higgs boson and a specific distribution of decay branching ratios. The code developed in this study is compatible with the FeynArXives format and is part of the 2L3P4P5S package, which provides a comprehensive set of MSSM phenomenological findings for on-shell, non-resonant processes within the standard model sector. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. This proposed framework aims to integrate existing models for cell mechanics, adhesive force-dependent cell shape analysis, and advection-diffusion on deformable surfaces. By bringing together these components, our approach will allow the computational examination of how the localization of specific proteins affects cell spreading and locomotion, therefore providing valuable insights for the interpretation of experimental data and clinical observations. Furthermore, this framework will facilitate the exploration of novel therapeutic strategies for a range of musculoskeletal disorders caused by misregulated cell behavior. In particular, our model will be applied to investigate the movement of myosin II and other proteins within locomotory fibroblasts, an area of study previously hindered by the absence of a computational tool that can analyze the complex interplay between cell motion and protein localization. In our implementation, we will utilize an actin network model that is characterized by a non-exhaustive set of governing equations but will also explore the possibility of substituting it with alternative models of living networks. Similarly, we will make use of a simplified advection-diffusion module on curved surfaces that is, to our knowledge, not widely available through existing software. Consequently, our project will involve the development of custom numerical integration methods for the actin network model, a simplified surface diffusion module, and a deformable surface solver, with a focus on accelerating these computations using high-performance parallel processing, an area that our approach currently only preliminarily leverages through a limited use of GPU acceleration. In line with the scope of this project, we will establish a working model, develop a basic protocol for implementing the proposed methodology, and demonstrate its applicability to our specific use case but will not delve into optimal algorithm optimization for the best possible performance. In the context of the project, the term 'living network' refers to a cell's actin network that exhibits homeostatic properties by continuously undergoing rearrangement upon external stimuli, as opposed to non-living networks like electrical or mechanical ones

The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for detecting malicious activities within blockchain transactions focus on the transactions themselves, neglecting the underlying money trails that indicate suspicious intentions. As a result, they have limited detection capabilities compared to traditional money laundering detection methods. In contrast, we propose an approach to identify the money trails of suspicious activities within a blockchain transaction graph. By modeling the transaction graph as a dual-phase directed graph and applying in-depth analysis techniques, we pinpoint the underlying money trails associated with malicious activities. When tested on the Ethereum blockchain transaction history, our method effectively detected a wide range of malicious activities, including (among others) 37 previously unknown malware-infected wallet addresses with potential receipts in the Ethereum block chain. Furthermore, our results highlight the practical applicability of our approach for anti-money laundering applications within cryptocurrency blockchain transactions. In addition, our method receives high scores from both rigorous scientific and practical metrics. In particular, we highlight the practical usefulness of our method by illustrating its capacity to monitor real-world malicious activities such as the Monero mining malware, WannaCry-like ransomware attacks, and Helo's user data theft malware, among others. In contrast to existing methods, our approach excels in detecting malicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchain transactions. In particular, we highlight the significant contribution of our method by comparing it with existing methods on the Ethereum blockchain transaction history. Notably, our method detects malicious activities at a rate that is up to 3 times greater than the next best method. In recognition of the critical importance of transparency in academic research, we release our implementation as an open-source software for the benefit of the broader research community. In particular, we provide theoretical justifications for our method by presenting a formal model for money trail detection within a blockchain transaction graph. Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, by first manipulating highly entangled quantum states before collecting information about an unknown variable through single measurements. Although this typically yields the most effective outcome, applying this method is extremely difficult when dealing with larger states. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and Binary Power Control (BPC) to examine the relationship between optimal power control and BPC in an interference network containing K users. By applying a previously developed framework, we determine the extremal GDoF gain resulting from optimal power control relative to BPC as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Moreover, we establish conditions under various GDoF scenarios, including the regime where some users exert control over other users' reception in an uplink scenario, in an extension to previous research. Additionally, we identify the sufficient and necessary number of degree-of-freedom values for users in an optimal power control setup. Furthermore, we derive the extremal GDoF gain in networks with Z-interferers, where the structure of optimal power control solutions follows an order of user indexing. Lastly, a near-optimal solution for an extremal GDoF gain of $\sqrt{K}$ is achieved using BPC with a $\Theta(K)$-sized binary tree. This finding provides a practical solution for large-scale networks. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of optimal power control in an extremal GDoF gain context, a previously unexplored area. As a result, many current strategies based on BPC are re-evaluated and re-defined in light of this discovery. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with established reference data. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, showing good agreement with simulations using the existing method but with significantly reduced computational cost. Our results indicate that using an artificially longer collision time step for convenience can lead to over 10 times increase in computational time without improvement in accuracy, while our algorithm achieves similar accuracy at one-third to half of this cost. Our study also highlights the importance of resolving particle rotation during collisions and neglecting it, as the existing method does, can lead to inaccurate results with high concentration of particles. Our algorithm is highly compatible with the SIMPFLOW simulator and its particle collision model and can be applied to various simulation tools with minor adjustments. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater control problem due to the fluctuating inertial frames of reference resulting from ground slippage. This study focuses on creating and testing an advanced modeling framework for a one-legged hopping robot in motion. A unique approach has been found where the ground's response can be viewed as a resistant force resisting the rate of descent, allowing the modeling of impact forces through a resistant layer. Numerical modeling involves using the resistive layer's parameters to generate force and torque responses. A critical condition must be met for these forces to align with the intended path, leading to the development of an optimal control system to manage force and torque discrepancies. When put into practice, this control system allows the robot to maintain balance while minimizing the needed control to overcome resistance, resulting in a significant reduction in energy expenditure. Simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this control method on various soft surfaces, showcasing the robot's ability to perform stable hopping movements. Due to the complex interactions between the robot and its environment, as well as the nonlinear and hybrid dynamics involved, this model remains a prime example for controlling a robot in dynamic interaction with soft terrain. Finally, the monopod design and the approach to modeling such a system are analogous to those that could be applied to bipedal robots, thereby holding broader implications for the field of legged locomotion. Additionally, the developed model highlights the value of high-fidelity simulation in its ability to accurately predict a variety of real-world hopping patterns and dynamics, even including the unique hopping gait commonly observed in birds and reptiles. This study has also identified the specific conditions under which a stable, walking gait may emerge from the robot's hopping motion, laying the groundwork for a more in-depth examination into the underlying mechanisms that govern this behavior. As a result, this research has significant implications for the pursuit of more advanced robotic locomotion methods, such as running and bounding, as well as for a deeper understanding of the dynamic interactions that shape animal movement patterns. Furthermore, the development of a robust and stable control system for robots navigating soft terrain, a critical milestone in the creation of more sophisticated robotic mobility systems, is also facilitated by this study. Consequently, this research has important implications for the creation of advanced robotic mobility systems that can efficiently and effectively navigate a variety of soft and deformable environments with ease

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our expectations from this endeavor are that researchers will leverage CONDAQA to craft more sophisticated and versatile models capable of grasping the intricacies of negation and related concepts. We anticipate these models to excel not only on our challenge but also on more broad-based reasoning tasks, such as figuring out the implications of particular statements. We look forward to observing the impact of this dataset on the evolution of NLP models. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Compared to flat-topic representations, HDTM enables users to explore related topics across any level of the hierarchy with only a few core nodes, achieving this while maintaining a topic diversity comparable to existing methods. In our experiments under HDTM, we found the ability to explore and drill down into topic hierarchies, a capability we demonstrated through an user study and performance benchmarks on document classification and clustering. Furthermore, our approach boasts a significant scalability improvement over its predecessors. Our implementation is available online for public use. In addition to HDTM, we developed a preprocessing technique called Stopword Removal using Cooccurrence Analysis (SRCO), a method that identifies unnecessary words with a high degree of accuracy in large networks, also making the text data significantly more manageable for our model. By integrating SRCO with HDTM, we achieved an even better outcome. In particular, our experiments showed that HDTM and SRCO reach 85% of the accuracy of a robust yet non-distributed baseline system when used with relatively small datasets of around 10,000 documents, while on much larger datasets such as Wikipedia, the models achieve a 90% accuracy with nearly 100% topic assignment precision. In our implementation, two million Wikipedia articles were processed in approximately 77 days by a single machine. In contrast to other hierarchical models, our approach not only generates more accurate and diverse topics but also does so with a higher level of scalability and a lower topic overlap rate, a potential issue in other models that could lead to incorrect conclusions. In our experiments, the average topic overlap rate with HDTM was less than 10%, a rate that could drop as low as 5% with the inclusion of SRCO. Furthermore, our implementation is highly versatile and can easily accommodate custom stopword lists, a feature that other distributed topic modeling solutions cannot match. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Additionally, the developed framework for interpreting quench data as an indicator of the annealing gap's behavior may be applied to other digital annealing simulations. Furthermore, the devised protocol for optimizing quantum annealing, leveraging machine learning techniques on quench dynamics, presents a viable approach for tackling inescapable computational issues in the large-scale simulation of quantum systems. Nonetheless, the method boasts the advantage of being computationally efficient. When comparing the proposed method to alternative strategies for optimizing quantum annealing, the novel approach demonstrates comparable performance when considering multiple initial conditions; nevertheless, it falls short of efficient Monte Carlo simulations in terms of precision. Nonetheless, when quantum annealing is performed across an overcomplete set of possible solutions, the proposed method outperforms all competing approaches by a substantial margin. These breakthroughs bring forward a viable solution for tackling the intricacies of digital annealing simulations through machine learning, providing a glimpse into the promising possibilities that arise at the intersection of these domains. Nonetheless, the study is confined to theoretical simulations, as the practical implementation of such a protocol on functional quantum annealing circuits necessitates the ability to obtain quench data from physical systems. Despite this limitation, the novel approach lays the groundwork for exploring the vast potential that lies within the intersection of machine learning and digital annealing. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band, leading to a
reduction in $d$-band's strong antiferromagnetic ordering. This results in
increased likelihood of self-trapping of an electron pair within the $d$-band,
favouring a state with mixed $d$-orbital pairing. Up to a certain strong
screening, the electronic properties remain close to those with moderate
screening. 
For strong screening, the model's physics is akin to that of an isolated,
highly-correlated $d$-band without a significant free $s$-electron component,
favouring a self-trapped, non-antiferromagnetic ground state with a mixed
$d$-orbital pairing state. 
However, in all situations examined, a one-dimensional projection of the two-
band model yields an unstable state. 
Experiments indicating no $s$-to-$d$ electron transfer in satellite peak
weight can serve as an empirical basis for determining the level of screening. 
Based on such experiments, the most plausible scenario is that with strong
screening, and thus a self-trapped, non-antiferromagnetic ground state should
be sought after in further theoretical investigations of infinite layered
nickelates.

feynman-diagram technique in self-consistent fashion, allow derivation of a
density of states displaying the experimentally observed double-hump structure,

This resolution offers a possible starting point for exploring whether local

By analyzing initial conditions with sufficiently small magnitudes regardless of the collision rate, the study reveals various dynamic processes arising from the combination of the phase-mixing/dispersive effects of the transport operator and the singular collision operator. In regions where high-frequency fluctuations are prevalent, an accelerated decay phenomenon is observed, characterized by an exponential decrease in a time scale that inversely correlates with the collision rate and the frequency magnitude. In contrast, for regions where fluctuations are minimal, Taylor dispersion leads to an accelerated decay governed by the inverse of the frequency squared, multiplied by the collision rate. Moreover, this research proves the existence of almost uniform phase mixing estimates. Consequently, for observable quantities such as density, almost uniform bounds in terms of the collision rate are derived for decay rates, influenced by Landau damping and dispersive decay processes. In the context of soft potentials, these results extend previous findings obtained under stronger collision conditions.
