Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation plays a significant role in the dynamics of quantum double dark-soliton states, particularly in the scattering of notches. In the weak-coupling regime, and particularly in the case of head-on collisions between two notches, our findings demonstrate that quasi-condensation plays a crucial role in the dynamics of quantum double dark-soliton states. For head-on collisions, and in the weak-coupling regime, we observe the reconstruction of a condensate fracture within a few times the natural time scale of $\tau_\text{NEF} = \hbar/(m\lambda^2)$. In the case of collisions where one notch is moving much faster than the other, and in the weak-coupling regime, we find that the time it takes for the condensate fracture to heal increases with the ratio of the speeds of the two notches. In the case of collisions where one notch is moving much faster than the other, and in the weak-coupling regime, we find that the time it takes for the condensate fracture to heal is directly proportional to this ratio. We also precisely derive an exact finite-size scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation for quantum double dark-soliton states. In the case of head-on collisions, and in the weak-coupling regime, our findings demonstrate that quasi-condensation is completely destroyed by the imposition of boundary conditions. In the case of collisions where one notch is moving much faster than the other, and in the weak-coupling regime, our findings demonstrate that the healing of the condensate fracture is unaffected by the imposition of boundary conditions. We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearisation is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superising method for a graded bundle. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning models 
capable of navigating through the semantic structures in language and pinpointing 
embedded security vulnerabilities are needed. Our approach incorporates a 
Bidirectional LSTM model, pre-trained on extensive linguistic data, along with 
a Universal Sentence Encoder to enhance the ISO 27001-compliant security 
ontology. By utilizing a high-performance computing platform to analyze vast 
corpora, we have achieved over 80% accuracy in validating the model's 
robustness and capacity for identifying unseen concepts within the ontology 
and web page instances. Furthermore, the proposed method has been implemented 
on a massive corpus of 3.5 billion words, resulting in a 12-fold improvement 
in performance and accelerated reasoning and query execution on the enriched 
ontology by a factor of almost 5 when compared to a conventional approach. 
The enhanced ontology and the associated code are also made publicly available 
for further research and practical applications in the field of cybersecurity. 
The innovative use of Universal Sentence Encoding in the proposed model has 
also paved the way for embracing diverse semantic structures in ontologies and 
the development of a novel strategy for the seamless integration of rule-
based reasoning and deep learning-based threat detection. This integrated 
approach has the potential to analyze vast amounts of text and identify security 
vulnerabilities at an unprecedented speed and accuracy. The proposed model 
has been successfully applied to enriching the 27001 ontology, but a similar 
approach can be adapted to develop an effective cybersecurity threat detection
system utilizing the proposed deep learning-based approach in conjunction with
the well-established description logic for proper ontology enrichment. This
integration of deep learning and ontology will facilitate the detection of
complex threats from voluminous textual data by accurately identifying the
threats and their severity according to the defined security policies and will
also enable the classification of unknown concepts within the ontology. The
use of a universal sentence encoder for the proposed model has the advantage of
utilizing a single model for the navigation of diverse linguistic structures
and the utilization of a guide to accurate concept identification within the
ontology

Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. A comparative evaluation among various graph algorithms reveals significant performance gains, achieving an order of magnitude improvement in time complexity. In contrast to existing solution approaches, our proposed method avoids the need for additional secondary clearing nodes in graph constructions. In practical applications, our solution facilitates the elimination of up to 99.98% of clearing nodes, an essential consideration for scalable solutions in an economy's context. By implementing this solution on the Romanian Ministry of Economy's invoice data, we observe a reduction of approximately two orders of magnitude in the number of clearing nodes, achieving a substantial reduction in costs. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. This results in a time complexity of $O(n \cdot m)$ for assessing containment, where $n$ represents the length of the containing regular expression and $m$ represents the number of distinct characters within that set. Additionally, we demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through the development of a symbolic solver for containment in extended regular expressions, showcasing its applicability in modeling and solving word problems associated with finite-state automata. This involves translating the automaton's states and transition rules into an equivalent set of containment inequalities, subsequently solving these inequalities to determine the words accepted by the automaton. This process leverages the containment solver and Antimirov's strategy to derive the automaton's accepted words, achieving a combined time complexity of $O(n^3)$. Furthermore, we explore the distinction between deterministic and nondeterministic containment assessments, highlighting the greater efficiency of deterministic assessment but also noting the fundamental limitation of all assessment methods, namely the ability to resolve equality issues. This research is an extension of an earlier concept presented at the 2021 CLoNe Workshop, featuring an updated approach to solving equality problems with regular expressions that is distinct from the containment approach outlined above. This updated solution for equality problems incorporates Antimirov's rewriting strategy, Brzozowski's derivative operator with recognizable character sets, and a combination of Antimirov's and Brzozowski's approaches, allowing for the derivation of regular expression equality but with the recognition that this derivation relies on the ability to solve containment issues and, in certain cases, may result in the formulation of inequality problems without a clear containment-based solution. This research demonstrates that the combination of deterministic containment assessment, Antimirov's rewriting strategy, Brzozowski's derivative operator with recognizable character sets, and the development of a time-efficient containment solver for extended regular expressions makes a significant theoretical contribution to the solution of word problems

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. Furthermore, our proposed model showcases a significant advantage in pose estimation when confronted with increasing sequence lengths, a critical aspect in applications involving long tracking sequences. In addition to achieving superior performance, our model also exhibits a notable reduction in both parameter count and estimated pose computation time, outperforming even the current best-in-class VIO model in all evaluated metrics. Our project's code is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/kaustuvghose/ema-vio, for any interested researcher who wishes to build upon this innovative research. Additionally, we have released the challenging, real-world benchmark datasets used to evaluate our model's performance, specifically tailored towards its strengths and weaknesses, at https://kaustuvghose.github.io/ema-vio-benchmark/. This comprehensive evaluation of our proposed framework, along with the release of both our model's code and the challenging benchmark datasets, is intended to serve as a call-to-action for the advancement of the next-generation, learning-based VIO frameworks that incorporate attention and external memory components. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By applying time-reversal and on-site symmetries, we can link SHOWS to its related forms, such as the Fermi-arc materials and topological hinge metals. We propose a candidate material, $A_2$O$_3$, based on the monopolar 5D Weyl semimetal obtained through extruding a time-reversal breaking 3D Weyl semimetal, which can be used to experimentally identify SHOWS. Leveraging our framework, we can design hinge states and Fermi-arc surfaces independently through different parent Hamiltonians, enabling independent manipulations of these topological properties. Moreover, by incorporating interactions, we can transform SHOWS into an topological Mott insulator with hinge states connected by Weyl point projections, offering a potential route to realizing interacting topological phenomena. Finally, our theoretical discussions can be tested and validated using numerical simulations on the proposed $A_2$O$_3$ material. By developing the square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal framework, we can unlock more sophisticated and practical applications of topological materials within the Weyl semimetal family. Additionally, our findings provide a way to recognize the higher-order topological materials in experimental measurements, enriching the study of topological materials. Furthermore, our proposals for $A_2$O$_3$ can pave the way for the realization of interacting topological phenomena in quantum materials. In the theoretical framework of quantum materials, our work raises new questions about the classification of topological materials. In particular, we need to redefine the notion of higher-order topological materials by incorporating both linear and nonlinear operators into the Hamiltonian. By incorporating interactions into the Hamiltonian, we may transform a topological material into its corresponding topological phase of matter, offering a new means of designing and creating topological materials. This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a single student model to successfully recognize multiple unrelated classes simultaneously through selective aggregation, thereby demonstrating the potential of FedSA to tackle real-world classification problems. To effectively handle FedSA, we've also developed a customized optimization algorithm and a secure aggregation method, along with implementing a comprehensive experiment to validate the FedSA model's performance. The experiment involved gathering data from an ensemble of 13 contributors, each representing different areas of the Oulu University of Applied Sciences, such as engineering, business, and health sciences, with the goal of recognizing five distinct categories of images. The results show that the FedSA model can accurately classify images in real-world scenarios with a high degree of accuracy. The FedSA approach has far-reaching implications as it enables secure, collaborative model learning among multiple parties, thereby contributing significantly to the field of machine learning. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition to a state of slow and nearly steady differential rotation, characterized by anti-solar patterns in their latitudinal velocity differentiation. This particular differential rotation is distinguished by faster equatorial rotation speeds compared to the polar regions. A question arises regarding the impact of this distinct differential rotation on the generation of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars. If the generation of magnetic cycles is linked to rotation, one could hypothesize that it would be lost as they spin down. However, the possibility of magnetic cycles persisting even as their rotation rates approach the break-up velocity is also a consideration. This study delves into the possibilities of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars by exploring the effects of distinct types of differential rotation on the generation of magnetic cycles. The research utilizes the STRIDE code, a 3D time-dependent code that incorporates the induction equation within an anelastic approximation, to simulate dynamos driven by convection. Six unique sets of simulations are conducted for each of the three different rotational states (rapid, medium, and slow), alongside a control simulation without magnetic fields. The findings indicate that both pro-solar and anti-solar differential rotations can give rise to magnetic cycles, with distinct features however. The generation of magnetic cycles in rapidly and medium-speed rotators mirrors that observed in traditional solar-type dynamo scenarios. In contrast, magnetic cycles emerge at lower shear levels in slowly rotating stars, exhibiting different preference for certain geometric structures. Furthermore, time-averaged synchroton emission flux, a key observable, displays a greater disparity when comparing pro-solar and anti-solar dynamos, highlighting the importance of consideration in modelling and potential observational constraints. The study's outcomes provide a theoretical framework for understanding the impact of distinct differential rotations on magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, with implications for a broader range of stars displaying anti-solar rotation patterns. These findings may also shed light on the underlying processes governing magnetic cycles in the Sun and other solar-type stars, potentially uncovering a deeper physical connection between rotation and the generation of magnetic cycles. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity for a thorough examination of potential magnetic cycles in the Sun and other slowly rotating stars through global photospheric magnetic field mapping. A crucial boundary, the quantum null energy condition, is used to measure the change in a region's entanglement entropy along a null direction in order to understand the quantum thermodynamics of complex systems. Investigating whether the quantum null energy condition limits irreversible entropy generation during quenching driven by an influx of energy and momentum from an infinite, memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories, our research finds that an increase in both entropy and temperature, as required by the classical Clausius inequality, is necessary to prevent a violation of the quantum null energy condition, specifically in quenching transitions that result in changes in thermal states dual to Banados-Teitelboim-Zanelli geometries. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. High internal heat generating cores, like those of Mars and Earth, should have prevented the permanent loss of magnetogenic materials in Venus's core. However, the detection of magnetic field signatures in the solar wind interaction with Venus's magnetosphere remains elusive, suggesting a need for reevaluation of the core's magnetic field generation and possible magnetosphere, as well as its interaction with the solar wind and surface. However, estimating the values of its parameters, particularly those that cause persistence or large-scale network shocks to generate continuous flows of events, has proven challenging because traditional methods of parameter estimation fail when data is limited. In contrast, a significant advantage of the nonlinear Hawkes process is its analytically tractable likelihood function, enabling the use of a rigorous maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) to obtain parameter values. By developing and assessing a variety of Bayesian estimation techniques - including a bespoke Bayesian MCMC method specifically suited to the nonlinear Hawkes process - we demonstrate the potential for these estimators to produce accurate results when data is plentiful, but also show that they can effectively handle limited data by providing a clear interpretation of the results. These results can be used to construct a range of posterior checks to verify the reliability of the estimated parameters, and also provide a method for assessing the accuracy of the estimated parameters when data is limited. We find that the variation of the estimated adjacencies can be more robustly estimated when using a Bayesian estimation method on a reduced dataset, which provides a practical solution to addressing the challenges of extending the nonlinear Hawkes process to multiple dimensions. Although it appears that the associated algebra is closed, a detailed examination in a simplified setting reveals the presence of a non-nilpotent BRS operator generated by the 1.5 order formalism. Consequently, this is also applicable to supergravity, suggesting the necessity of formulating revised nilpotent transformations to accurately comprehend 3+1 dimensional supergravity. We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half. Both of these decoding strategies are deterministic and provide guaranteed performance in the worst-case scenario. Additionally, our approaches can be implemented efficiently using current computational technology. As a code rate of $\frac{n-k}{2}$ is a key threshold in our findings, we also investigate the performance of this specific rate threshold in the context of rank metric codes. Leveraging the insights gained, we develop a heuristic inference procedure that can accurately identify whether an error of rank $\frac{n-k}{2}$ exists. This heuristic can determine whether an error matrix is equivalent to another, differing by an isometry. Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation of conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of massless Witten operators in AdS$_3$, enabling a more intricate understanding of conformal block dynamics. This new insight allows us to derive an explicit formula for spinning conformal blocks in CFT$_2$, utilizing the lightcone vertex operators proposed by \cite{Maldacena:2011kd}, \cite{Maldacena:2011np}, \cite{Costa:2011jaw}, \cite{Hofman:2011bet}, \cite{Hofman:2011js}. Furthermore, our approach reveals that a block characterized by both spin and charge can be represented as a linear combination of scattering states within AdS$_3$, comprising interacting massless fields and primary fields in CFT$_2$. This new framework also facilitates the representation of block operators as higher-spin conserved charges, emerging from the combination of Noether's charge and the charge associated with symmetry transformations in AdS$_3$. Lastly, our formalism allows us to express a spinning conformal block in terms of a higher-spin conserved charge operator in CFT$_2$. This connection between conformal blocks and higher-spin conserved charges provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between AdS$_3$ and CFT$_2$. Moreover, our work reveals that a spinning conformal block can be represented as a combination of scattering states within AdS$_3$, comprising both massless fields and primary fields in CFT$_2$. This new insight offers a novel perspective on the scattering matrix of massless fields in AdS$_3$, paving the way for a more comprehensive exploration of conformal blocks and higher-spin conserved charges in both AdS$_3$ and CFT$_2$. Moreover, our work also raises intriguing questions regarding the consistency of massless fields in AdS$_3$, sparking the need for further analysis of the scattering matrix of massless fields in this context. This new understanding of conformal blocks and higher-spin conserved charges opens up a broader discussion on the relationship between AdS$_3$ and CFT$_2$, shedding light on the nature of massless fields in AdS$_3$ and, by extension, the scattering matrix of massless fields in this theory

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects. Therefore, we need to reevaluate our assumptions about the neural network's performance in order to make certain that its predictions are actually accurate. We plan to conduct a more in-depth analysis of the neural network's performance in an iterative framework that is presented in this paper. This includes a section where we discuss the implications of combining the neural network with an iterative cleaning algorithm of foreground contaminants. This issue is particularly relevant because the neural network is highly susceptible to biases introduced during its training, which in turn affects its delensing performance. We were able to delens a significant amount of the foreground contaminated map, but the challenge remains to determine the optimal number of iterations for this combined approach. We hope that this analysis will contribute to the development of more sophisticated delensing methods in the future. We anticipate that future experiments will be able to determine the value of the parameter $r$ accurately if they are able to delens at least $20\%$ of the lensing power. We hope to investigate the issue of foreground contamination in more detail in our upcoming papers. We will then be delving into the specifics of how to combine the results of the neural network and quadratic estimators in a more general manner. We will also be exploring the possibility of applying the neural network in a more general context, in other words without assuming that the map is Gaussian. We will be using a data set that will be relevant to the CMB experiments carried out in 2019 and 202

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. By exploring these ideas, we successfully adapt the combinatorial version of the Pontrjagin classes to conform to the orientation requirements in a higher-dimensional manifold. As a result, we are able to demonstrate the applicability of the combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes within a specific oriented manifold. Furthermore, we are able to derive an innovative, non-inductive formula for the Pontrjagin classes in a higher-dimensional manifold. We also examine the circumstances under which the classical Pontrjagin classes can be obtained from their combinatorial counterparts. Additionally, we provide an intuitive explanation for the values obtained using the combinatorial approach and shed light on the underlying relationship between the classical and combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Finally, we outline the potential benefits of adopting the combinatorial approach in place of the classical definition of differentiable manifolds. Leopoldo A. Saldana's earlier work builds upon this discussion and is also highlighted in the concluding section. Additionally, we include an appendix with the complete derivation of the modified Pontrjagin class formula for the combinatorial differentiable manifolds. This modified formula can be expressed using the fundamental class of an oriented manifold within a specific higher-dimensional manifold. This expression is analogous to the classical formula proposed by Gillet and Sourau. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the classical and combinatorial approaches by demonstrating that the latter is an extension of the former. This relationship is rooted in the fact that the classical Pontrjagin classes can be derived from their combinatorial counterparts by integrating over the manifold. This integration is made possible by applying the combinatorial approach within a specific higher-dimensional manifold. This connection highlights the unique benefits of the combinatorial approach and underscores the value of exploring this concept further. This includes investigating other geometric objects such as vector fields, maps, and submanifolds to gain a deeper understanding of its scope and potential. This discussion also brings to light the intriguing link between the combinatorial approach and the novel application of the degree functor in algebra. This connection suggests that the combinatorial approach may have far-reaching implications that extend beyond the realm of geometry

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data on SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range, indicating it likely resulted from the collapse of an hydrogen-rich massive star. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested SN~2020jfo experienced little to no extended pre-explosion mass loss. SN~2020jfo's light curve behaviour during the plateau and hydrogen line-dominated spectra are comparable to that of SNe~1999em and~2001elt, which exploded from similar massive progenitors. SN~2020jfo's low initial nickel abundance and its relatively fast [Ni~II] to [Fe~II] line strength ratio make it an intriguing object of study in supernova science. Additionally, we propose that SN~2020jfo's faint peak magnitude could be an indicator of a distinct subclass of Type~II supernovae. Moreover, its relatively fast [Ni~II] to [Fe~II] line strength ratio suggests that a diverse range of heavy element formation processes occur in the explosions of hydrogen-rich massive stars. SN~2020jfo's rapid [Ni~II] to [Fe~II] line strength ratio, characterised by its super-solar nickel abundance and short plateau duration, set it apart from other low-luminosity Type~II supernovae. This distinct ratio of line strengths may provide a new marker for identifying supernovae resulting from the collapse of hydrogen-rich massive stars. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing a single detector into multiple sectors, each covered by separate LE layers. When an X-ray source is detected, the associated angle of incidence can determine which LE layer has captured the signal. As a functional proof of the MuLE concept, we used a single 1-inch CCD detector to create four virtual LE layers. During observations with the MuLE setup utilizing the Large X-ray Detector (LXD) on the Hard X-ray Telescope (HXT) aboard the Stratospheric Balloon Satellite (SBS), we collected data that showed a count rate ratio of approximately 1:10,000 between the highest and lowest rate pixels. These findings demonstrate that the MuLE technique can effectively reduce the necessary image sensors by a factor of ten to ten thousand for wide-field X-ray monitors utilizing LE optics, without significantly decreasing the field of view. Furthermore, MuLE optics can also offer enhanced anti-pixelation capabilities through the use of empty pixels in the overlaying LE layers. By applying the MuLE concept, even smaller and more expensive image sensors can be utilized in wide-field X-ray monitors utilizing LE optics. As a result, this new optics configuration can further enhance the sensitivity of such instruments. As a functional proof of the MuLE concept, the collected data also demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing this technology with high-density, next-generation image sensors equipped with pixel anti-pixelation protection. Lastly, the MuLE configuration can easily integrate with superconducting transition-edge sensors (STES). Additionally, our team envisions the MuLE concept to have a profound impact on future wide-field X-ray absorption line spectroscopy experiments utilizing LE optics. However, the MuLE technique may introduce a minor increase in data processing requirements. Furthermore, enforcement of identical exposure times across all LE layers in the MuLE configuration may be necessary to avoid creating flat-field images with varying intensities. Lastly, the MuLE optics configuration can also benefit time-resolution X-ray monitoring applications. Nonetheless, the MuLE technique does not significantly impact either the optical depth or the geometric area of the detector. Consequently, the MuLE optics configuration remains suitable for a wide range of scientific targets in the high-energy astrophysics field. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard halo occupation distribution (HOD) method, no improvement was seen in the prediction of halo mass function (HMF). By examining the features learned by the neural network, it was found that velocity field data does not significantly contribute to the prediction of HMF. This suggests that halos with similar masses and at comparable redshifts have similar formation histories, which can be predicted using a single path in phase space. Furthermore, when testing a simplified model that maps initial conditions to halos, a improvement was seen in the inclusion of velocity field data, indicating that the minimal benefit seen in the deep learning case was an artifact of the training process. Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing issues with noise sensitivity and note duration misclassification. Notably, our research indicates that incorporating only a few reference examples per note is insufficient, with optimal results achieved when at least 10-20 examples per note are provided under certain conditions. Furthermore, we explore ways to integrate our low-rank factorization framework with neural network-based note onset detection methods, highlighting the potential for further integration with such models. The implementation and experimental results on the MAPS dataset are detailed, with the source code available online. The proposed method continues to fall short of leading transcription models, prompting suggestions for future improvements, specifically integrating our factorization framework with onset detection models using latent variables and incorporating external music knowledge, such as MIDI files, into the factorization process. The MAPS dataset and our implementation are available online at the specified addresses. The transcription model, specifically the CNMF method, was evaluated on the previously unpublished piano dataset PIANOMI, with the aim of determining if there is a correlation between the amount of training data and the accuracy of the transcription. The results showed that all CNMF-based methods exhibited a linear increase in accuracy with additional training data, offering a theoretical basis for future research, while the previously mentioned suggestions for model improvement remain relevant and applicable. The available training and testing datasets, as well as our CNMF-based transcription model, are commonly referred to as the PIANOMI dataset. The study proposed two novel applications for the PIANOMI dataset, prompting the development of two new evaluation metrics, specifically the note-based precision and the super-note precision, with the aim of assessing the transcription of larger musical phrases. The proposed CNMF method demonstrated linearity in accuracy with increasing training data, while all music notes contained in the dataset have distinct low-rank representations, thereby eliminating the need for explicit class labels during the factorization process. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning physical properties to computational control volumes. Our method encompasses a comprehensive set of neutron star and white dwarf physics phenomena, including endothermal mass absorption, surface pressure conditions, and zero surface velocity. It also enables the direct computation of stars with complex, dynamic shapes throughout their evolution, making it particularly well-suited for modeling the dynamical formation of compact binaries and supernovae explosions resulting in compact object formation. Our preliminary configurations demonstrate a high degree of alignment with established numerical models and the standard laws of physics. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the seamless integration of physical and numerical processes that occur during the formation and subsequent evolution of compact stars, a combination that cannot be achieved using existing numerical models. Our researchers at the University of Innsbruck and the University of Warsaw collaborated on this project and are currently utilizing this model to study the dynamics of neutron star binary mergers. Our new approach has provided valuable insights into the composition of neutron star mergers and the origins of short-duration heavy element formation, and we believe it holds the key to a more comprehensive understanding of the evolution of compact stars. Our study has further revealed that high-energy degrees of freedom, including quarks and magnetic fields, play a crucial role in the behavior of neutron stars. Our research has also shown that the conversion of electromagnetic energy into matter plays a significant part in the development of central oscillations in neutron stars following a merger. Our study has further found that the detection of gravitational waves by the LIGO collaboration in GW170817 is consistent with our model, and we believe that our approach provides valuable predictions that can be tested by future observations. Our new approach has also raised interesting questions about the behavior of rotating stars, and we are confident that it will contribute significantly to our understanding of the evolution of compact stars and the universe. Our study has further demonstrated that the computation of neutron star and white dwarf stars is a critical aspect of our understanding of the universe, and we believe that our approach will facilitate further research in this field. Our researchers at the University of Innsbruck and the University of Warsaw are committed to continuing this research and are currently utilizing this model

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, we found that models trained with partially labeled data can achieve comparable or even better performance than their fully labeled counterparts, as measured through the F1 score. Our findings suggest that selective labeling holds significant potential to make visually rich document extraction more practical and feasible for a broader range of applications and use cases. Our code and models have been made available for public accessivity. Additionally, we launched a ongoing active learning project on invoices that can be accessed through a user-friendly web interface, where anyone can participate by labeling and contributing to the dataset. The models trained on this data are also being utilized in real-world settings and are currently among the top-performing models in certain competitions. They have also been integrated into production environments by several companies. Our research also raised the issue of whether models can overfit on the basis of background information, which has been verified through additional experiments. In response to this risk, a subsequent line of research focused on developing a new kind of robust model that is trained to ignore any potential distractions in its background, resulting in a more efficient use of labeling data. This model is less prone to overfitting and requires a significantly smaller amount of labeling data, making it even more suitable for a broad range of document extraction applications. Our experiments have demonstrated that this new kind of model outperforms the previous generation of models by a substantial margin. Furthermore, it has been found that this model can effectively be trained on a dataset that includes images with diverse levels of quality, without any noticeable decline in performance. Our research on active learning has led to the development of a first practical sampling strategy that is both efficient and accurate, reducing the cost of labeling by yet another order of magnitude. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries, which comprise binary black hole, binary neutron star, and neutron star-black hole events for themselves. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to directly recognize gravitational waves from real-time LIGO data. Our model successfully identifies 28 out of 31 merging neutron star and black hole events with 89% accuracy, which is an improvement over the current matched-filter method. Furthermore, a separate experiment using a smaller dataset consisting of cleaned signals identified all 11 neutron star-neutron star events with 100% accuracy and 89% accuracy for neutron star-black hole events. Moreover, our approach extends to binary black hole events with low signal-to-noise ratios, detecting 50 out of 51 events with 98% accuracy. Our research lays the groundwork for real-time gravitational wave analysis in the next generation of detectors, which will observe binary mergers at a rate of up to 200 per year. In such a scenario, our model can efficiently filter out suitable events for electromagnetic observations within 2 seconds following a detection. The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the quality of care and healthcare disparities have long been acknowledged. However, many social determinants remain unstructured and un-coded within electronic health records, often only present in the free-text notes made by healthcare professionals. As a result, there is a pressing need for an automated method to extract this valuable information from clinical notes. Our research centers on the development of an innovative multi-stage system combining techniques like named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract relevant social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention.

We utilized the N2C2 Shared Task data consisting of 4480 annotated sections on twelve different social determinants of health sourced from MIMIC-III and University of Washington Harborview Medical Centers to test our proposed system. Given the challenge posed by entities that overlap with each other, our entity recognition team designed a marker-based multi-classifier model, comprising twelve individual NER models, to assign labels to connected text spans. Once entities were correctly identified, our relation classification model, built using a bidirectional LSTM with a simple linear structure, determined the relationship between these entities. Subsequently, our text classification model, comprising a bidirectional LSTM with multiple layers, established whether the described situation indicated the patient was experiencing a housing issue. Notably, our proposed system performed better than the baseline models across all categories, achieving a precision of 0.346, a recall of 0.323, and a F1-score of 0.334 for all social determinants combined, according to the official evaluation metrics provided by the N2C2 Shared Task. Our system particularly excelled in identifying patients with housing issues, achieving a precision of 0.378, a recall of 0.351, and a F1-score of 0.364. Our experiments used two GPUs and took approximately 14 days to complete. Our research demonstrates that a marker-based multi-classifier model is an effective approach for extracting social determinants of health information from clinical notes. Our marker-based entity recognition model specifically proved particularly useful in handling text spans with overlapping markers. Furthermore, our proposed system highlights the potential of a combination of named entity recognition, relation classification, and text classification to identify and extract a broad range of social determinants of health information from clinical notes with minimal human intervention. Our research paves the way for the use of automated marker-based multi-classifier models in accurately identifying and extracting a wide variety of social determinants of health information from clinical notes containing connected text

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with associated implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. To this end, this study finds that targeted promotional campaigns designed to encourage people to visit different income segments in urban areas during the pandemic successfully increased diversity by up to 15 percent, a figure consistent with the overall decline of 15% observed in New York City. These campaign effects lasted into late 2021 and beyond, suggesting they may have contributed to mitigating the long-term adverse impacts of COVID-19 on urban diversity. A discussion on policy recommendations and future research directions is also presented. Due to the widespread impact of the pandemic, which was characterized as a public health crisis with far-reaching economic and social consequences, its effects on urban diversity are expected to influence policy decisions in response to similar public health emergencies. Furthermore, the findings of this study may also be applicable to other contexts in which individual behavior is influenced by similar health-related risks and varying levels of government enforcement, such as the response to the pandemic in different countries or regions with distinct levels of mobility restrictions. In such scenarios, people's behavioral changes during the pandemic led to a decline in income diversity of urban encounters that lasted well into 2021, resulting in a 15% to 30% drop in diversity in the four most populous US cities. Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects can produce different effects, such as mergers rather than bursts, and object disruptions that could result in super-Eddington outflows affecting their surroundings. These findings imply that mergers can significantly impact the development of massive stars and contribute substantially to their growth. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of text passages. Specifically, we utilize BERT to enhance the reliability of annotations for text featuring emotion-related content and complex sentence structures. Our results indicate that the combined efforts of human annotators and BERT lead to substantially improved label accuracy compared to sole human input. Additionally, we observe that annotators' confidence in their labels tends to align with the complexity of the underlying text. This is exemplified by the substantial improvement in annotation quality for relatively simple texts, accompanied by only a modest increase in the time required for annotation. Our research also highlights the scope for a more nuanced understanding of how to model the text's inherent complexity. Ultimately, our findings suggest that collaborative efforts between humans and BERT can yield high-performance models, as evidenced by our best model achieving a 79.04% F1 score on the test dataset. This outcome surpasses the 76.37% F1 score attained by a model trained on data annotated solely by humans. Furthermore, when deployed on the Amazon Mechanical Turk annotation platform, our approach resulted in reduced annotation costs and improved work quality for annotators. Our implementation and modification of the BERT-based annotation scheme enabled our models to accurately predict emotion-related question types and achieve a 77.41% F1 score on the Semeval 2017 task. This includes a 4% relative improvement in the F1 score for the subtask involving multi-label predictions. Our work also facilitated the creation of a BERT-based sentiment classification model, which achieved a 90.35% F1 score on the test dataset. This model outperformed a baseline model integrating various sentence representations, including BERT-based models. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the use of BERT-led annotations yields a 12% relative improvement in the estimated number of required annotated samples. This, in turn, results in a greater than proportional reduction (by 18%) in the required annotation budget. Our research provides a novel approach that integrates human and artificial expertise to produce high-quality annotated data, thereby enabling the development of precise machine learning models. Kopczyński (ICALP 2006) hypothesized a link between the existence of preemption-independent scheduling equilibria and the computability of Pareto optimal preemption patterns in multiple-resource systems. We refute his computability assertion by constructing a computable system where no preemption-independent equilibria exists, thereby demonstrating the necessity of allowing preemptions in such analysis. Furthermore, we present a non-deterministic polynomial-time algorithm determining whether a given system admits a preemption-independent scheduling equilibrium when our model of equilibrium is employed, in contrast to the undecidability of general energy games. We observe that both our positive and negative findings rely on the utilization of totally ordered resource vectors. Finally, we outline an extension of our findings to a specific class of partial orderings. Additionally, we explore implications of these findings on the study of energy games and scheduling theory. Our research also facilitates a broader examination of the relationship between preemption patterns and the existence of equilibria in multi-resource systems. As a result, we are able to derive insights into the underlying structure of systems that support the existence of preemption-independent scheduling equilibria or the Pareto optimal preemption patterns when compared to their counterparts that do not support such equilibria or patterns. Our analysis highlights the significance of the order of resource vectors in determining the computability of preemption patterns or the existence of equilibria, indicating a level of undecidability that is inherent to systems with certain types of partial orderings. Consequently, our research paves the way for further exploration into the realm of scheduling theory and energy games through the lens of computability, equilibria, and preemption patterns, offering a richer understanding of the intricate relationship between these concepts and the structure of multi-resource systems. This understanding, in turn, fosters a deeper appreciation for the complexity that arises when tackling concurrency issues in concurrent systems with multiple resources. As such, our findings serve as a cautionary reminder of the importance of considering the order of resource vectors in concurrent systems when seeking a preemption-independent scheduling equilibrium or the most efficient preemption pattern, emphasizing the necessity of a thorough examination of the underlying structure of these systems before drawing conclusions regarding the existence of such equilibria or patterns. Our research on the computability of energy games under different equilibria conditions provides valuable insights into the complexities of concurrency, which can be applied across a variety of scheduling domains. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Further examination of their hard X-ray spectrum components also reveals differences in their overall brightness, with a possible correlation with the duration of their accretion flows. Lastly, our findings suggest that accretion in asynchronous polars tends to be more transient, which may be a key factor contributing to their harder spectrum when compared to their synchronized counterparts. Further study and a larger sample size are needed to fully understand this relationship. Additionally, considering other variables such as binary mass ratio and outburst history may also be crucial in understanding the spectral hardness of polars. Our research also utilizes the full capacity of available data, including hardness ratios, which were previously underutilized in the context of the RXTE database. Utilizing these ratios allows for a fair comparison between different systems despite differences in count levels and net detection limitations. As a result, this research sets a useful precedent for analyzing other types of X-ray binaries using similar data sets. Our analysis of the full sample also identifies notable variations in the spectrum of the well-known asynchronous polar, AM CVn, which exhibits signs of both increased hard X-ray flux and higher hardness ratio during its brighter phases, further supporting the detection of transient accretion in this subclass. Our study includes a detailed analysis of AM CVn's spectrum, confirming that its harder spectrum when compared to standard polars is due to its increased hard X-ray flux and higher hardness ratio during its brighter phases, consistent with the findings of a more detailed analysis of its hard spectrum components, which reveals that its higher hard X-ray flux is likely a result of a greater duration of accretion flow. Our study also includes a detailed analysis of the spectral comparison between the asynchronous polar, AM CVn, and the standard polar, DQ Leo, using their full available spectra, with a focus on their hard X-ray spectrum components, with a length of ~450 ks for AM CVn

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This could potentially enable the calibration of magnetic sensors and metrological applications of superconducting materials. Furthermore, this method allows for the distinction between external magnetic fields and the Meissner effects caused by superconducting currents, achieving a sensitivity of $10^{-18}$ Amereats with atomic interferometry, supplementing the presently limited assessment via magnetic susceptibility measurements. It's also possible to design an experiment where atomic interferometry can distinguish between different superconducting states (e.g., ME-SS and ME-NS) under the influence of external magnetic fields, paving the way for the development of atomic sensors capable of measuring a material's magnetic susceptibility and the associated phase transition in magnetic field strength. Moreover, this method can be extended to detect not just local magnetic field strengths but also magnetic field gradients with a comparable sensitivity, or the tiny magnetic fields generated by the movement of a superconductor within a constant external magnetic field, or the fragile quantum states of superconductors, all with an unprecedented sensitivity. Additionally, this experiment demonstrates the feasibility of controlling an atomic interferometry system with a superconductor's expelled local magnetic field, a previously unattained level of control, allowing for the development of a new generation of atomic sensors capable of accurately measuring this effect and a wide range of other sensitive applications. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This reduction essentially minimizes the discontinuity at the gap edges, thereby preventing excessive field amplification. We further validate our findings with numerical experiments using the time-domain finite difference method. Alternatively, the hydrodynamics model can also be enhanced to give accurate results with a modified local response approach. This modification involves an effective reduction in the imaginary part of the dynamic tensor that accounts for the spillover and nonlocal effects, especially in regions farther than a few lattice parameters from the gap. This modified local approach can be employed to analyze complex geometries that cannot be readily handled with the hydrodynamics model. We apply this modified local approach to investigate a variety of nanostructures with gaps, demonstrating that it provides an accurate and efficient analysis of the electromagnetic field within these structures. This approach may be utilized in high accuracy numerical simulations of the time-dependent response of metallic nanostructures. Additionally, we demonstrate that our modified local response model is equivalent to the time-integrated hydrodynamics model, thereby confirming its validity. This confirmation is further supported by our numerical experiments that demonstrate the hydrodynamics model's ability to accurately reproduce the time-dependent response of the electron gas through its integration over time. This accurate representation of the electron gas's behavior using the hydrodynamics model's time-integrated form highlights the model's ability to capture the spillover and nonlocal effects that influence the behavior of the electron gas. This understanding of the hydrodynamics model's time-integrated form also provides insight into the relationship between the Thomas-Fermi approximation and the model's time-integrated form, revealing that the former is equivalent to considering the time-integrated hydrodynamics model in its limit of small time steps. This equivalence is further confirmed by our numerical experiments that demonstrate how the time-integrated hydrodynamics model can be successfully used to analyze nanostructures with gaps by treating the gap size as an effective parameter that takes into account the spillover and nonlocal effects. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Initially, we discuss the initial proofs provided by Coquand and Huet in 1985, focusing on the application of the Tarski theorem and the leverage of construction trees to justify the strong normalization property. Next, we delve into the collection of proofs that followed, highlighting key differences, such as the use of the modification rule and the application of the proof by logical induction. Finally, we explore the most recent proofs, discussing the various ways in which the constructivity of the proofs has been interpreted and the potential for extending the Calculus of Constructions with modification rules while upholding the strong normalization property. Throughout this survey, the underlying mechanisms underlying the proofs are revealed through the presentation of the relevant proofs and the discussion of their key components. Although primarily focused on the Calculus of Constructions, the survey also touches on the related theory known as the Calculus of Algebraic Constructions, highlighting the connection between the modification rule and the type generalization rule. Through its comprehensive examination of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, this survey provides a thorough understanding of the underlying principles and the unique goals of the researchers involved. Its comprehensive nature makes it an invaluable resource for the further development of programming languages and type theory. We derived a two-loop amplitude formula for four graviton supermultiplets in AdS$_5$ times S$^5$ using a preamplitude construction, confirming the findings of Huang and Yuan. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL) for effortless GPU integration, and a simple C API for easy integration with existing code.  The innovative memory allocator designs included in DynaSOAr, such as the hybrid free block list, the hybrid size classification, the forward-looking thread block allocation, the reverse spiral memory pattern, and the memory allocator lock-free implementation using atomic operations, significantly reduce fragmentation, speed up memory allocation, and enable parallel memory allocation.  The DynaSOAr DSL's unique features, such as reverse spiral memory pattern support and backward compatibility with existing C code, allow for a seamless and safe transition of object-oriented code to GPU-compatible code.  The DynaSOAr framework has been put through its paces by rewriting several well-known benchmark programs, including K-Means, FLAT, FM-Index, and Bag-of-Words, and the results show substantial speed-up gains, with some achieving speeds over 500 Gflops.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr has been found to be highly adaptable, yielding positive results with different compiler versions and demonstrating its potential as a viable option for a wide range of GPU programming applications.  The framework's raw speed and potential for further optimization make it an exciting development in the field of GPU programming.  The source code of DynaSOAr has been openly released and is available for use and adaptation by other researchers.  In line with the principles of reproducibility and ease of use, a step-by-step guide on how to use DynaSOAr has also been provided in the appendix of this paper. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed the breaking of the four-fold symmetry. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance on the MS COCO dataset while delivering superior results at higher resolutions. Furthermore, FourierMask shows superiority to Mask R-CNN in high-resolution images and exhibits resolution-invariance in experiments. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/AmirGattal/FourierMask. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography, a three-dimensional imaging technique, offers a promising alternative for studying these complex clouds. Although conceptually straightforward, implementing cloud tomotherapy in practice is fraught with difficulty because it requires precise information about cloud geometry and tomographic reconstruction methods can be computationally intensive when applied to large datasets from satellite imagery. This research focuses on applying cloud tomography to analyzing convective clouds from space using the high-fidelity imaging capabilities of the MISR satellite. By leveraging the higher spatial resolution of MISR's nine individual cameras and utilizing a veiled core model, researchers can simulate the three-dimensional nature of these clouds and reconstruct their geometry more accurately. This results in significantly improved retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size when compared to traditional methods. Notably, when evaluated using in situ measurements from ground stations beneath the clouds, the new method yields a significantly lower mean absolute error. The method also identifies and excludes cloudy pixels that contain hanging edges or are geometrically distorted, effectively locating the "veiled core" of the clouds. This allows for more precise estimation of the relationship between cloud geometry and optical properties. The method has potential applications for recovering three-dimensional geometries of opaque clouds using satellite imagery from multiple sources, such as the joint MODIS-MISR dataset covering the period from 2000 to 2020. This in turn enables more accurate retrievals of cloud properties and their effects on the Earth's energy balance and climate. Furthermore, the method enables the investigation of how cloud geometry influences the recovery of cloud optical thickness and particle size, with implications for climate models and retrievals of cloud properties using tomography. Additionally, the method allows for the exploration of how the resolution of satellite imagery affects the reconstruction of cloud geometry and the recovery of cloud optical thickness and particle size.
